summary: This single-arm open-label trial tested ropinirole in 16 patients with primary or secondary RLS recruited from a movement disorders clinic. Among the 13 patients who completed the trial (mean dose 2.8 mg/day), IRLSSG abbreviated questionnaire scores improved from 18.6 to 7.7 (58.7% improvement; p = 1.08 × 10⁻⁸ by two-tailed paired t-test). Three patients discontinued due to adverse events or extenuating circumstances; the medication was otherwise generally well tolerated, with sedation and nausea being the most common side effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm open-label study, not an RCT; there is no control group and no randomization, so many RCT-specific fields (n_randomized, allocation concealment, etc.) are not applicable and set to null. The paper reports a within-arm pre-post paired t-test (p = 1.08 × 10⁻⁸); this is captured in between_group_effects as a pre_vs_post comparison. Treatment duration varied by patient (range 2-7 months per Table 1; mean 3.9 months); no single study duration is reported. The paper_id provided in the template appears to be from a different paper and has been retained as given. The 16 enrolled vs 13 completing means 3 discontinued; all 3 discontinuation reasons are described narratively. Per-arm IRLSSG scores for all 13 individual patients are available in Table 1 and were used to confirm the reported means. Outcome 3 (degree of improvement) partially overlaps with outcome 2; both are reported because the paper distinguishes 'marked improvement' (n=10) from 'moderate improvement' (n=3). The enrolled-16 total is used as the denominator for withdrawn (n=3), but n_analyzed=13 is verbatim for the primary outcome.

summary: This open-label single-arm trial enrolled 21 patients (mean age 70 years) with restless legs syndrome who were treated with amantadine 100-300 mg/day (titrated). The mean RLS rating scale score decreased from 9.8 ± 0.6 at baseline to 6.6 ± 3.8 posttreatment (p=0.001), with 52% of patients reporting subjective benefit (mean improvement 69% among responders). The study was uncontrolled and open-label, so placebo effects cannot be excluded, but results suggest amantadine may be an effective and well-tolerated treatment option for RLS.

summary: This double-blind, double-dummy RCT (n=94 analyzed) compared IV ferumoxytol (1020 mg total) versus oral ferrous sulfate (650 mg/day for 6 weeks) for treatment of restless legs syndrome in patients with iron deficiency anemia at a single US hematology clinic. Both treatments produced marked improvement in RLS symptoms (IRLSS and CGI-I scores), with 68% of IV iron patients and 75% of oral iron patients reporting improvement at Week 6. No statistically significant between-group differences were found for either co-primary outcome (IRLSS change p=0.27; CGI-I score p=0.70) or the secondary PGI-S outcome (p=0.35), though IV iron produced significantly greater increases in ferritin (p<0.0001) and significantly greater decreases in TIBC (p=0.004); oral iron was better tolerated in terms of hematological response but far worse in adverse events (55% vs. 11% AE rate, predominantly gastrointestinal).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 had some parsing ambiguity due to merged cells and garbled formatting in the OCR (particularly for the IRLSS change row which showed n=48/n=46 but no mean/SD values in the parsed text — these appear to only be presented in Figure S1 referenced in the text, so change-from-baseline IRLSS means/SDs are not_reported from text alone). The Table 2 row for 'Change in TIBC' reported absolute change values of 105.7 (60.4) and 64.3 (52.5) which appear to represent decreases; these were recorded as negative values (-105.7 and -64.3) to reflect direction of change from a high baseline. The paper states 'p < .0001' for ferritin change — recorded as p_value_exact=false. The n for MCV change in IV iron arm was not explicitly stated in Table 2 text. AE counts for arm 1 (n=5) and arm 2 (n=15) were calculated by counting patients listed in Table 3 per arm; the text states 11% for IV iron and 55% for oral iron, implying approximately 5/48 and 25/46 respectively — the text-stated percentage of 55% for oral iron (suggesting ~25 patients) does not match the 15 patients listed in Table 3, suggesting Table 3 may be incomplete or the percentage refers to a different denominator. Baseline ferritin difference between arms (22.6 vs 13.5 µg/L) was noted as statistically significant in text (p<.05) despite Table 1 showing p=0.17 — this apparent contradiction exists in the source paper. IRLSS and PGI-S intermediate timepoint data (Days 7, 14, 28) are mentioned as collected but not reported numerically in the paper text.

summary: This single-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group RCT enrolled 46 drug-naive RLS patients randomly assigned to a single dose of pramipexole (0.25mg), clonazepam (0.5mg), or placebo, each receiving one baseline and one treatment night of full polysomnography. Pramipexole significantly suppressed PLMS and improved sleep efficiency and stage 2 sleep but did not reduce EEG instability (CAP) or cortical arousals, while clonazepam reduced CAP rate and A1/A2 indices without affecting PLMS; both active drugs improved subjective RLS symptom severity on VAS relative to placebo. These results demonstrate that PLMS and cortical arousals can be pharmacologically dissociated, suggesting an indirect rather than causal relationship between the two phenomena.

summary: This double-blind randomized crossover trial tested bromocriptine 7.5 mg at bedtime versus placebo (each for 30 days with a 2-week washout) in 6 patients with severe idiopathic restless legs syndrome. On bromocriptine, patients showed a statistically significant 57% reduction in periodic movements of sleep per hour compared to placebo (86 vs. 37 per hour; p<0.025) and 5 of 6 patients reported partial subjective improvement in restlessness and paresthesias. Non-significant improvements in total sleep time and sleep efficiency were also observed, driven primarily by 2 patients with very poor baseline sleep.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 1 values for sleep efficiency and % Stages 1+2 appear garbled due to OCR/typesetting errors (e.g., sleep efficiency shown as '95q', '009;', '7o/r' in control/placebo/drug columns; % Stages 1+2 shown as '43', '48', 'ih'); exact numeric values for these could not be reliably extracted and are left null. Table 2 (individual patient data) is severely garbled with merged/misaligned cells due to OCR failure — individual patient values for PMS/night, PMS/hour, total sleep time, sleep efficiency, and sleep stage % are partially extractable but not reliably parsed for all patients and conditions. The bromocriptine mean PMS/hour at end of treatment (37) was calculated from the stated 43% decrease from control value (65): 65 × (1-0.43) ≈ 37. The paper states two analysis findings: (1) significant decrease in total PMS/night p<0.025, (2) significant decrease in PMS/hour p<0.025 (43% from control, 57% from placebo). No SDs are reported for any outcome. This is a crossover study — the 'placebo' arm values represent the placebo phase results (not a separate group), and the control condition represents pre-treatment baseline polysomnography. The note 'n=4' for PMS outcomes vs 'n=6' for sleep parameters reflects that PMS were quantitated in only 4 of 6 patients. summary: This 3-arm parallel-group RCT in 18 patients with primary RLS compared 8 weeks of supervised treadmill aerobic exercise (3x/week) and stretching exercise (3x/week) to a no-exercise control. Both exercise programs significantly reduced IRLSSG-RS symptom severity (aerobic: p=0.025; stretching: p=0.034) and improved subjective and total sleep quality (PSQI) and RLS-specific quality of life (RLS-QoL) compared to within-group pre-post changes, with very large effect sizes; aerobic exercise uniquely reduced wake after sleep onset on actigraphy (p=0.048) while stretching exercise uniquely reduced self-reported sleep disturbances (p=0.025). No significant between-group differences were found between the two exercise types on any primary outcome.

Table 2 between-group note 'CO-AE' indicates significant difference between control and aerobic groups for IRLSSG-RS at post-treatment (Group x Time p=0.024). 4. Table 3 between-group note 'CO-SE' indicates significant difference between control and stretching groups for subjective sleep quality (Group x Time p=0.016). 5. Table 4 WASO between-group comparison: group x time F=4.862, p=0.024; post-treatment F=4.677, p=0.026 with annotation '2-3' indicating arm1 (AE) differs from arm3 (SE); AE also had within-group p=0.048. 6. Sleep medicine (PSQI) subscale: all zeros for control and SE groups at both timepoints; not extracted as separate outcome. 7. summary: This single-arm, open-label 12-month extension study evaluated long-term treatment with combined regular-release (RR) and sustained-release (SR) levodopa/benserazide in 23 severely affected RLS patients who had responded to this combination in a preceding double-blind crossover trial. Using ITT-LOCF analysis, significant improvements were observed in primary sleep outcomes (satisfaction with sleep improved by 3.5 points on 7-point scale, p=0.0001; total sleep time increased by 190 minutes, p=0.0001) and in RLS severity at bedtime and during the night (reductions of 6.5 and 6.0 points respectively on 11-point scales, p<0.0001), but daytime RLS severity worsened non-significantly (+1.9 points, p=0.076). Only 10 of 23 patients (43%) completed the 1-year study, with 8 discontinuing due to probable augmentation (worsening daytime RLS), indicating that while efficacious for nocturnal symptoms, long-term levodopa therapy led to augmentation requiring treatment discontinuation in the majority of patients.

summary: This was an uncontrolled open-label pilot study testing alpha-dihydroergocryptine (DHEC, 10–40 mg/day) in 16 patients with idiopathic or secondary RLS over 5 weeks (1-week baseline + 4-week treatment). The primary outcome — overall RLS complaints assessed by patient-rated VAS — improved significantly from baseline to end of treatment for both daytime (28.0 to 10.0, p<0.0001) and nighttime (55.7 to 20.1, p=0.003) symptoms, with a mean 63.9 ± 38.1% reduction in nocturnal complaints. All secondary VAS outcomes (paresthesia, motor restlessness, involuntary movements) and sleep parameters (sleep duration, onset latency) also improved significantly, though the study lacked a control arm, precluding conclusions about efficacy beyond placebo response.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This is a single-arm uncontrolled open-label pre-post study, NOT a randomized controlled trial; 'between_group_effects' fields represent pre-post within-arm comparisons rather than true between-group contrasts, and are labeled as 'baseline_vs_end_of_treatment'. 2. The p-value for overall daytime complaints is reported as 'P > 0.0001' in the original paper (likely a typographic error for P < 0.0001); extracted as p<0.0001. 3. Exact VAS values for paresthesia, motor restlessness, and involuntary movements sub-domains are presented only in a figure (Figure 1 lower panel) with no numeric values in the text or tables; these outcomes have null means/SDs with result_source='not_reported'. 4. Table 1 contains garbled merged cells with multiple patients' data condensed into single rows (e.g., patients 11–15 listed together); individual VAS baseline/end values extracted per-patient from table are partially readable but overall study means were taken from the results text. 5. The paper states all four VAS parameters showed statistically significant improvement (sign-rank test, p<0.05) but does not report exact p-values or means/SDs for the sub-domains (paresthesia, motor restlessness, involuntary movements). 6. N analyzed is listed as 16 for baseline and 15 for end of treatment (1 dropout after 4 days); however, Figure 1 caption states 'Mean values of the 16 patients are given' suggesting the dropout's partial data may have been included in some analyses. 7. RLS duration mean is given as 12 years (from table footnote).

summary: This 1-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group pilot RCT tested three fixed doses of transdermal rotigotine patch (1.125 mg, 2.25 mg, and 4.5 mg/day) versus placebo in 63 patients with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS including daytime symptoms. The highest dose (4.5 mg/day) produced a statistically significant 15.7-point reduction in IRLS total score compared to 8.0 points with placebo (adjusted difference 7.7 points; 95% CI 2.0–13.5; p=0.0095), with all doses also significantly improving daytime RLS severity on the RLS-6 scale. Rotigotine was generally well tolerated with no serious adverse events, supporting further development of the transdermal patch for RLS.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 reports IRLS change-from-baseline and RLS-6 changes as ANCOVA least-square means ± SEM (not raw SD). Exact p-values for RLS-6 daytime scales at doses 1.125 mg and 2.25 mg are reported only as p<0.05 (threshold only). The RLS-6 baseline data for items 1 (bedtime), 2 (night), and 4 (active) are not provided in the paper tables; only item 3 (day at rest) baseline is given. summary: This 12-week, double-blind, randomized, parallel-group, placebo-controlled trial (TREAT RLS 2) enrolled 267 outpatients with moderate-to-severe RLS and compared flexible-dose ropinirole (0.25-4.0 mg/day) to placebo taken 1-3 hours before bedtime at 46 centers across Australia, Europe, and North America. Ropinirole produced a significantly greater reduction in IRLS score at week 12 compared to placebo (-11.2 vs. -8.7, adjusted treatment difference -2.5, 95% CI -4.6 to -0.4, P=0.0197), with benefits evident as early as week 1 and extending to CGI-I responder rates, all four MOS sleep scale domains, and disease-specific and generic quality-of-life measures. The drug was generally well tolerated, with predominantly mild-to-moderate adverse events typical of dopamine agonists (principally nausea, dizziness, and vomiting) and no reports of augmentation during the treatment period.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm SDs for the IRLS change-from-baseline at week 12 were not reported (only SE provided). MOS Sleep Scale domain change-from-baseline values per arm were not reported in text or tables; only adjusted between-group treatment differences were given. SF-36 remaining domains (physical functioning, role-physical, bodily pain, general health, role-emotional) showed numerical improvement favoring ropinirole but were not statistically significant and per-arm values were not reported. WPAI questionnaire results were non-significant and no quantitative values were reported. The overall effect size (Cohen's d = -0.29) was reported verbatim in the paper. Baseline IRLS score SD was reported (ropinirole: 5.9, placebo: 5.4). The paper notes a planned sample size of 116 per arm but enrolled 131 and 136. The ITT population was 266 (1 placebo patient had no post-dose assessments). Median time to CGI-I response was in days (ropinirole: 14 days, placebo: 22 days). Figure 2 contains week-by-week IRLS scores but per-arm values beyond baseline and week 12 were not extractable from text.

summary: This single-center cohort study in Germany validated a home-based diagnostic 'L-DOPA test' using a single 100/25 mg dose of levodopa/benserazide in 48 treatment-naive patients with suspected RLS (40 confirmed RLS, 8 non-RLS after expert evaluation). Using ≥50% improvement in VAS scores as a positive test threshold, the L-DOPA test achieved 88% sensitivity and 100% specificity for 'severity of symptoms in the legs,' and 80% sensitivity with 100% specificity for 'urge to move the legs,' outperforming polysomnographic PLMS arousal index (58% sensitivity, 63% specificity). The test also predicted 100% of subsequent responses to continuous dopaminergic treatment, supporting its clinical utility for diagnostic decision-making in uncertain RLS cases.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a diagnostic accuracy/cohort study, NOT an RCT. Arms represent post-hoc diagnostic groups (RLS vs non-RLS), not randomized treatment allocation. All patients received the same L-DOPA test; arm grouping is by final expert diagnosis. The VAS time-course data for the 2-hour observation period is presented only in Figure 1 (as percentage change medians over time) with no tabulated values per timepoint — only the change-from-baseline at best assessment within 2 hours is tabulated in Table 3. Validity metrics (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, accuracy, AUC) for L-DOPA test and PSG indices are in Table 2. Final visit timing is described as 'approximately 4 weeks of routine therapy' (inferred from discussion); exact weeks not stated. Duration of RLS-like symptoms: RLS group 12.9 ± 12.6 years, non-RLS group 4.2 ± 4.1 years. IRLS baseline total score: RLS 26.5 ± 4.6, non-RLS 27.9 ± 6.2. CGI Item 2 full breakdown: RLS — very much improved 24 (60%), much improved 16 (40%); non-RLS — slightly improved 1 (12.5%), unchanged 6 (75%), slightly worse 1 (12.5%). The 3 patients excluded from final analysis (51 performed test, 48 completed per protocol) had no details provided.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group withdrawal trial enrolled 150 RLS patients who had responded to 6 months of open-label pramipexole (mean dose 0.50 mg) and randomized them to continue pramipexole (0.125–0.75 mg/day) or switch to placebo for 3 months. Patients switched to placebo reached the primary composite endpoint (CGI-I worsening plus IRLS >15) significantly more often (85.5% vs. 20.5%) and faster (median 7 days vs. >84 days to 50% event rate), with large, statistically significant differences across all secondary outcomes including IRLS scores, CGI subscales, patient global impression, quality of life, and sleep VAS ratings (all p<0.0001). The findings confirm sustained efficacy of pramipexole for RLS through 9 months of total treatment, with no augmentation observed in this responder population.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This is an RLS (not Long COVID) trial; long_covid fields are not applicable and set to null. 2. The primary outcome was time-to-event by Kaplan-Meier analysis; no HR with CI was reported verbatim (only p<0.0001 and KM time estimates at specific survival probabilities: 5 days vs 42 days to 0.85 survival, 7 days vs >84 days to 0.50 survival). 3. For RLS-6 VAS outcomes, only placebo arm change-from-baseline median values were reported in text; pramipexole arm was described as 'virtually unchanged' with no numeric values given. 4. For RLS-QOL, only baseline medians and the final between-group median difference (12.5 points) were given; no end-of-Period-2 per-arm medians reported. 5. The n_analyzed values for final-analysis population are 69 (placebo) and 78 (pramipexole) based on text stating total final-analysis population of 147, with placebo n=69 derived from Table 1 (69 in final-analysis population). 6. AE counts by arm (n_any_ae) were calculated from percentages: pramipexole 39.7% of 78 = ~31; placebo 23.6% of 72 = ~17. 7. Period 1 (6-month open-label run-in) data is pre-randomization; IRLS baseline in Table 1 refers to pre-Period 1 scores. 8. Augmentation was monitored but no cases occurred; not extractable as a binary outcome with events. 9. CGI-I improved/unchanged/worse distributions fully reported in Table 2 and extracted in outcome 3. 10. ESS end-of-Period-2 per-arm values not explicitly reported; only baseline values and the ANCOVA p-value were given.

summary: This randomized withdrawal trial enrolled 202 adults with primary RLS who received open-label ropinirole for 24 weeks; responders (≥6-point IRLS reduction) were then randomized to continue ropinirole (n=45) or switch to placebo (n=47) for 12 weeks. The primary endpoint showed significantly fewer patients relapsed on ropinirole than placebo (32.6% vs. 57.8%; adjusted OR 0.33, 95% CI 0.13–0.81, P=0.0156). Secondary outcomes including IRLS scores, CGI-I ratings, sleep (MOS sleep scale), and quality of life (RLSQoL, SF-36) all favored ropinirole over placebo, with most differences reaching statistical significance.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This is a randomized withdrawal design (not a traditional parallel-group RCT): all patients received single-blind ropinirole for 24 weeks, then only responders were randomized. Arm_id=0 is used for single-blind phase data (entire enrolled cohort, n=202) which is distinct from the double-blind arms. 2. The RLSQoL change scores are reported as 2SE (twice the standard error) not SD; SE values were calculated by dividing reported 2SE values by 2 (ropinirole: 2SE=5.76, SE=2.88; placebo: 2SE=5.58, SE=2.79). 3. Per-arm means and SDs for MOS sleep scale domains at week 36 are not reported in text or tables — only between-group treatment differences are given for the double-blind phase; double-blind phase data only in figures for most subscales. 4. SF-36 domain changes during the double-blind phase (Fig 5B) appear to be presented only in a figure without exact numerical values — only between-group treatment differences and CIs were extractable from text. 5. Omitted SF-36 domains with non-significant between-group differences: Physical Functioning (CI -2.0 to 10.9, p not stated as significant), Bodily Pain (CI -8.2 to 8.4), Role Emotional (CI -7.0 to 20.3), General Health (CI -4.5 to 6.4). 6. N=202 for single-blind safety analysis vs n=92 for double-blind ITT. Primary analysis excluded 4 patients (2 per arm) who did not meet relapse or completion criteria, giving n=43 (ropinirole) and n=45 (placebo) for primary endpoint. Time-to-relapse analysis excluded 12 patients, giving n=41 (ropinirole) and n=39 (placebo). 7. The median time to relapse for the ropinirole group could not be estimated (fewer than 50% relapsed). 8. The IRLS change from single-blind baseline to randomized baseline (week 24) was reported as a mean reduction of 12.8 points for the overall single-blind cohort but per-arm SDs for change scores during double-blind phase were not provided.

summary: This 6-week multicenter double-blind RCT (Effect-RLS Study) enrolled 345 patients with moderate-to-severe primary RLS, randomized 1:2 to placebo (n=115) or pramipexole (n=230) with individually optimized dosing from 0.125 to 0.75 mg/day. Pramipexole produced significantly greater reductions in IRLS score (adjusted mean change -12.3 vs. -5.7 points; difference -6.6, 95% CI -8.6 to -4.5, P<0.0001) and higher CGI-I responder rates (62.9% vs. 32.5%, P<0.0001), with all secondary endpoints (IRLS responder rate, PGI responder rate, and VAS symptom severity) also significantly favoring pramipexole. Pramipexole was well tolerated at the low doses required for efficacy in RLS, with predominantly mild adverse events and no serious adverse events in the active treatment arm.

No subgroup analyses were reported in the paper. 7. The participant flow diagram (Fig. 1) is described but exact numbers for each attrition step by arm are not fully itemized in text.

summary: The CALDIR trial was a 30-week multicenter double-blind RCT comparing cabergoline (2-3 mg/day) to levodopa/benserazide (200-300 mg/day) in 361 adults with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS. Cabergoline demonstrated statistically superior efficacy to levodopa on both primary endpoints: IRLS score improvement at 6 weeks (LS-mean difference -6.6 points, 95% CI -8.6 to -4.7, p<0.0001) and time to discontinuation due to augmentation or loss of efficacy over 30 weeks (11.9% vs 24.0%, p=0.0029). summary: This quasi-experimental study assessed cortical plasticity using paired associative stimulation (PAS) TMS in 12 idiopathic RLS patients and 10 healthy controls, then re-examined 8 RLS patients after 4 weeks of dopaminergic treatment (cabergoline or pramipexole). PAS significantly increased MEP amplitudes for up to 30 minutes in healthy controls but had no effect in untreated RLS patients, demonstrating impaired LTP-like motor cortex plasticity. After 4 weeks of dopaminergic treatment, PAS-induced plasticity was restored in RLS patients (significant MEP increases at T0, T15, and T30; p<0.003 for all), and IRLS-RS clinical severity scores were significantly reduced (p=0.003), though correlation between symptom improvement and plasticity restoration was not significant.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is NOT an RCT — it is a non-randomized quasi-experimental study with no placebo arm. The study has three comparison groups: healthy controls (n=10), untreated RLS patients (n=12), and treated RLS patients (n=8, within-subject pre-post). Per-arm MEP amplitude values are only presented in a figure (Figure 1) with no numerical data in text or tables; result values are set to null with result_source 'not_reported'. RMT data are reported numerically in text as mean ± SEM. The IRLS-RS follow-up mean is not reported in text (only individual patient values visible in Table 1). WASO SD is reported in text as 85.2 (likely SD), SE% SD as 17.2, arousal index SD as 15.3, PLMS index SD as 32.8 — these appear to be SDs not SEMs based on context but are placed in the arm_results mean field only as the field labels are ambiguous; placed as mean only since the paper uses '±' without specifying SD vs SEM for sleep variables. The n=8 treated subgroup is a subset of the n=12 RLS patient group; 4 were lost to neurophysiological follow-up. The paper does not report p-value for IRLS-RS improvement with exact t-statistic t(1,11)=5.3, p=0.003.

summary: This 12-month double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT compared intravenous iron sucrose (1000 mg total over 3 weeks, n=29) with saline placebo (n=31) in 60 patients with primary RLS and mild-to-moderate iron deficiency (S-ferritin <45 µg/L). summary: This prospective, multicenter, 66-week study evaluated the incidence of augmentation in patients with moderate-to-severe restless legs syndrome (RLS) treated with ropinirole (0.25–4.0 mg/day) versus placebo over 26 weeks of double-blind treatment, followed by 40 weeks of open-label ropinirole. Confirmed augmentation rates were 4% for ropinirole and <1% for placebo during the double-blind phase, with clinically significant augmentation in 3% vs <1%, representing a 3.1% absolute excess risk with ropinirole; IRLS scores improved significantly more with ropinirole than placebo at weeks 12 and 26 (adjusted mean difference −2.1 and −2.5 points respectively, both p<0.05). No predictors of augmentation were identified and new cases continued to accumulate at a stable rate throughout the study duration, suggesting ongoing long-term risk.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a RLS trial, not a Long COVID trial; all Long COVID-specific fields (long_covid_definition, time_since_infection, percent_vaccinated, percent_previously_hospitalized, required_symptoms as COVID symptoms) are null/not applicable. The open-label phase does not have a separate randomized control arm; arm_id=1 is used for all open-label data. The 95% CIs reported in Table 4 for augmentation appear to be absolute numbers of cases (not percentages), not the usual proportion CIs — extracted as approximate percent CIs where possible. The IRLS change-from-baseline values for DB ropinirole (−15.9 ± SE 0.76) and placebo (−13.4 ± SE 0.77) are reported in the abstract with § interpreted as ± per instruction; the between-group difference of −2.5 at week 26 (p=0.023 with CI −4.6 to −0.3) is stated for the GSK clinical study register, not in the paper text directly. The open-label ropinirole IRLS change (−20.4 ± SE 0.55) references week 66 but n=269 reflects those who entered OL. The time-to-augmentation range values (62–183 days for DB ropinirole; 46–285 days for OL) are reported as ranges not IQR; stored in iqr_low/iqr_high fields as range proxies. Kaplan-Meier survival curves are in figures only with no tabular data. AE data for OL phase (n=269 ropinirole only, no placebo comparator) is included under arm_id=1. Discontinuation rate of 42% is mentioned for OL phase but per-arm completion numbers are not explicitly tabulated.

summary: This phase 4 RCT compared a single 1000-mg intravenous dose of ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) versus placebo in 110 iron-deficient nonanemic adults with moderate to severe RLS (IRLS >= 15). The primary endpoint — mean change in IRLS score from baseline to week 4 — was not statistically significant (treatment difference -2.9, 95% CI -5.93 to 1.02, p=0.163), but FCM produced a significant improvement by week 12 (treatment difference -4.66, 95% CI -8.59 to -0.73, p=0.021), suggesting that the full therapeutic effect of IV iron in RLS requires more time to manifest than the 4-week primary endpoint captured.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT randomized 70 adults with moderate-to-severe RLS and PLMS index ≥10/h to 6 weeks of rotigotine (up to 3 mg/24h transdermal) or placebo to assess effects on nocturnal blood pressure dipping patterns by 24-hour ABPM. At end point, significantly fewer patients in the rotigotine group had systolic (47% vs 72%) and diastolic (21% vs 47%) nondipping BP profiles compared with placebo (OR ~2.9–3.5, P<0.05), and mean systolic and diastolic BP dips were significantly greater with rotigotine. Rotigotine also significantly improved PLMS, PLMA, PLMW, IRLS, sleep efficiency, CGIs, and total sleep time compared with placebo, while endothelial function and absolute 24-hour BP values did not differ between groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 3 (Changes in BP values) had heavily garbled/merged cell structure in the OCR'd text, making row/column alignment ambiguous. Values were cross-referenced with Table 2 and narrative text to resolve discrepancies. The 'between-group difference' column in Table 3 reports mean change differences, and these were extracted as mean_difference effect sizes. The OR values in Table 2 for continuous dip measures (outcome IDs 3, 4, 5) represent the per-unit increase in odds of dipping per 1% increase in BP dip (continuous logistic regression), not a standard between-group mean difference OR — this context is preserved. The 'n_any_ae' for each arm was calculated from the reported percentages (rotigotine 36.4% × 33 ≈12; placebo 33.3% × 33 ≈11). Daytime diastolic BP, daytime mean BP, daytime heart rate, nighttime mean BP, nighttime heart rate, and dipping mean BP were available in Table 3 but omitted from outcomes to manage output size; their endpoint values and change-from-baseline for placebo/rotigotine are available in Table 3. Sleep efficiency, sleep latency, wake after sleep onset, micro-arousal index, and sleep stage percentages from Table 4 (per-protocol PSG outcomes) are also omitted from detailed outcome extraction but were reported as significant for sleep efficiency in Table 4.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial (n=28) tested oral dipyridamole (mean dose 218 mg/d) versus placebo over two 2-week treatment periods in treatment-naive patients with idiopathic RLS. Dipyridamole significantly reduced IRLS scores (mean change -13.0 vs -5.0 points, P<0.001) and improved CGI, m-SIT subjective and motor scores, PLM indices, and multiple polysomnographic sleep measures compared with placebo. All between-group differences favored dipyridamole and were statistically significant (P<0.001 for primary outcome), supporting the adenosine hypothesis of RLS pathogenesis.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Two slightly discrepant PLM index values reported: abstract states dipyridamole 8.2±3.5 vs placebo 28.1±6.7; Table 2 text states PLM index 7.5±4.0 vs 19.1±8.2. Both extracted as separate outcome objects (outcome_id 5 from Table 2 text, outcome_id 14 from abstract). The sleep latency effect estimate in Table 2 is listed as -722 which appears to be a garbled value (likely -7.22); the CI is -12.07 to -2.38 and P=0.007, suggesting the true estimate is approximately -7.2 minutes — extracted as -7.2 with verbatim CI. summary: This open-label, single-arm trial treated 15 patients with severe idiopathic (n=13) or uremic (n=2) RLS who had experienced augmentation under prior L-dopa therapy with pergolide (mean dose 0.41 mg nightly) plus initial domperidone for 6 months. All 15 patients reported dramatic improvement in nocturnal RLS symptoms within 3–5 days, and all were classified as having 'no RLS' at 6-month follow-up, with daytime symptoms also resolving completely. No control group was included and no formal statistical testing was performed, so these results reflect uncontrolled observational data only.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm open-label trial with no randomization, no control group, and no validated RLS rating scale (e.g., IRLS). The only outcome instrument is a study-specific 3-category severity classification. No per-arm means or SDs for continuous outcomes were reported as there is only one arm. Duration of treatment with pergolide varied considerably per patient (6–24 months per Table 1, though the follow-up evaluation was at 6 months for all). Patient 3 was listed as age 72 in Table 1, slightly inconsistent with the stated range of 46–71 years in the text. Patient 5 discontinued pergolide due to lack of perceived efficacy but is still counted in the 6-month analysis group. No polysomnographic (PLM) data were reported at follow-up despite baseline PSG being performed. The paper does not report formal statistical analyses or p-values for any outcome.

summary: This quasi-experimental before-after study examined TMS cortical silent period (CSP) duration and polysomnographic PLM indices in 20 patients with primary RLS and 15 healthy controls before and after 1 month of dopaminergic treatment (levodopa n=8, cabergoline n=8, ropinirole n=4). CSP duration was significantly shorter in RLS patients than controls at baseline (e.g., right TA: 97.7±18 ms vs 128.9±11 ms, p<0.01), and dopaminergic treatment significantly prolonged CSP in the tibialis anterior muscles (p≤0.05) but not in the upper-extremity APB muscles. No significant correlation was found between CSP duration and PLM-related polysomnographic parameters, suggesting these neurophysiological measures reflect different inhibitory mechanisms.

Post-treatment SD values for CSP are not reported in text or table. 7. The paper reports that the 3 patients who did not attempt sleep studies are excluded from PSG results (n=17 for PSG outcomes). 8. summary: This double-blind, randomized, 2-period crossover pilot trial tested carbamazepine (titrated up to 600 mg/day) versus placebo over two 4-week periods in 6 patients with restless legs syndrome. Three patients (responders) showed marked benefit from carbamazepine, with week-4 symptom severity on carbamazepine being only 21% of the corresponding placebo value, while three nonresponders also had lower symptom scores on carbamazepine than placebo. No patient preferred placebo over carbamazepine on global evaluation, though the study was too small and lacked formal statistical testing to draw definitive conclusions.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This is a very small pilot crossover trial (n=6); no formal statistical tests were reported — all comparisons are descriptive. 2. Table 1 and Table 2 present per-patient, per-week data rather than means with SDs; means could not be calculated for arm_results without knowing which patients were in which treatment period at each week (crossover design). Individual patient values are preserved in notes fields. 3. summary: This single-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study investigated the acute effects of pramipexole 0.27mg (split evening/bedtime dose) on objective and subjective sleep quality via polysomnography in 11 RLS patients, followed by an open-label 4-week titration phase. summary: This randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, 3-arm crossover trial (n=20 idiopathic RLS patients) compared slow-release valproic acid (600 mg) and slow-release levodopa/benserazid (200/50 mg) to placebo, each given for 3 weeks. summary: This prospective open-label 6-month multicenter study (N=60 evaluable) examined the incidence and severity of augmentation during levodopa/benserazide treatment (flexibly dosed 200-600 mg/day; mean maximum 311 mg/day) in patients with idiopathic RLS across eight European centers. Augmentation was diagnosed by independent expert consensus in 60% (36/60) of patients, with a median time to onset of 71 days; augmenters showed significantly less improvement in IRLS severity (-6.4 vs -12.4, p=0.039), CGI, and treatment satisfaction compared to non-augmenters, and were more likely to be on doses >=300 mg/day (83% vs 54%, p=0.031). Most augmenters (80.6%) tolerated the complication during the 6-month period, with only 11.7% of all patients discontinuing due to augmentation, suggesting that while augmentation is common with levodopa it varies in severity and clinical impact.

summary: This open-label pre-post study with healthy control comparison tested whether 4 weeks of dopaminergic treatment (cabergoline or pramipexole) normalized deficient short latency afferent inhibition (SAI) — a TMS measure of sensory-motor integration — in 10 drug-naive idiopathic RLS patients. At baseline, SAI was significantly reduced in RLS patients compared to healthy controls (conditioned MEP 90% vs. 65% of unconditioned MEP; F(1,9)=59, p=0.00003), and 4 weeks of treatment restored SAI to near-normal levels (64%, p=0.001 vs. pre-treatment), while the IRLS-RS score also improved significantly (p=0.003). Short intracortical inhibition (SICI) showed a parallel pattern of deficit and normalization, while long latency afferent inhibition (LAI) and intracortical facilitation (ICF) were unaffected.

summary: This 12-week multicenter double-blind RCT (3:1 randomization) compared ropinirole immediate release (flexible doses up to 4 mg/day) versus placebo in 231 patients with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS and at least mild depressive symptoms (MADRS >= 12). Ropinirole also significantly reduced RLS severity (IRLS adjusted treatment difference -4.8 points, p<0.001), improved sleep quality on 3 of 4 MOS Sleep Scale subscales, and showed superior results on all three depression rating scales (MADRS, HAMD, BDI-II), indicating that treating RLS with ropinirole can substantially ameliorate comorbid depressive symptoms.

summary: This quasi-experimental study compared computerized posturographic measures of postural control in 12 unmedicated RLS patients versus 12 healthy controls, then assessed changes within the RLS group after a single-day open-label pramipexole intervention (0.88 mg twice daily). Unmedicated RLS subjects showed significantly lower center-of-force velocity with eyes open (0.68 vs. 0.99 cm/s, p=0.008) and higher Romberg's quotient (2.42 vs. 1.69, p=0.01) than controls, indicating compensatory visual dependence for postural stability. After pramipexole, the eyes-open velocity difference from controls was no longer statistically significant (p=0.052), and subjective symptom severity (VAS) and akathisia scores (BAS) improved significantly, supporting a dopaminergic mechanism for postural dysfunction in RLS.

summary: This double-blind, sham-controlled pilot RCT tested high-frequency (5 Hz) repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) over the supplementary motor area in 19 patients with idiopathic RLS already taking pramipexole. After 10 sessions (once every 3 days), the real rTMS group (n=11) showed a statistically significant improvement in IRLS-RS scores (mean 31.7 to 12.7) versus no meaningful change in the sham group (mean 29.6 to 28.6), with significant between-group differences after both the 5th and 10th sessions (p<0.001). A crossover subsample of 5 patients who crossed from sham to real stimulation confirmed a significant benefit of real rTMS (IRLS-RS declined from 25.8 to 5.8) with no augmentation or adverse events observed.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The crossover subsample (n=5) was extracted as a separate outcome (outcome_id=2) because these 5 patients received sham then real stimulation sequentially (not simultaneously), with different baselines for each phase (sham baseline mean 28.2 vs real baseline mean 25.8), making them non-comparable to the primary parallel-group analysis. Between-group p-values for the crossover subsample at each timepoint are verbatim from the text (Mann-Whitney test comparing sham vs real within the 5 patients); between-group mean differences for the crossover subsample were not calculated because the two phases had different baselines at different time points. The p-value reported as 'p=0.000' in the text for after-5th-session between-group comparison was recorded as p_value_exact=false. The calculated mean differences for the primary parallel-group analysis at baseline, after 5th session, and after 10th session are: +2.1 (real minus sham), -9.5, and -15.9 respectively. summary: This single-arm pilot study treated 12 patients with idiopathic RLS and vitamin D deficiency (mean baseline vitamin D 21.7 nmol/l) with oral or intramuscular vitamin D supplementation for 3–8 months until vitamin D levels normalized. The mean IRLSG RLS severity score improved from 26 at baseline to 10 after treatment (p=0.002, Wilcoxon signed-rank test). The authors conclude that vitamin D correction may significantly improve RLS symptoms, though the absence of a control group precludes causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm uncontrolled pre-post pilot study, not an RCT. No randomization occurred. The paper reports 'mean' values for RLS score and vitamin D, but the statistical analysis section states data were presented as 'median and range' and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used — so values labeled 'mean' in the text (RLS score 26 and 10; vitamin D 21.7 and 61.8) may actually be medians; this is ambiguous and both mean and median fields are populated with the same values. Ranges are given as parenthetical values (e.g. 15–35 for RLS score at baseline) and stored in iqr_low/iqr_high fields as the closest available approximation. No SDs are reported for outcome measures. Treatment duration ranged 3–8 months but no single week-value can be assigned. RLS score and vitamin D figures (Fig. 1, Fig. 2) show data only graphically without additional numeric precision beyond what is stated in the text. The between_group_effects entries represent within-arm pre-post paired comparisons, not between-group effects; the effect_value for RLS score (−16) is calculated as post minus pre mean (10 − 26). The study has no comparator arm and should not be pooled in a meta-analysis of controlled trials without careful handling.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) This study is quasi-experimental (not a true RCT): participants were assigned to groups by clinic site using non-probability sampling, not true randomization — this is explicitly stated in the paper. 2) PSQI Component 6 (Use of Sleeping Medication) was scored as zero for all participants and excluded from analysis; no numeric data are reported for this subscale. 3) Between-group t-test statistics are reported in Table 2 (t values and p values) but no confidence intervals are provided for between-group effects — CIs were not extractable. 4) Within-group t-test statistics from Table 3 are also provided (pre vs post within each arm) but these were not converted to between_group_effects entries as they represent pre-post within-arm changes, not between-arm comparisons. 5) The paper labels variables as 'independent' and 'dependent' in a reversed manner from standard convention, but this does not affect data extraction. 6) No RLS-specific severity scale (e.g., IRLS) was used; only PSQI sleep quality was measured as the outcome.

summary: This 12-week double-blind RCT randomized 35 adults with primary RLS in Saudi Arabia to weekly oral vitamin D 50,000 IU (n=17) or placebo (n=18). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 footnote labels (a = independent t-test, b = chi-square) clarify p-value test type. The n_analyzed values at week 12 are inferred from the Discussion (12 in vitamin D group, 10 in placebo group completed the study). The number of vitamin D-deficient completers per arm at week 12 is not reported — only that 11 per arm were deficient at baseline. The between-group p-value of 0.32 and CI (-12.8 to +4.4) are stated in the text but not in Table 4. Within-arm paired t-test p-values are reported separately for each arm (vitamin D: p=0.54; placebo: p=0.04) and recorded under outcome_id 4. The reported CI direction suggests intervention mean minus control mean (vitamin D minus placebo = positive value), meaning vitamin D group had higher (worse) end scores than placebo, consistent with Table 4 values. The withdrawal note mentions 'two left the country, two refused to continue' in the placebo week 4 group totaling 4 withdrawals plus 4 other reasons reported — the total of 8 withdrawals from placebo is calculated (4 at wk4 + 1 consent wk8 + 3 AE wk8). Bone profile outcomes were measured but not reported quantitatively.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Generalized Linear Model showed thyroid comorbidity was a significant predictor of post-operative RLS severity (OR=-24.752, p=0.001), indicating patients with thyroid disease had significantly lower RLS scores after bariatric surgery.

Greater BMI reduction after surgery was significantly correlated with greater reduction in RLS severity (r=-0.410, p=0.014); in multivariate GLM, BMI difference remained a significant predictor of post-operative RLS (OR=-0.490, p=0.049).
Greater BMI reduction was significantly associated with lower post-operative BSQ-OSAS scores in both correlation (r=-0.143, p=0.048) and GLM analysis (OR=-0.041, p=0.027).

summary: This retrospective cross-sectional survey study evaluated the effect of bariatric surgery on sleep disorders in 454 morbidly obese patients (207 with sleep complaints) at three Turkish university hospitals, with patients self-reporting sleep quality before and 6 months after surgery. RLS severity (IRLSSG) scores decreased significantly from 20.30±9.14 to 17.26±8.64 (p=0.001), and all other sleep measures (ISI, ESS, BSQ, most PSQI subscales) also improved significantly post-operatively. Greater BMI reduction was significantly correlated with greater improvements in RLS severity and OSA symptoms; however, the retrospective design, lack of a control group, and reliance on recalled pre-operative data severely limit causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is NOT an RCT — it is a retrospective pre-post observational study with no randomization and no control arm. The JSON schema has been adapted accordingly: single arm, design_type set to quasi-experimental, risk_of_bias overall=high. The table reports scores for all patients together (no per-group split for n=247 without complaints vs n=207 with complaints in Table 2). summary: This open-label, non-randomized, single-dose parallel-group pharmacokinetic study compared the absorption, distribution, and elimination of transdermal rotigotine (2 mg/24 h patch) in 24 healthy Japanese and 24 healthy Caucasian subjects. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a pharmacokinetic study in healthy volunteers comparing ethnic groups (Japanese vs. Caucasian), not an RLS clinical trial with efficacy outcomes. No RLS-specific outcomes (IRLS, PLMS, QoL, sleep scales) are reported. Per-arm pharmacokinetic values in Table 2 are geometric means with CV%; individual female/male subgroup means are reported separately rather than combined arm means — combined arm means for outcomes 1-4 are calculated as geometric averages of female and male subgroups. SD values for pharmacokinetic parameters are not directly reported (only CV%); SD could be reconstructed from CV% and geometric mean but this was not performed to avoid introducing calculation errors. summary: This 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (with 40-week open-label extension) tested prolonged release oxycodone/naloxone (OXN PR) in 304 patients with severe RLS inadequately controlled by prior dopaminergic therapy. OXN PR significantly improved sleep outcomes compared to placebo across multiple domains, including sleep disturbance (mean difference -18.6, 95% CI -24.4 to -12.9, p<0.0001), sleep adequacy (difference +14.9, 95% CI 7.9 to 21.9, p<0.0001), sleep quantity (+0.77 h/night, p<0.0001), sleep satisfaction, and RLS-specific quality of life (sum score difference -9.02, 95% CI -12.85 to -5.19, p<0.001); all improvements were sustained over the 40-week open-label extension. The safety profile was consistent with known opioid effects, with drug withdrawal symptoms observed in only 3 of 176 patients assessed at follow-up.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a secondary analysis of a previously published RCT (Trenkwalder et al., Lancet Neurology 2013) focusing on sleep and QoL outcomes; the primary efficacy outcome (IRLS sum score) is not reported here. Domain-level MOS sleep scale change-from-baseline values with 95% CIs are reported in the text and figure (Fig. 3) but not in tabular form per arm — domain-level between-group effect values (mean differences with CIs and p-values) were extracted verbatim from text. Individual MOS item-level per-arm means and SDs were extracted from Table 2. AE percentages reported but absolute n not given for most AEs. RLS-QoL dimension scores at baseline and end of double-blind phase are shown only in figures (Fig. 4, Fig. 5) without per-arm means/SDs in text, so arm_results were left unpopulated for outcomes 17-21. The overall RLS-QoL baseline mean of 45.4 is stated as an overall figure without per-arm breakdown. Completion rates stated as percentages (71% OXN PR, 63% placebo) allowing calculation of approximate n completed. IRLS sum score at randomization (post-washout) was OXN PR 31.7±4.4, placebo 31.6±4.7 (not extracted as separate outcome since primary IRLS outcome is in parent paper). MOS sleep scale items 'Rested when waking up' and 'Getting the amount of sleep needed' score direction: lower scores = more often rested/getting enough sleep (scale 1=all the time to 6=never), so at baseline higher scores indicate problems — the table shows these were high at baseline (~4.65-4.86) and decreased under OXN PR, consistent with improvement; higher_is_better set to false (lower score = better). Withdrawal symptom follow-up at 4 weeks post-extension conducted in 176 patients. Extension phase n at week 40 differs by outcome: n=157 for MOS, n=152 for RLS-6, n=190 for RLS-QoL sum score.

summary: This double-blind, randomized, crossover, placebo-controlled trial tested 2 weeks of suvorexant (10 mg week 1, 20 mg week 2) versus placebo in 41 adults with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS and significant sleep disturbance. summary: This cluster-randomized crossover pilot trial (n=23 hemodialysis patients with RLS) tested 4 weeks of acupressure at 12 bilateral lower-limb acupoints (36 min, 3×/week during dialysis) versus observation alone. No adverse events were reported with acupressure.

The per-arm means reported at each timepoint (T0, T1, T2) reflect the sequence groups, not the intervention condition per se. The between-group treatment effect from the GLMM (which properly isolates the acupressure vs. observation contrast across both periods) is the key effect estimate — reported verbatim with 95% CIs. The S4 (sleep efficiency) baseline was significantly different between sequences (p=0.0165), which may confound interpretation. The PSQI S6 (sleep medication) and S7 (daytime function) treatment effect CIs were partially garbled in the source table; p-values extracted as stated. Age was reported categorically only (35–64 and ≥65 groups), not as mean±SD per arm. The CA sequence SD for sleep duration (S3) at baseline was not cleanly legible in the table but cross-referenced with the overall SD.

summary: This double-blind, sham-controlled crossover pilot study (n=20 idiopathic RLS patients) tested a single 15-minute session of anodal, cathodal, or sham transcutaneous spinal direct current stimulation (tsDCS) over the thoracic spinal cord during the symptomatic evening phase. Anodal tsDCS significantly reduced RLS symptom severity on the VAS at both immediately post-stimulation (mean 65.2 to 37.5, p<0.001) and at 30 minutes (mean 44.4, p<0.001), with significant superiority over sham at both timepoints; cathodal tsDCS produced significant improvement only at the immediate post-stimulation timepoint (p=0.008). Anodal tsDCS also significantly reduced elevated H2/H1-ratios at ISIs of 0.2 s and 0.3 s in the 14-patient neurophysiology subgroup, supporting the spinal cord hyperexcitability hypothesis, though symptom relief was short-lasting (a few hours) and did not correlate with H2/H1-ratio changes.

summary: This post hoc analysis of the PEARLS double-blind RCT evaluated the relationship between the IRLS patient-rated severity scale and polysomnographic PLMS indices in 100 RLS patients randomized to pergolide or placebo for 6 weeks. At baseline, IRLS correlated significantly with PLMS-arousal index only in the PEARLS population pre-selected for high PLMS activity (r=0.22, p=0.033), not in an unselected outpatient cohort. Over the 6-week treatment period, changes in IRLS score correlated significantly with changes in both PLMS index (r=0.42, p<0.001) and PLMS-arousal index (r=0.38, p<0.001) across all treated patients combined, supporting use of both measures to track treatment response.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is primarily a post hoc correlation analysis of the PEARLS RCT; it does not report between-group treatment efficacy statistics (p-values, CIs, mean differences) for the RCT arms directly — these are referenced to Trenkwalder et al. 2004 (Neurology). The table reports change values labeled as 'change under treatment' for each arm with mean ± SD, but these are presented as descriptive data to contextualize the correlation analyses, not as formal between-group comparisons. The change values in the table appear to represent the magnitude of change (not signed — paper states 'change' values; context implies reduction, so signs were inferred as negative for symptom worsening outcomes). The correlation outcomes (outcomes 5 and 6) report pooled results across both arms combined (n=100), not per-arm; Spearman r values for these are: ΔIRLS vs ΔPLMS index r=0.42, p<0.001; ΔIRLS vs ΔPLMS-arousal index r=0.38, p<0.001. summary: This single-arm pre-post study with a separate healthy control group examined cutaneous silent period (CSP) electrophysiology in 157 RLS patients before and after one month of dopamine agonist treatment, compared to 60 healthy controls at baseline. At baseline, RLS patients had significantly longer CSP duration than controls (61.0 vs 52.01 ms; p=0.003) but similar CSP latency, and after one month of treatment both CSP duration (63.33 to 52.2 ms; p<0.001) and IRLS scores (25.70 to 12.9; p<0.001) improved significantly, though changes in CSP variables did not correlate with changes in IRLS score. The study had no randomization, no control arm for the treatment phase, and did not report adverse events, limiting causal inference.

summary: This single-center quasi-experimental study (Turkey) compared cutaneous silent period (CSP) electrophysiology parameters between 25 RLS patients and 25 healthy controls, then assessed the effect of 1-week pramipexole (0.5 mg/day) treatment within the RLS group using a pre-post design. At baseline, RLS patients showed significantly prolonged lower-extremity CSP latency (106.22 vs. 91.67 ms, p<0.001) and shortened lower-extremity CSP duration (35.50 vs. 49.47 ms, p<0.001) compared to controls, suggesting small-fibre neuropathy and altered spinal inhibition. After 1 week of pramipexole, CSP durations were significantly prolonged in both upper (40.88→46.84 ms, p=0.006) and lower extremities (35.50→44.91 ms, p=0.005), suggesting pramipexole may restore cortical and spinal inhibitory mechanisms, though this was an uncontrolled pre-post comparison without randomization.

summary: This was a Phase I, randomized, double-blind, 4-period crossover thorough QT/QTc study in 54 healthy volunteers evaluating the cardiac repolarization effects of single oral doses of gabapentin enacarbil (1200 mg and 6000 mg — the latter being supratherapeutic) compared with placebo, with moxifloxacin 400 mg as an active control. The primary finding was that gabapentin enacarbil at both doses did not prolong the QTcIb interval — the upper one-sided 95% CI for the double-delta QTcIb was below 10 ms at all 14 time points over 22.5 hours, meeting the negative thorough QT study criterion per ICH E14 guidance. Moxifloxacin demonstrated the expected positive QTc prolongation signal (up to 7.4 ms ddQTcIb), confirming assay sensitivity, while adverse events (predominantly dizziness and somnolence) were dose-dependent with gabapentin enacarbil, occurring in 46% at 1200 mg and 98% at 6000 mg versus 33% with placebo.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a Phase I cardiac safety/pharmacokinetic study in healthy volunteers and is NOT an RLS efficacy trial — it contains no RLS symptom outcomes, IRLS scores, sleep measures, or patient-reported RLS outcomes. The paper was included in the meta-analysis corpus but contributes only safety/tolerability and pharmacokinetic data. Table II reports LS mean ddQTcIb/ddQTcF as 'point estimate (upper confidence limit [1-sided])' for gabapentin enacarbil arms and Table III as 'point estimate (lower confidence limit [1-sided])' for moxifloxacin — these asymmetric CI presentations are preserved as-is in the between_group_effects fields (ci_95_high for GEn arms, ci_95_low for moxifloxacin arm). No per-arm raw QT means or SDs are reported — only the between-group ddQTc values from the mixed-effects model are tabulated. Tmax values for gabapentin PK were reported as median (range) rather than mean (SD); median values are: GEn 1200 mg Tmax 6.00 h (range 4.00-15.0), GEn 6000 mg Tmax 7.00 h (range 3.00-12.0), moxifloxacin Tmax 3.00 h (range 1.00-4.05) — these are omitted from arm_results as the JSON schema does not have a median/range field for PK parameters. The study had 7-day washout periods between the 4 crossover periods; total study duration not explicitly stated. Baseline demographics are reported only at the overall study level, not per-arm. The overall study N was 54 enrolled; the safety population per arm was n=50 for GEn 1200 mg, n=50 for GEn 6000 mg, n=50 for moxifloxacin, and n=51 for placebo (crossover, same subjects in each arm).

summary: This open-label pre-post study enrolled 20 never-treated idiopathic RLS patients and 15 healthy controls; patients received 0.25 mg pramipexole nightly for 3 months. At baseline, RLS patients showed significantly worse performance than controls on multiple cognitive domains including working memory (Digit Span Backward 4.0 vs 6.4, p<0.001), decision making (IGT 60.0 vs 83.7, p<0.001), and executive function (WCST perseveration errors 7.3 vs 1.2, p=0.001). After 3 months of pramipexole treatment, PSG-measured sleep improved significantly (PLMs index decreased from 53.6 to 8.4, p=0.001; TST increased from 341 to 429 min, p=0.001), and cognitive performance improved across nearly all tested domains, reaching levels comparable to healthy controls, though the absence of a placebo control limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is NOT a randomized controlled trial — it is a quasi-experimental pre-post study with a separate cross-sectional healthy control group. The 'between_group_effects' fields have been used to capture two types of comparisons: (1) controls vs. iRLS at baseline (cross-sectional comparison, Mann-Whitney U test), and (2) iRLS follow-up vs. iRLS baseline (pre-post treatment comparison, Wilcoxon test). These are labeled accordingly in the 'comparison' field. Note that Table 2 reports n=20 for iRLS at baseline while Table 3 uses n=18 (after 2 dropouts); baseline values in Tables 2 and 3 differ slightly (e.g., Digit Span Backward: 4.00 vs 3.89) because Table 2 includes all 20 patients while Table 3 includes only the 18 who completed follow-up. Both sets of baseline values are captured. Quality of life (SF-36 subscales), PSQI, BDI, and STAI scores are mentioned qualitatively but specific means/SDs are NOT reported in tables — these outcomes could not be extracted numerically. The article keywords listing 'Vortioxetine, Antidepressant, Memory, LTP, Novel object recognition, Neurogenesis' appear to be a publishing error (wrong keywords were assigned to this paper). The article also notes an 'Uncited reference' (Ferini-Strambi et al., 1995) flagged by the journal. Withdrawals were due to low compliance, not adverse events. Adverse events were not systematically reported.

summary: This 8-week double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT tested gabapentin enacarbil (GEn, 300-600 mg/day) vs. placebo in 147 older adults with Alzheimer's dementia, comorbid RLS, and nighttime agitation across 31 long-term care sites. summary: This double-blind RCT enrolled 105 Iranian hemodialysis patients with chronic renal failure and randomized them to 4 weeks of effleurage leg massage with lavender oil (1.5%), glycerin oil (2%), or no additional treatment (control), with RLS severity (IRLSSG 0-40 scale) assessed at baseline and one week post-intervention. summary: This phase III open-label extension study evaluated 52 weeks of flexible-dose pramipexole (0.125-0.75 mg/day) in 141 Japanese patients with primary RLS who had completed a prior 6-week double-blind trial. The IRLS total score improved markedly from 22.3±4.7 at baseline to 4.9±5.9 at week 52, with IRLS responder rates of 67.4% at week 12 and 86.6% at week 52 and CGI-I/PGI responder rates exceeding 90% at week 52. summary: This single-blind, parallel-group pilot RCT (n=35) compared whole body cryotherapy at -60°C (verum), whole body cryotherapy at -10°C (sham), and local cryotherapy at -17°C for idiopathic RLS, with 2 weeks of daily treatment and 4 weeks of follow-up. summary: This single-center quasi-experimental study compared quantitative sensory testing (QST) profiles in 40 previously untreated primary RLS patients versus 40 age- and gender-matched healthy controls, and also followed 8 patients longitudinally after L-DOPA treatment. RLS patients demonstrated 3- to 4-fold pinprick hyperalgesia (MPS 322-425% of controls, p<0.001), tactile hypoesthesia (50-67% threshold increase, p<0.05), and excess paradoxical heat sensations at the foot (p<0.05), with no accompanying dynamic mechanical allodynia. In the 8-patient L-DOPA substudy (uncontrolled, open-label), pinprick hyperalgesia was significantly reduced by 60% (p<0.001) and tactile sensitivity improved by 50% (p<0.05) after treatment, suggesting these sensory changes reflect functional central disinhibition reversible by dopaminergic therapy.

Table 1 provides geometric means for most QST parameters (log-transformed); individual SDs are not provided — only log10 mean ± SEM values in parentheses. summary: This single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled withdrawal trial enrolled 33 RLS patients who first received open-label ropinirole titration over 4 weeks and were then randomized (n=26; completers n=22) to continue ropinirole (n=9) or switch to placebo (n=13) for 2 weeks. Continued ropinirole significantly prevented rebound worsening of PLMSI (Group x Time interaction p<0.007) and PLMSAI (p<0.04), with median PLMSI increasing from 7.3 to 85.6 events/hour in placebo-randomized patients versus remaining stable (9.9 to 0.9) in ropinirole-maintained patients. IRLSSG symptom scores also worsened significantly more in the placebo group at visit 6 (p<0.03 between groups), though both groups showed increased scores after randomization, possibly reflecting anticipatory anxiety or augmentation effects.

Adverse events during open-label phase are reported for all 26 entrants combined, not by double-blind assignment. 7. summary: This open-label, single-arm study evaluated repeated supplemental IV iron gluconate (450 mg per course as 3x150 mg infusions) in 5 RLS patients who had previously responded completely to an initial 1000 mg IV iron dextran infusion but experienced symptom recurrence. The study found that supplemental iron courses could sustain previously achieved symptom improvements for most patients, and that repeated treatments were associated with a progressive decrease in the abnormally rapid rate of serum ferritin decline (mean 6.6 mcg/l/week after initial infusion vs. 2.3 mcg/l/week after last supplemental course). No inferential statistics on symptom outcomes were reported due to the small sample size and uncontrolled design, limiting conclusions about efficacy; the rate-of-ferritin-decline to symptom-duration correlation was statistically significant (r=0.71, p<0.006).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is NOT an RCT — it is a single-arm open-label longitudinal study with no control group and no randomization; the study_design.design_type is quasi-experimental. The paper does not report group-level mean or SD for age (individual ages per subject are: 51F, 68M, 51F, 54M, 58F — mean=56.4 years, 3 female out of 5 = 60%). Individual-level GRS scores are provided in Table 1 (initial=0 for all 5; best=10 for all 5; last varies: 5, 4.5, 5, 10, 10) but no group mean or SD is given. Individual ferritin values from Table 1: initial ferritin: 26, 188, 8, 84, 9 mcg/l; final ferritin: 291, 514, 140, 296, 145 mcg/l. Individual rates of ferritin decline after initial treatment: 2.6, 11.6, 7.3, 8.9, 6.0 mcg/l/week (mean=7.28 but paper reports mean=6.6, likely excluding one subject or using different rounding). Final rates: 0.3, 1.1, 7.4, 1.0, 1.5 mcg/l/week (mean=2.26 mcg/l/week, paper reports 2.3). Ferritin figure (Fig. 1) shows individual trajectories — data not extractable from text. The correlation statistic r=0.71 p<0.006 is between rate of ferritin change and log of duration — this is reported as a correlation, not a between-group comparison, but stored in between_group_effects as the closest available field. The between_group_effects effect_value field for outcome_id=5 stores the r value (0.71), not a mean difference — this is a limitation of the schema applied to this non-RCT study.

summary: This proof-of-principle study tested a transdermal lisuride patch (dopamine agonist) in 10 patients with severe idiopathic RLS, using a 2-week open-label phase followed by a 1-week double-blind randomization to lisuride (n=5) or placebo (n=4). During the open-label phase, IRLS scores improved markedly from a mean of 32.4 to approximately 10 points in all 10 treated patients. In the double-blind phase, patients maintained on lisuride showed continued improvement (mean final IRLS 6.8) while those switched to placebo deteriorated significantly (mean final IRLS 18.5), supporting efficacy of the transdermal formulation, though no formal statistical tests were performed given the exploratory pilot design.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a mixed open-label/RCT design: all 10 patients received lisuride in the open-label phase, then 9 responders were randomized (1 non-responder excluded). Baseline demographics (age, sex) are only reported for the overall group of 10 treated patients, not per randomized arm. The open-label change-from-baseline values in Table 2 are reported for subgroups of 'one patch' (n=3) and 'two patches' (n=7), and also combined (n=10); all combined values were extracted. The double-blind period 'change from week 2' values from Table 2 are the within-period changes, not changes from the original baseline. Final IRLS endpoint values (6.8±12.0 for lisuride, 18.5±7.5 for placebo) are quoted in the text and used as endpoint results at week 3. Adverse events are not separated by double-blind arm; all drug-related AEs (n=10 events in 4 patients) occurred in the open-label lisuride period and were assigned to arm 1. IRLS scores 'about 15' at end of week 1 and 'about 10' at end of week 2 are narrative approximations only and were not extracted as they lack SDs. Individual patient IRLS data appear in Fig. 2 but were not extracted as they lack SDs. No formal p-values or confidence intervals were reported for any outcome.

summary: This 3-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group RCT evaluated four fixed doses of pramipexole (0.125, 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75 mg/d) versus placebo in 107 Finnish patients with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS confirmed by polysomnography. All active doses produced highly significant reductions in the primary endpoint (PLMI) compared to placebo (p<0.001 for all comparisons by both ANCOVA and nonparametric testing), with median PLMI reductions ranging from 26.55 to 52.70 versus 3.00 for placebo. Subjective RLS severity (IRLS) also improved significantly with all pramipexole doses (adjusted mean changes -11.87 to -17.01 vs -6.08 for placebo, all p≤0.001), and pramipexole was generally well tolerated with an adverse event profile comparable to placebo.

summary: This phase II, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-response study evaluated the efficacy and safety of sumanirole (a selective dopamine D2 agonist) at doses of 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 mg/day in 270 patients with idiopathic RLS over 8 weeks. On the primary endpoint (IRLS-10 change from baseline), none of the sumanirole doses achieved statistical significance versus placebo, though the 4.0 mg dose showed the numerically largest difference (LS mean difference -2.59 points); a large placebo response (mean improvement ~9.6-13.1 points across all groups) made it difficult to detect a drug effect. Sumanirole 2.0 mg and 4.0 mg produced statistically significant, dose-dependent reductions in PLMS index versus placebo (treatment ratios 0.39 and 0.27, respectively; both p<0.0001), demonstrating objective polysomnographic benefit despite the lack of a significant subjective symptom response.

summary: This was a 52-week, open-label, single-arm, multicentre study evaluating the long-term safety, tolerability, and efficacy of ropinirole (0.25–4.0 mg/day) in 309 patients with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS, most of whom had previously participated in controlled parent studies. The primary finding was that ropinirole was generally well tolerated, with nausea as the most common adverse event (37.2%) and only 8.4% withdrawing due to adverse events; no cases of fibrotic complications, sudden onset of sleep, or postural hypotension were observed. IRLS total score improved by a mean of 12.0 points (OC) from baseline at week 52, with 82.8% of patients rated much or very much improved on the CGI-I, alongside improvements in sleep, quality of life, and work productivity; however, as an uncontrolled open-label study, no formal inferential statistics were performed and improvements cannot be definitively attributed to ropinirole.

summary: This single-blind, parallel-group RCT evaluated the acute effect of a single oral dose of pramipexole 0.25 mg versus placebo on RLS symptoms and polysomnographic parameters in 32 drug-naive patients with severe idiopathic RLS, using a within-patient baseline-to-treatment-night design. Pramipexole produced a marked and statistically significant reduction in PLMS indices (whole-night, NREM sleep) and subjective symptom severity on VAS (p<0.00001) versus no significant change with placebo. The between-group differences in PLMS change index and NREM PLMS index after treatment were highly significant (p<0.004 to p<0.00007), demonstrating immediate objective and subjective efficacy from the first night of therapy.

The ANOVA p-values for Group effect on LM parameters (p=0.004, 0.004, 0.014, 0.013) appear to represent the treatment night between-group comparison per post-hoc analysis context; these were assigned to treatment timepoint comparisons. The between-group p-value for VAS (p<0.00001) is stated for within-arm baseline vs. treatment comparison in pramipexole group only; no between-group VAS p-value at treatment timepoint was explicitly stated. summary: This retrospective pooled analysis of four 12-week double-blind placebo-controlled RCTs (N=996) examined whether clinical response to ropinirole (0.25–4.0 mg/day) in moderate-to-severe RLS differed by age at symptom onset. Neither continuous age-at-onset nor a dichotomous split at 35 years moderated the treatment effect on IRLS score or CGI-I responder rates, with interaction p-values all >0.35. Ropinirole produced significantly greater improvements than placebo in both early-onset (<35 years) and late-onset (≥35 years) subgroups, with adjusted mean treatment differences of approximately −3.0 IRLS points and odds ratios of 1.7–2.1 for CGI-I response.

Overall pooled between-group effects for the primary endpoint are not explicitly stated numerically (only visible in figures). summary: This 26-week single-arm open-label extension (PRELUDE extension) evaluated flexible-dose pramipexole (0.125–0.75 mg/day once nightly) in 107 patients with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS who had completed a prior 3-week double-blind phase. At week 30, pramipexole produced a mean IRLS reduction of 16.9 points (73.5% reduction from a baseline of 23.0) and an IRLS responder rate of 81.3%, both statistically significant (p<0.05); 89.7% of patients rated themselves as 'much/very much better' on the PGI. The trial lacked a control arm, precluding causal inference, but findings suggest durable and well-tolerated efficacy across the dosage range studied, with 93.5% of patients completing the open-label phase.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm open-label extension study; there is no comparator arm, so all between_group_effects arrays are empty. SF-36 domain-level numeric data (means and SDs) are presented only in a figure (Fig. 2) with no accompanying table or text values — quantitative SF-36 domain scores were therefore not extractable and are noted as not_reported. The RoB2 tool is designed for RCTs; it has been applied here in spirit, but the single-arm design means most domains are intrinsically high risk. The n_analyzed for ESS and CGI-I were not explicitly stated. Baseline for the open-label phase is the treatment-naive baseline of the prior double-blind phase (week 0), not the end of the double-blind phase. The '30-week' timepoint refers to week 30 counting from the original double-blind baseline, which includes 3 weeks of double-blind treatment, 1 week washout, and 26 weeks of open-label treatment.

summary: This 12-month single-arm open-label extension study (SP710) enrolled 295 patients with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS who had completed a preceding 6-week double-blind placebo-controlled dose-finding trial (SP709) of rotigotine transdermal patch (0.5–4 mg/24h). After one year of treatment, mean IRLS total score improved by −17.4 points (SD 9.9) from a baseline of 27.8, with 68.1% of patients meeting responder criteria (≥50% IRLS improvement) and 53.2% achieving remission (IRLS ≤10); all within-group pre-post comparisons were statistically significant (p<0.001) with effect sizes exceeding 1.0. No augmentation was reported; the main tolerability concern was application site reactions leading to discontinuation in 13.2% of patients.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm open-label extension study, not an RCT; design_type was set to quasi-experimental accordingly. No randomization occurred in SP710 itself. Between-group effects are not applicable (no control arm in this study). The IRLS figure (Fig. 1) shows data from the preceding SP709 trial arms alongside this study's maintenance data, but those SP709 arm-level data were not extractable as they pertain to a separate study. Completer vs. ITT analyses are reported in Table 3 — arm_results entries with n_analyzed=220 correspond to completers and those with n_analyzed=295 to ITT. QoL-RLS completer n is approximately 200 per the note 'varying between 200 (QoL) and 220 (IRLS)'. The RLS-6 satisfaction with sleep scale is scored 0–10 with higher scores indicating worse satisfaction (i.e., higher_is_better=false). Responder/remitter binary outcomes (outcomes 12–17) are reported for both ITT (N=295) and completers (N=220) in Table 4; only ITT values extracted in arm_results for these binary outcomes to avoid duplication; completer percentages are also available verbatim in the paper.

summary: This 3-week double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group dose-ranging trial (n=107 ITT) evaluated four doses of pramipexole (0.125, 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75 mg/d) versus placebo in adults with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS verified by polysomnography. All pramipexole doses significantly reduced the primary endpoint (PLM index) compared to placebo (median reductions of 26.55-52.70 vs. 3.00 for placebo; p<0.01 for all), with all doses normalizing the PLMSI to below 5/hour, and all doses also significantly improving subjective RLS severity on the IRLS (p≤0.0274). No dose-dependent increase in adverse events was observed and daytime somnolence remained within normal range across all groups.

Most polysomnographic outcome data (PLMI, PLMSI, PLMWI, PLMAI, sleep latency, TST, stages 2-4/REM) are reported as medians and median changes without SDs or IQRs, severely limiting meta-analytic pooling. Only baseline values in Table 1 provide means and SDs. 2. Stages 2-4/REM baseline medians: 276.50-338.25 for pramipexole groups, 316.00 for placebo; individual arm medians not specified. 7. summary: This 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 357 ITT patients with moderate-to-severe RLS tested flexible-dose pramipexole (0.125–0.75 mg nightly) versus placebo across 49 European centers. Pramipexole produced significantly greater reductions in RLS symptom severity (IRLS adjusted mean change -13.4 vs -9.6; treatment difference -3.8, p=0.0001) and MOS sleep disturbance score (adjusted mean change -25.3 vs -16.8; treatment difference -8.5, p<0.0001) compared to placebo. Secondary outcomes including IRLS responder rate, MOS sleep adequacy, RLS-QOL, PGI, and CGI-I all significantly favored pramipexole, and the drug was well tolerated with similar AE-related withdrawal rates (~9%) in both groups.
