summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT enrolled 18 patients with RLS and low-normal serum ferritin (15-75 ng/ml) and randomized them to ferrous sulfate 325 mg twice daily (n=11) or lactose placebo (n=7) for 12 weeks, with all patients also receiving vitamin C. The iron group showed a significantly greater reduction in IRLS scores compared to placebo (mean decrease 10.3 vs 1.14 points; p=0.01) and a significantly greater increase in ferritin levels (25.1 vs 7.5 ng/ml increase; p=0.04). A non-significant trend toward improved quality of life was observed in the iron group (p=0.07), making this the first double-blind placebo-controlled trial to demonstrate significant RLS symptom improvement with oral iron in patients with low-normal ferritin.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper reports IRLS score change at 12 weeks as a decrease (10.3 and 1.14 for iron and placebo respectively); these are presented as positive numbers representing reduction from baseline in the paper tables but have been coded as negative change values (-10.3, -1.14) to reflect direction of change. No endpoint (absolute) IRLS scores at week 12 were reported, only change from baseline. The between-group effect for quality of life used Fisher's exact test (not OR/RR); the p-value is reported but no effect size with CI was given. Intermediate timepoint data (6 weeks) was collected per protocol but not reported numerically in the paper. Adverse events were not systematically reported. The study mentions stool color change as a potential unblinding risk but provides no AE data.

summary: This 6-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT evaluated pramipexole (0.125-0.75 mg/day, forced titration) versus placebo in 41 Japanese patients with primary RLS and PLMI >= 5/hour. Pramipexole produced significantly greater reductions in PLMI (adjusted ANCOVA p=0.0019), IRLS total score (p=0.0005), PGI (p<0.0001), CGI-I (p=0.0488), and PSQI total score (p=0.0016) compared to placebo at 6 weeks. The drug was well tolerated with gastrointestinal adverse events more common in the pramipexole group (55% vs 28.6%) but no withdrawals due to adverse events in either arm.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Primary endpoint PLMI was analyzed by ANCOVA on log-transformed data (p=0.0019) and confirmed by Wilcoxon rank-sum test on raw data (p=0.0146); both p-values extracted. Per-arm means and SDs not reported for PLMI (only medians and ranges); ANCOVA adjusted means at week 6 not numerically reported in text. IRLS change from baseline of -16.1 (pramipexole) and -6.4 (placebo) stated in text and confirmed by calculating from per-arm endpoint values. ESS change from baseline values of -0.2 (pramipexole) and 0.4 (placebo) stated in text. Note substantial baseline age imbalance between arms (48.7 vs 62.3 years) and baseline PLMI imbalance (median 27.75 vs 38.45). Table 2 placebo group shows n=18 for PSG data despite n=21 randomized (3 patients likely excluded from PSG analysis). Secondary PSG outcomes omitted from outcome objects: PLMWI, PLMAI, total number of awakenings/arousals, total number of PLM during sleep with arousals, sleep latency, sleep efficiency, total sleep time, time in stages 2-4 and sREM, percentage sREM, percentage delta sleep, amount of time in delta sleep, and SIT parameters for all patients and SIT-VAS subgroup data — all available in Table 2. PSQI sub-items sleep latency, habitual sleep efficacy, use of sleep medicine, and daytime dysfunction omitted from outcome objects (non-significant; available in Table 3).

summary: This single-center crossover study in 8 drug-naive RLS patients tested the effects of oral melatonin (3 mg at 19:00h) and bright light exposure (3000 lux, 19:00h to midnight) on RLS motor and sensory symptoms measured by the Suggested Immobilization Test (SIT) at two evening timepoints. Exogenous melatonin significantly worsened motor symptoms (SIT-PLM index increased ~70 movements/hour vs. baseline, p=0.038; and was greater than bright light, p=0.011), while bright light exposure significantly reduced sensory discomfort (MDS) compared to baseline (p=0.032) but had no significant effect on periodic leg movements. These findings support a role for melatonin in the circadian worsening of RLS and suggest potential therapeutic interest in bright light treatment, though the small sample limits generalizability.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a 3-condition within-subject crossover design, not a traditional parallel-group RCT; arm_id=3 (baseline) serves as the reference/control condition. The ANOVA p-values reported (p=0.038 for melatonin vs baseline PLM; p=0.011 for melatonin vs bright light PLM; p=0.032 for bright light vs baseline MDS) apply across both SIT timepoints combined (no SIT main effect found), so the same p-values are assigned to both timepoints. Salivary melatonin values in the text are reported as approximate means (e.g., 'mean of 70 and 60 pg/ml') without SDs. Discomfort score time-course data (Fig. 2) is only in a figure and was not digitized; figure shows n=7 (one subject excluded from figure but included in analyses). The between_group_effects p_value for melatonin vs baseline and melatonin vs bright light for PLM are assigned to both timepoints as the ANOVA showed no SIT effect and post-hoc p-values appear to be for the overall condition effect. The duration of the study per se is one evening per condition with one-week washout between melatonin and bright light conditions; total study duration was approximately 2-3 weeks but not explicitly stated.

summary: This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (NCT00275236) tested rotigotine transdermal patch (up to 3 mg/24 h) versus placebo over 7 weeks (3-week titration + 4-week maintenance) in 67 patients with moderate to severe idiopathic RLS and polysomnographically confirmed PLM. Rotigotine significantly reduced the primary endpoint PLMI from 50.9 to 8.1 PLM/h TIB versus 37.4 to 27.1 PLM/h under placebo (adjusted treatment ratio 4.25, 95% CI 2.48–7.28, p<0.0001), and also significantly improved PLMSAI (p=0.0072), IRLS sum score (p=0.0107), and CGI-1 (p=0.0168), with rotigotine well tolerated and most adverse events mild to moderate.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Primary PLMI values are geometric means (not arithmetic means); the between-group effect is reported as an adjusted LS mean ratio (not a mean difference), which is appropriate given log-transformation. SDs for PLMI endpoint values are reported as geometric coefficients of variation (CV%), not standard deviations; these cannot be directly used as arithmetic SDs. The placebo FAS n=20 (one excluded for missing data from n_randomized=21). PSG outcomes (Table 2) use the completer set (n=41 rotigotine, n=20 placebo), while subjective outcomes (Table 3) use FAS (n=46 rotigotine, n=20 placebo). The MOS sleep quantity subscale change values (+1.0 rotigotine, +0.3 placebo) were extracted; note this subscale is in hours. Several RLS-6 subscale outcomes (daytime resting, daytime active, daytime sleepiness) and additional MOS subscales (snoring, short of breath, somnolence, sleep indices I and II) are fully tabulated but between-group effect sizes were not reported for these. Non-REM 1 latency, Non-REM 3/4 latency, and REM latency PSG data were fully extracted in Table 2 but omitted from the outcomes array to stay within reasonable length; data are available in Table 2 of the paper.

summary: This 6-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, six-arm dose-ranging phase 2b study evaluated pregabalin (50, 100, 150, 300, or 450 mg/day once daily) versus placebo in 137 patients with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS. The primary endpoint—change from baseline in IRLS total score at week 6—showed a dose-dependent reduction characterized by an exponential decay model, with ED50 at 37.3 mg/day and ED90 at 123.9 mg/day; statistically significant reductions versus placebo were observed for doses ≥150 mg/day (nominal p≤0.04). Secondary outcomes including actigraphy total sleep time showed significant improvements at doses ≥150 mg/day (p<0.01), and dizziness and somnolence were dose-related adverse events, with 10 patients discontinuing due to pregabalin-related AEs.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. CGI-I responder percentages and IRLS responder percentages for most dose groups appear ONLY in Figure 4 and are not reported numerically in text or tables (except that 80% of arm 5/450mg IRLS responders is stated in text). 2. The table reports 'least squares means' (LS means) from mixed-model analysis, not arithmetic means or raw change scores — these are placed in a 'least_squares_mean' note field within arm_results since the schema lacks a dedicated LS mean field; the 'mean' field was left null to avoid confusion. 3. For between-group effects, the paper states significance thresholds (nominal p≤0.04 or p<0.05 or p<0.01) rather than exact p-values; p_value_exact is set to false. 4. The paper identifies which dose arms reached significance vs placebo (≥150 mg for IRLS total) but does not provide exact p-values or CIs for pairwise comparisons. 5. Actigraphy n_analyzed is 88/132 total across all arms but per-arm breakdown not provided. 6. SSQ Sleep Latency, Number of Awakenings, Wake Time After Sleep Onset, and MOS-SS Somnolence, Snoring, Awaken Short of Breath subscale data are available in Table 2 but between-group effects were not explicitly stated as significant; these were omitted from between_group_effects arrays. 7. Arm IDs reassigned for clarity: arm_id 1=pregabalin 50mg, 2=100mg, 3=150mg, 4=300mg, 5=450mg, 6=placebo (control). Note this reverses the convention of arm_id=1 for primary intervention, but was necessary to accommodate the six-arm structure. 8. RLS-QoL and SF-36 outcomes are mentioned but no numerical data provided in tables — omitted from outcomes.

summary: This single-blind placebo-controlled RCT examined the effects of a single dose of pramipexole (0.25 mg) versus placebo on heart rate variability (HRV) and PLMS-related heart rate changes during polysomnography in 23 RLS patients, with a separate comparison to 10 healthy controls. Pramipexole strongly suppressed the PLMS index (from 30.9 to 7.1 events/hour vs. 36.9 to 37.0 in placebo) and significantly reduced the amplitude of PLMS-related heart rate rises, normalizing them to levels seen in healthy controls. No significant effects were found on basal tonic sympathovagal balance (LF/HF ratio, spectral HRV parameters) in either treatment condition, suggesting pramipexole selectively targets phasic autonomic responses without disrupting overall autonomic regulation during sleep.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Primary outcome of PLMS-related HR changes (outcome_id 6) is presented only in figures (Figs. 2-4) as percentage-of-baseline time series curves with SEM error bars — no tabulated means or SDs are provided, so arm_results values could not be extracted numerically. The study includes a third group (healthy controls, n=10) used for comparison with RLS patients at baseline but not part of the RCT randomization; control group sleep architecture data from Table 1 (Controls Baseline night: TIB 488.7±72.72, SPT 449.6±37.22, TST 343.7±92.63, SOL 19.9±23.94, SE 71.2±20.63, WASO 23.5±20.77, S1 4.7±3.71, S2 43.9±16.19, SWS 12.4±9.03, REM 15.5±8.86, PLMS index 10.0±12.33) and HRV data from Table 2 were not included as separate arm results since controls were not randomized. summary: This 12-week multinational double-blind RCT randomized 404 adults with moderate-to-very-severe idiopathic RLS and at least moderate RLS-related mood disturbance to flexible-dose pramipexole (0.125–0.75 mg/day) or placebo. Pramipexole was significantly superior to placebo on all three primary endpoints: IRLS total score reduction (-14.2 vs -8.1, p<0.0001), BDI-II total score reduction (-7.3 vs -5.8, p=0.0199), and IRLS item 10 mood responder rate (75.9% vs 57.3%, p<0.0001). Pramipexole also improved anxiety (HADS-A), quality of life (RLS-QOL), and most RLS-6 subscales, and was well tolerated with fewer withdrawals than placebo.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CGI-I and PGI responder rates at all intermediate timepoints (day 9, weeks 2 and 4) and the pramipexole arm's week-12 CGI-I responder rate and PGI responder rate appear primarily in a figure (Fig. 2D and 2E) with no precise numeric values given in text except the ARR and NNT at week 12. Per-arm event counts for IRLS item 10 responders, IRLS 50% responders, and PGI/CGI-I responders were not stated numerically in the text. The n_withdrawn_due_to_ae for placebo (11) was derived from 5.5% of 200 (safety population). The withdrawal reason breakdown by arm includes only partial data: 3.4% pramipexole vs 10.0% placebo for lack of efficacy; 4.4% pramipexole vs 5.5% placebo for AEs. The RLS-6 table reports n=195 for placebo and n=202 for pramipexole; HADS-A baseline medians are from the safety population table (n=200 placebo, n=203 pramipexole). The 95% CI for the HADS-A treatment effect [-1.1, -0.9] is unusual (very narrow) and appears to represent median difference CI from the non-parametric test. The between-group effect for HADS-A effect_value of -1.0 is the median difference (pramipexole minus placebo). The RLS-QOL CI [7.2, 7.8] similarly appears to be the median difference CI.

summary: This paper reports a secondary analysis of RLS-related limb pain as a secondary outcome in two double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group RCTs (Trial 615: n=357 ITT; Trial 604: n=398 ITT) evaluating pramipexole (0.125–0.75 mg/day for 12 weeks) in patients with idiopathic RLS. In both trials, approximately 75% of patients had clinically meaningful baseline limb pain (VAS >30 mm), and pramipexole produced significantly greater reductions in VAS pain scores than placebo by as early as day 5. At week 12, median VAS reductions were -33.5 vs. -11.0 (p<0.0001) in Trial 615 and -31.0 vs. -11.0 (p<0.0001) in Trial 604, with responder rates (>=30% reduction) of 72.5% vs. 51.4% and 68.7% vs. 45.7% respectively.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper reports two separate RCTs together; all outcomes are presented per trial, not pooled. Arm-level sample sizes for ITT populations are reported in the results section (Trial 615: pramipexole n=178, placebo n=179; Trial 604: pramipexole n=201, placebo n=197), but the baseline demographics table uses randomized n (Trial 615: placebo 187, pramipexole 182; Trial 604: placebo 200, pramipexole 203). The between-group median difference reported in the paper appears to be from the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney rank test (not a simple arithmetic difference of medians); the stated values are -4.0 (Trial 615) and -12.0 (Trial 604) with very narrow CIs, suggesting these are Hodges-Lehmann estimators — extracted verbatim under median_difference comparisons. The calculated mean difference was derived from per-arm mean change values. Intermediate timepoint data (days 1, 5, 9, weeks 2, 4) appear only in figures (Fig. 1), so result_source is 'not_reported' for those timepoints. Withdrawal rates expressed as percentages only (Trial 615: 9.3% pramipexole, 8.6% placebo AE-related withdrawal; Trial 604: 4.4% pramipexole, 5.5% placebo), exact n not calculable without confirmed analyzed n. The primary outcomes of the two trials (sleep for Trial 615, mood for Trial 604) are not reported in this paper — only the secondary pain VAS outcome is presented here.

summary: This 26-week double-blind RCT enrolled 331 adults with idiopathic RLS (IRLS >15, ferritin >30 ng/mL) across 42 European sites and randomized them 1:1 to optimized pramipexole (0.125–0.75 mg/day) or placebo. summary: This study examined leg movement (LM) activity during wakefulness and sleep in 90 idiopathic RLS patients and 28 controls, with a subset of 35 patients randomized to a single dose of 0.25 mg pramipexole (n=17) or placebo (n=18) before a second polysomnographic night. RLS patients showed significantly higher LM activity during both wakefulness and sleep compared to controls, but the periodicity index during wakefulness did not differ between groups, indicating that wakefulness LM is less periodic than sleep LM. Pramipexole produced only limited effects on wakefulness LM, significantly reducing only the number of PLMW sequences (p=0.026) and periodicity index (p=0.027), without affecting total LM or PLMW index, while placebo had no effect on any parameter.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is primarily an observational/mechanistic study with a small embedded RCT component (n=35). The RCT arm IDs (1=pramipexole, 2=placebo) differ from the observational cohort groups (arm_id 3=RLS patients n=90, arm_id 4=controls n=28) used in outcomes 8-12 — these are noted in arm_results with arm_id 3 and 4 respectively to distinguish the two study designs within one paper. The t-test p-values reported in Table 4 are within-arm (paired, baseline vs. post-treatment) comparisons, not between-arm comparisons; between_group_effects for outcomes 1-7 are labeled accordingly. summary: This single-arm before-after study enrolled 13 drug-naive patients with moderate-to-severe RLS (IRLS >19) and treated them with pramipexole (median 0.25mg/day) for 12 weeks, evaluating effects on working memory via the Sternberg ERP paradigm. These findings suggest pramipexole improves both RLS symptoms and working memory performance, though the lack of a control group limits causal inference.

The paper reports the ANOVA F-statistic for hit rate as F(1,12)=13.980, p=0.003. The omission error ANOVA F-statistic F(1,12)=1.840 with p=0.006 appears inconsistent in the original text (low F but significant p) — extracted verbatim. summary: This was a prospective observational pilot study of 19 consecutive patients admitted for opioid/opiate detoxification in India, examining prevalence and treatment of restless legs syndrome (RLS) during withdrawal. Ten of 19 patients (approximately 53%) developed RLS meeting IRLSSG criteria, far exceeding the 2.1-2.5% population prevalence; RLS onset occurred a mean of 1.7 days after abstinence and appeared related to mu-receptor affinity of the opioid and concomitant cannabis use. Pregabalin (75-150 mg/day) was added for the 8 subjects who did not respond to buprenorphine substitution alone, with clinician-reported resolution of RLS symptoms and improved sleep quality in all treated patients, though no formal statistical comparison was conducted due to the uncontrolled design.

summary: This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial conducted in South Korea tested a single intravenous 500mg dose of ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) versus saline placebo in 64 adults with moderate-to-severe primary RLS (IRLSS ≥15). At the primary endpoint of 6 weeks, FCM showed a trend toward greater improvement in IRLSS scores (−8.3 vs −4.8) and VAS severity (−23.4 vs −13.3) compared to placebo, but neither difference reached statistical significance (p=0.100 and p=0.077, respectively). summary: This pilot neurophysiology study compared the effects of a single session of low-frequency (1 Hz) rTMS over the primary motor cortex on cortical plasticity (indexed by motor evoked potential suppression) in 13 RLS patients versus 10 healthy controls. At baseline, rMT and MEP amplitudes did not differ between groups, but after rTMS RLS patients showed significantly less MEP suppression than controls at both intermediate (T1: 1.9 vs 1.3 mV, p=0.016) and final (T2: 1.7 vs 0.3 mV, p<0.0001) timepoints. The findings indicate that short-term inhibitory rTMS-induced cortical plasticity is impaired in RLS, consistent with GABA-mediated disinhibition of motor cortex as part of the disease pathomechanism.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a neurophysiology mechanistic sub-study of a larger single-blind RLS rTMS trial (Lanza et al., Ther Adv Neurol Disord, in press at time of publication). The study design is technically a comparison of RLS patients vs healthy controls both receiving real rTMS — not a classic RCT with randomization to treatment vs control arms. The JSON structure has been mapped with arm_id=1 (RLS patients) as intervention and arm_id=2 (healthy controls) as comparator. Only median and range (not mean and SD) are reported for TMS parameters in Table 2; IQR fields used to store the range values. PSG data in Table 1 are means ± SD for RLS patients only (no control PSG data). Between-group effect p-values are verbatim from Mann-Whitney U test results in Table 2. The Mann-Whitney U statistic is: rMT U=48.0 (NS), MEPs T0 U=50.0 (NS), MEPs T1 U=25.5 (p=0.016), MEPs T2 U=0.5 (p=0.000075). No clinical RLS symptom severity scores (IRLSRS) or quality-of-life outcomes are reported with numeric data in this paper; these were stated to be reported in the parent trial reference [13]. This paper is primarily a neurophysiology mechanistic study, not a clinical outcomes trial.

GEn produced substantially greater improvements in IRLS score (mean change -14.98 vs -8.43), IRLS responder rate (67.5% vs 30.0%), and CGI-I responder rate (74.0% vs 36.2%) compared to placebo. The primary analytic finding was that baseline SIT leg discomfort scores and change-from-baseline in SPSD sleep quality were the strongest and most consistent predictors of treatment response for both GEn and placebo in stepwise logistic regression models.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a post-hoc predictor analysis, not a primary efficacy report; between-group effect sizes (mean differences, CIs, p-values) for most outcomes are not reported — only the change-from-baseline per-arm means and SDs are given in Table 1; between-group mean differences were therefore calculated. The baseline values in Table 1 are reported for the overall ITT population (n=131) and are not disaggregated by treatment sequence arm; the crossover design means all subjects received both treatments. The footnote Ns (a–j) in Table 1 indicate different sample sizes for specific variables; these have been applied to the relevant arm_results entries. SIT baseline value (n=125) and SIT PLMI baseline (n=126) applied to overall baseline. The SD column for the placebo/GEn changes represents SD (not SE), based on the table format, though the header says 'mean change (SE)' — values are large (e.g., 7.86, 8.22 for IRLS) suggesting these are SDs, but the table header explicitly says SE; extractor retained them as SD per magnitude. The follow-up total duration is estimated: 4-week treatment period 1 + 1-week taper + 1-week washout + 4-week treatment period 2 + 1-week taper = ~15 weeks. Ferritin baseline: mean 99.18 (SD 89.68) µg/L — not extracted as a standalone outcome. Correlation coefficients reported in the text (Spearman r values) were not extracted as outcomes per instructions. Logistic regression p-values from Tables 2-3 are extracted in the subgroup/predictor results section only as described in discussion; they are not represented as between-group effects since they address predictors, not arm comparisons. NOTE: The table header states 'mean change (SE)' but the SD column values (e.g., IRLS SD=7.86 for placebo change, 8.22 for GEn change) are too large to be standard errors for n~120; they are almost certainly SDs mislabeled as SE in the header. Extracted in the sd field accordingly.

summary: This double-blind, randomized, crossover, placebo-controlled trial compared the response to 2 weeks of gabapentin enacarbil (600 mg/day) versus placebo in 39 adults with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS who were either dopamine-treatment naive (Group A, n=20) or had been continuously treated with dopamine agonists for at least 5 years without augmentation (Group B, n=19-20). summary: This single-arm, open-label, longitudinal study in 30 adults with RLS/WED evaluated the effect of intravenous ferric carboxymaltose (1000 mg) on substantia nigra iron deposits (measured by transcranial sonography SNEI) and RLS symptom severity (IRLS) over approximately 160 days. summary: This open-label RCT evaluated 4-session individual CBTI versus sleep hygiene education alone in 25 Korean RLS patients with comorbid insomnia on stable dopaminergic therapy. summary: This single-center sham-controlled RCT (n=30 RLS patients) tested 14 days of daily anodal transcutaneous spinal cord direct current stimulation (tsDCS) at 2 mA for 20 minutes versus sham stimulation. The anodal tsDCS group showed significant reductions in IRLS-RS scores (27.2 to 15.0, p<10^-6) and PSQI scores (14.9 to 10.3, p<10^-4), while sham showed no significant change, with clinical improvement sustained at the 2-week post-treatment assessment. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) MRI (VBM and fMRI) data were collected ONLY in the anodal tsDCS arm and healthy controls — sham arm had no neuroimaging, severely limiting neuroimaging outcome interpretation. 2) All neuroimaging outcome data (GMV values, FC z-scores) are presented only in figures with no numeric values in text or tables; result_source set to 'not_reported' for these. 3) The paper reports p<10^-6 for IRLS-RS and p<10^-4 for PSQI within-group changes for the active arm — these are threshold p-values not exact values. 4) Between-group (anodal vs sham) statistical comparisons for IRLS-RS and PSQI are not reported; only within-group pre-post comparisons are provided. summary: This paper reports a post hoc pooled analysis of two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Japanese trials (Phase II/III and post-marketing) evaluating gabapentin enacarbil (GE) 600 mg/day versus placebo over 12 weeks in 610 patients with moderate-to-very-severe idiopathic RLS, where neither individual trial had demonstrated statistically significant superiority of GE 600 mg. Post hoc subgroup analyses identified positive family history of RLS, prior dopaminergic agonist use, and higher baseline ferritin (≥50 ng/mL) as predictors of greater GE response, while higher baseline IRLS score and higher BMI were associated with greater placebo responses. A predictive enrichment analysis identified 57% of the pooled population as an 'enrichable subpopulation' in which the GE-placebo difference was statistically significant (LS mean difference −2.8, 95% CI −4.3 to −1.4, p<0.001), suggesting that patients with typical idiopathic RLS characteristics may derive greater benefit from GE treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a post hoc pooled analysis, not a primary RCT report. The paper reports LS means with 95% CIs from MMRM models rather than raw means and SDs for change-from-baseline outcomes; SD values for change from baseline are therefore not available and were not extracted. summary: This multicenter, parallel-group, sham-controlled RCT evaluated 2 weeks of active versus sham tonic motor activation (TOMAC), a noninvasive bilateral peroneal nerve stimulator, in 45 adults with moderate-to-severe RLS (20 medication-naïve, 25 medication-refractory). summary: This 6-month randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested transdermal rotigotine at 1, 2, and 3 mg/24h versus placebo in 458 adults with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS (mean baseline IRLS 28.1). summary: This small double-blind crossover RCT (n=6) tested clonazepam (titrated to up to 2 mg/day) versus placebo over two consecutive 4-week periods in patients with restless legs syndrome, using a daily 5-point self-rated discomfort score as the primary outcome. Acute exercise resulted in statistically significant reductions in number of leg movements (PLM + RLS: 33.0 ± 54.1 vs. 10.0 ± 12.3, p<0.03, a 69.7% reduction), as well as significant improvements across all other sleep parameters including total sleep time, sleep stage changes, awakenings, and REM sleep duration.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is not an RCT — it is a within-subjects repeated-measures (quasi-experimental) study with a fixed condition order (basal night always first, exercise night always second), so arm_id assignment here uses arm_id=1 for the intervention condition (post-exercise) and arm_id=2 for the control/basal condition. RoB2 tool is not ideally suited for this design type. The p-values reported are all threshold values (e.g., p<0.03, p<0.04, p<0.01), not exact values. Mean differences in between_group_effects were calculated as arm1_mean minus arm2_mean (post-exercise minus basal). Total sleep time was analyzed by paired Student's t-test; all other outcomes were analyzed by Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test. The paper does not specify exact weeks from randomization as there was no randomization; timepoints are within a 3-day laboratory stay (basal night = Day 2, post-exercise night = Day 3). summary: This randomized double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial enrolled 16 hemodialysis patients with RLS and tested gabapentin 300 mg orally three times weekly after dialysis sessions versus placebo for 6 weeks each (with 1-week washout), with 13 patients completing the study. Post-gabapentin mean RLS questionnaire score was 3.0 ± 2.2 versus 5.8 ± 2.3 post-placebo (p < 0.01), and 12 of 13 completers responded to gabapentin versus 2 of 13 to placebo (McNemar p < 0.006). The study concluded gabapentin is an effective and generally well-tolerated treatment for RLS in hemodialysis patients, with somnolence/lethargy as the primary limiting side effect.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Crossover design: per-arm means and SDs are reported combined across both periods (i.e., pooled post-gabapentin and post-placebo scores from all completers), not separated by sequence group. Baseline score of 6.9 ± 0.7 applies to all 16 patients before treatment. The mid-study washout score of 6.7 ± 1.2 is reported for completers and attributed to the placebo arm timepoint as it occurred after the first 6-week period before crossover. Figure 1 contains individual patient score data but no aggregate values beyond what is stated in the text; per-arm figures data not extractable numerically. Between-group mean difference of -2.8 was calculated (3.0 - 5.8). The responder counts in the binary outcome (events=12 for gabapentin, events=2 for placebo) are calculated from the binomial table: gabapentin effective in 12/13; placebo effective in 2/13. The death occurred in the placebo arm at time of death and the patient never received gabapentin; the 2 dropouts from adverse events both occurred during gabapentin administration. Baseline demographics are only reported for the overall cohort (N=16), not by randomization sequence arm. The p < 0.01 for t-test and p < 0.006 for McNemar test are threshold values, not exact; p_value_exact set to false.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT tested a single IV infusion of 1,000 mg iron dextran versus normal saline in 25 ESRD patients with RLS confirmed by IRLSSG criteria. RLS severity scores improved significantly in the iron dextran group at week 1 (median change −2 vs −0.5; p=0.03) and week 2 (median change −3 vs 0; p=0.01), with iron-treated patients also showing significant increases in serum ferritin and iron saturation. summary: This pilot diagnostic test study validated a Holter-monitored suggested immobilization test (SIT) performed during hemodialysis for detecting periodic limb movements (PLMs) in 32 uremic patients with RLS and 29 dialysis controls. The 30-minute SIT achieved 63% sensitivity and 90% specificity for RLS diagnosis, and SIT-PLM correlated moderately with IRLSRS severity scores (r=0.53, p=0.03). In an uncontrolled pre-post pilot of 18 RLS patients, 4 weeks of pergolide significantly reduced both IRLSRS scores (24.9±9.1 to 9.5±6.8, p<0.01) and SIT-PLM counts (41.9±24.2 to 11.3±12.3, p<0.01), though changes in the two measures were not significantly correlated (r=0.27, p=0.3).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a diagnostic test study and uncontrolled pre-post treatment pilot — not an RCT. RoB2 is not strictly applicable but has been applied to flag the non-randomized design. summary: This double-blind RCT (RENALYS) tested rotigotine transdermal patch (1-3 mg/24h) versus placebo in 30 adults with moderate-to-severe RLS and ESRD requiring hemodialysis, over a 5-week treatment period with polysomnographic assessment. Rotigotine significantly reduced the primary outcome (PLMI ratio end of maintenance/baseline: 0.7 vs 1.3; treatment ratio 0.44, 95% CI 0.22-0.88, p=0.02), and also improved PLMSI, sleep efficiency, and TST versus placebo; IRLS improvement (-15.9 vs -8.6 points) approached but did not meet significance (LS mean difference -6.08, p=0.05). The study was small (n=25 analyzed), all dropouts occurred in the rotigotine arm, and confirmed that no dose adjustment is needed for hemodialysis patients.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The primary outcome is the PLMI ratio (a ratio of endpoint/baseline), reported as mean±SD per arm; the between-group effect is expressed as a treatment ratio (ANCOVA on log-transformed ratio), not a mean difference — this is captured under rate_ratio. 2. End-of-maintenance absolute PLMI value for rotigotine (58.1±37.6) was reported in text only, not in the table; extracted verbatim from text. 3. The end-of-maintenance PLMI absolute value for the placebo arm was not explicitly stated (only the change: +10.3), so it can be calculated as 85.3+10.3=95.6 but is not extracted as an arm_result to avoid imputed values. 4. CGI-1 per-arm means and SDs at baseline and endpoint were not reported in tabular form — only the LS mean treatment difference is available; arm_results left empty for outcome_id 15. 5. The SF-36 table footnote references 'SF-16' in the paper but this is clearly a typo for SF-36. 6. Follow-up duration: titration up to 21+3 days (~3.4 weeks) + 2-week maintenance = ~5.4 weeks treatment; plus 30(+3)-day safety follow-up (~4.7 weeks post-treatment); total ~10 weeks excluding washout/screening. Treatment period conservatively estimated as 5 weeks (titration max 3 weeks + maintenance 2 weeks), post-treatment follow-up ~4 weeks (30-day safety follow-up). 7. Safety set n=20 rotigotine, n=10 placebo; full analysis set (FAS/primary efficacy) n=15 rotigotine, n=10 placebo. 8. Blood pressure data (day/night SBP/DBP changes) available in text for rotigotine safety set but not tabulated with SD for placebo; not extracted as formal outcomes due to incomplete per-arm data. 9. IRLS remitter (IRLS<=10) and symptom-free (IRLS=0) responder counts reported in text (rotigotine: 8/15 remitters, 3/15 symptom-free; placebo: 1/10 remitter, 0 symptom-free) but not extracted as separate outcomes to conserve space.

summary: This open-label randomized exploratory trial compared amantadine (100–300 mg/day) versus ropinirole (0.5–2 mg/day) over 12 weeks in 46 Indian adults with moderate-to-severe RLS (IRLS >10). Both drugs produced significant reductions in RLS severity, sleep disturbance, and quality-of-life impairment, with comparable IRLS scores through week 8; from week 10 onward, ropinirole was significantly superior (week-12 IRLS: 17.0 ± 5.7 vs. 9.0 ± 4.4, p<0.001), and also showed greater improvements in ISI and RLS-QOL at week 12. Ropinirole was better tolerated, with fewer adverse events and no treatment discontinuations due to side effects, compared to two discontinuations in the amantadine group.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IRLS score data at intermediate timepoints (weeks 2, 4, 6, 8, 10) appear only in Figure 3 with no numeric values in text or tables — these were set to not_reported. The ITT and per-protocol analyses use different n values; ITT baseline data (n=19/18) are from Table 1, while per-protocol ISI/RLS-QOL week-12 data (n=15/15) are from Table 2; these were captured in separate arm_results entries where identifiable. The between-group IRLS p-value at week 12 was stated as p<0.001 (text: 'amantadine vs ropinirole: 17.0±5.7 vs 9.0±4.4; P<0.001') — mean difference of 8.0 was calculated. For ISI, the paper reports p=0.001 in the abstract and p=0.01 in Table 2; the Table 2 value (0.01) was used. The SE reported for CGI-I Mann-Whitney U test (SE=23.05) was placed in the SE field of between_group_effects. CGI-I individual arm medians/distributions not reported. Per-protocol baseline IRLS values for both arms also captured as separate arm_results rows (n=15 each). summary: This 52-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled and active-comparator trial (N=731) compared pregabalin 300mg/day versus pramipexole (0.25mg or 0.5mg/day) or placebo in adults with moderate-to-severe primary RLS. At 12 weeks, pregabalin significantly reduced IRLS scores vs. placebo (mean difference -4.5 points, p<0.001) and was superior to both doses of pramipexole on IRLS at 12 and 52 weeks; at 52 weeks, pregabalin was associated with significantly lower augmentation rates than pramipexole 0.5mg (2.1% vs. 7.7%, p=0.001), though not vs. 0.25mg pramipexole (5.3%, p=0.08). Pregabalin showed superior sleep maintenance outcomes (waking after sleep onset, quality of sleep, awakenings, total sleep time) compared to pramipexole, while pramipexole showed greater reduction in sleep latency.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The IRLS score at 12 weeks is reported as an average over the first 12 weeks (mixed model), not a single endpoint measurement. 2. The between-group CIs for IRLS comparisons of pregabalin vs pramipexole are reported as 97.5% CI (not 95% CI) due to the noninferiority testing framework; only the upper boundary was reported. 3. Placebo arm was re-randomized at 12 weeks, so placebo data is only available at baseline and 12 weeks. 4. CGI-I data at 52 weeks was only reported as percentages without n_analyzed. 5. Per-arm n_analyzed for secondary outcomes (sleep, QoL, limb pain) was not reported in the paper. 6. The p<0.001 values were reported as thresholds, not exact values. 7. Figure 1 shows longitudinal IRLS and CGI-I trajectories at intermediate timepoints (26 weeks), but only specific numeric values from Table 2 and text were extracted. 8. Some serious adverse events occurred in placebo-to-active switch patients (Table 4) and are not included in the primary arm AE counts. 9. Augmentation data at 40 weeks includes only the originally-placebo patients who were re-randomized to active treatment, while 52-week data is for those originally randomized to active treatment.

summary: This small (N=10) exploratory placebo-controlled crossover trial tested ecopipam (25-100 mg/day), a D1/D5 dopamine receptor antagonist, in patients with dopaminergic augmented restless legs syndrome who continued their background dopamine agonist therapy. Ecopipam was well tolerated with sedation as the most common adverse event; no extrapyramidal effects or withdrawal exacerbation were observed. The study was not powered for efficacy, but all exploratory measures (IRLS change of -4.6 vs -2.4 on placebo, CGI improvement in 7/10 vs 4/9, RLS diary hours 10.2 vs 15.0) numerically favored active drug, though none reached statistical significance (all NS), and results were confounded by a substantial carry-over effect.

summary: This single-center parallel-group sham-controlled RCT tested a single session of low-frequency transcutaneous electronic stimulation (3Hz, individualized intensity) versus sham (zero intensity) in 46 adult primary RLS patients in South Korea. The primary outcome was Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) symptom severity assessed over 20 minutes of stimulation; 77.3% of the active group versus 33.3% of the sham group were classified as responders (chi-square p=0.003), and repeated-measures ANOVA showed a significant time-by-group interaction (F=4.441, p=0.031), indicating greater VAS improvement in the active group. No follow-up beyond the acute session was reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) Per-arm VAS values at each of the 4x5-min intervals during and after stimulation are not reported numerically in tables or text — only the ANOVA statistics are given; repeated-measures data are not extractable per timepoint. 2) The sham group responder count in Table 1 appears discrepant: the table lists '5 (33.3%)' but the text states '8 responders (33.3%)' — the text value (8/24=33.3%) is internally consistent; the table appears to contain a typographic error. The text value (8) was used for extraction. 3) Randomization allocation: the paper states 1:1 but 48 patients enrolled and 22 active + 24 sham completed (46 completed), with 2 active and 1 sham withdrawn — implying starting allocation was approximately 24/24, but exact pre-withdrawal allocation per arm is not stated; n_randomized per arm is estimated. 4) Sleep scale and PSG results (N1, N2, total sleep time, etc.) are described as non-significant with the exception of N2, but no numerical values are provided in the text — only the statement that active group showed shorter N2; these could not be extracted. 5) Study duration is a single evening session; no multi-week follow-up was conducted. 6) Adverse events are not formally reported.

summary: This open-label crossover trial compared gabapentin (200 mg post-hemodialysis) versus levodopa (125 mg nightly) over 4 weeks each, with a 2-week washout, in 14–15 hemodialysis patients with RLS in Turkey. Gabapentin produced a statistically superior reduction in RLS severity (median score 3 vs. 10 for levodopa vs. baseline 17; p<0.001) and was effective in all patients versus 13 of 14 for levodopa. Gabapentin also significantly outperformed levodopa on SF-36 body pain, social function, and general health subscales, and on PSQI sleep quality, sleep latency, and sleep disturbance (all p<0.001), though per-arm numeric data for sleep outcomes were not reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This is a crossover RCT; baseline values in Table 3 (SF-36 subscales) are shared between arms and reported once — they were assigned to both arms for extraction purposes. 2. Per-arm numeric data (means/SDs) for PSQI sleep subscale outcomes (sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep disturbance, sleep duration) are not reported in the paper — only p-values are given in the text. 3. The RLS rating scale uses medians (not means) with only min/max reported; no IQR was given. 4. The between-group p-value for sleep disturbance is reported in the paper as 'p<0.000', which is likely a typographic error for p<0.001. 5. The study notes RLS symptoms recurred immediately on drug discontinuation, suggesting no meaningful post-treatment follow-up period. 6. Total duration calculated as 4 weeks treatment 1 + 2 weeks washout + 4 weeks treatment 2 = 10 weeks. 7. Levodopa improved body pain (p=0.002) and improved sleep quality (p<0.001), sleep latency (p<0.001), and sleep duration (p=0.014) vs. baseline — these within-arm p-values are stated but no numeric scores are given for levodopa sleep outcomes. 8. SF-36 subscales not reported as significantly different (physical function, role-physical, role-emotional, mental health, energy/vitality) are omitted as no data were provided.

summary: This single-arm pre-post pilot study examined the effects of an 8-week gentle Iyengar yoga program (2 classes/week plus home practice) on RLS symptoms, sleep, mood, and perceived stress in 10 community-dwelling women with moderate-to-severe RLS. Participants showed a significant 49% mean decline in IRLS total score (21.1 to 10.8, p=0.01) and a 62% reduction in overall symptom severity (4.7 to 1.8, p=0.0006), with large effect sizes (Cohen's d 1.6–2.2); significant improvements were also observed in sleep quality, mood, and perceived stress. However, the absence of a control group means these findings cannot exclude placebo effects or natural disease progression as contributing factors.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post study (not an RCT); the design_type field is set to 'quasi-experimental' and num_arms to 1. The paper reports SE (not SD) throughout Table 3; all variability values placed in 'se' field with 'sd' as null. Between-group effect comparisons are pre-vs-post within the single arm (not true between-group contrasts); effect_source set to 'calculated' for mean differences. The paper reports Cohen's d effect sizes for all outcomes (IRLS total=1.62, severity subscale=1.82, impact subscale=0.88, RLS severity scale=2.16, Sleep Problems Index I=1.27, Sleep Problems Index II=1.62, sleep disturbance=1.09, snoring=0.11, short of breath=0.45, sleep adequacy=-1.66, somnolence=1.09, sleep duration=-0.47, POMS total=0.95, tension-anxiety=0.85, anger-hostility=0.70, vigor=-0.66, fatigue=1.17, confusion=0.63, depression=0.66, PSS=0.99, systolic BP=0.00, diastolic BP=0.02, heart rate=-0.01) but these are within-group pre-post effect sizes, not between-group SMDs; they are not extracted into the between_group_effects fields to avoid conflating them with between-group comparisons. N for BP outcomes appears to be 9 or fewer based on the trailing decimal (83.89 diastolic suggests n=9 averaged), but paper states n=10 completers; leaving n_analyzed=10. The RLS severity scale category data (binary outcome showing 90% none-mild post) is noted but not separately extracted as a binary outcome object to keep extraction concise; the ordinal scale continuous data in outcome_id 4 captures the same measure. The paper states IRLS score SE at baseline for completers was 2.01 in Table 2 but BMI SE is 2.28/2.3 in text; slight discrepancies in text vs table rounding noted but values taken from Table 3 as authoritative.

summary: This post hoc analysis of a double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT evaluated cannabidiol (CBD, 75-300 mg/day orally for 12 weeks) versus placebo for RLS/WED symptom severity in 18 patients with Parkinson's disease and REM sleep behavior disorder. The primary outcome, IRLSSG rating scale score, showed no significant difference between groups across follow-up (ANOVA interaction p=0.869), and no secondary outcomes (sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, quality of life, polysomnography variables) differed significantly between arms. The study was substantially underpowered due to small sample size and was not designed primarily to evaluate RLS.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm means and SDs for all outcome measures (IRLSSG, PDSS, PSQI, ESS, PDQ-39, sleep diary variables, polysomnography variables) across all timepoints are reported only in Supplementary Tables S1-S5, which were not provided in the paper text — thus all arm_results values are null with result_source 'not_reported'. The IRLSSG primary outcome data appears only in Figure 1 as a box-and-whisker plot with no tabulated values in the main text. The interaction p-value of 0.869 for the primary outcome is explicitly stated in the text. The placebo group had a significant nocebo effect at week 4 (per Supplementary Table S5, not available). Baseline imbalances in levodopa dose (CBD: 916.67 mg vs placebo: 637.5 mg, p=0.037) and Hoehn-Yahr stage (p=0.018) are noted. The study is a post hoc analysis of a trial registered as RBR-5fwhf7.

summary: This was a 12-week parallel-group pilot feasibility RCT comparing Iyengar yoga (n=19) to an educational film program (n=22) in 41 adults with moderate-to-severe RLS. Overall retention was 73% (below the pre-specified 80% benchmark), but among completers, class attendance exceeded 80% in both arms and homework log completion was 100% in both groups, with no serious adverse events. The study was primarily a feasibility and acceptability trial; RLS symptom and sleep quality outcomes were not reported in this paper but were published separately, and both programs were deemed acceptable to participants based on high satisfaction ratings.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper reports only feasibility and acceptability outcomes; clinical outcomes (RLS symptom severity, sleep quality, mood, quality of life) measured with validated instruments such as the IRLS scale are explicitly stated to be reported in a separate companion paper (Innes et al., J Clin Sleep Med 2020;16:107-119, reference 41). No per-arm means or SDs for clinical outcomes are available in this paper. The paper reports age as mean ± SE (not SD) — SE values used throughout. The exact n_analyzed for yoga schedule preference questionnaire items is not specified in the text; values are presumably from all completers. Withdrawal reasons by arm are not individually disaggregated in the text (only totals by reason category across both arms combined), though 3 non-completers came from each arm before attending any classes. summary: This single-blind RCT (n=35 completers) tested acupuncture (12 sessions over 4 weeks at leg acupoints) versus sham acupuncture (seed patches at nonacupoints) in hemodialysis patients with moderate-to-severe RLS. Acupuncture significantly reduced IRLSRS scores compared to sham at post-treatment (mean difference −2.9 points by GEE, p<0.001) and at 1-week follow-up (−1.3 points, p=0.003), and also significantly improved ISI insomnia scores at post-treatment (−1.5 points, p=0.006). Acupuncture also significantly increased parasympathetic HF% and reduced sympathetic LF% compared to sham at post-treatment (p=0.021), suggesting autonomic modulation as a possible mechanism.

summary: This parallel-group RCT randomized 24 haemodialysis patients with uraemic RLS to 6 months of intradialytic progressive aerobic exercise (cycling at 60-65% max capacity, 3x/week) versus no-resistance cycling (active control). Progressive exercise training reduced IRLS severity scores by approximately 58% (from 25.4 to 10.7) versus a non-significant reduction in controls (22.0 to 18.3), with a statistically significant between-group difference (p=0.017); depression scores and sleep quality also improved significantly in the exercise group. The study concluded that systemic training adaptations rather than acute leg movement are responsible for RLS symptom improvement.

summary: This double-blind randomized crossover trial tested oxycodone (mean dose ~15.9 mg/night, titrated to effect) versus placebo over 2-week periods in 11 patients with idiopathic restless legs syndrome (RLS). Oxycodone significantly reduced subjective leg sensations (p<0.009), motor restlessness (p<0.006), and daytime drowsiness (p<0.03) compared to placebo or baseline. Polysomnographic measures also significantly improved on oxycodone: PLMS/hour sleep decreased (p<0.004), sleep efficiency increased (p<0.006), and arousals/hour sleep decreased (p<0.009); 10 of 11 patients preferred oxycodone over placebo.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a crossover design; each patient served as their own control. N=10 for subjective outcomes (patient #4 excluded due to incomplete data); N=9 for most polysomnographic outcomes excluding PLMS/hour sleep and arousals (patients #1 and #6 had <15 min sleep at baseline or placebo and were excluded from PLMS-related and arousal indices); N=11 for sleep efficiency, sleep latency, %REM, and %stage 3&4. No SDs are reported for any outcome — only group means and p-values from Friedman nonparametric test with post-hoc Wilcoxon signed rank. The subjective rating scale is described as '1-4' in the abstract but '0-4' in the methods; patient data in Table 1 includes zeros, confirming the 0-4 range. Patient-level data is available in both tables for all outcomes. Oxycodone mean dose for polysomnographic phase (15.9 mg/day) differs from subjective rating phase (11.39 mg/day) as they represent different averaging periods. Total study duration estimated as ~10 weeks: 2 weeks baseline PSG + 2 weeks titration phase 1 + 2 weeks phase 1 PSG + approximately 0.5 weeks taper/washout + 2 weeks titration phase 2 + 2 weeks phase 2 PSG. No carryover analysis reported. Age range stated as 36-74; mean and SD not reported. Paper published ~1993; no DOI confirmed in text — paper_id used is an estimated journal DOI.

summary: This randomized double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial tested a single bedtime dose of L-dopa 100-200 mg plus benserazide in 28 patients with idiopathic (n=17) or uremic (n=11) restless legs syndrome, with each period lasting 4 weeks. L-dopa significantly reduced total PLM count (327 vs 459, p=0.003), PLM index (45 vs 63, p=0.005), and PLM arousal index (42 vs 56, p=0.020) by polysomnography, with the benefit concentrated in the first 4 hours of sleep; subjective sleep quality (4.9 vs 3.0, p=0.002) and quality of life also improved significantly. The drug was well tolerated in both RLS subtypes, with only minor adverse events (headache, dry mouth, GI symptoms) more frequent on L-dopa than placebo.

Arm-level baseline demographics are not reported separately per treatment arm as arms are the same patients in a crossover. summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled 3-period crossover trial (n=10) compared clonidine (mean 0.5 mg/day, titrated) versus placebo in patients with idiopathic restless legs syndrome over 2-3 weeks per treatment period. Clonidine significantly reduced subjective paresthesias (p=0.021), motor restlessness (p=0.001), and daytime fatigue (p=0.014), and decreased PSG-measured sleep latency (12 vs 30 minutes, p=0.006). However, clonidine also caused significant adverse effects including a marked reduction in REM sleep (4% vs 16%, p=0.001) and prolonged REM latency (195 vs 70 minutes, p=0.028), and did not improve PLMS, total sleep time, or sleep efficiency.

summary: This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 5 chronic hemodialysis patients with severe RLS tested single nightly doses of controlled-release levodopa/carbidopa 100/25 mg versus placebo over 1 week per arm. Active treatment significantly reduced leg movements per hour of sleep (101.0 vs 61.0, p=0.006), percentage of sleep time with leg movements (15.1% vs 8.6%, p=0.014), and arousals associated with leg movements (209 vs 108, p=0.03), and increased slow-wave sleep (22.8% vs 9.0%, p=0.01). summary: This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled crossover trial tested incremental doses of pergolide (up to 0.25 mg at bedtime) versus placebo in 8 uremic patients on dialysis with severe restless legs syndrome and sleep disturbance. Five of eight patients (62.5%) reported subjective improvement in RLS symptoms and sleep quality on pergolide, and leg EMG activity during the first hour in bed was significantly reduced (20.5% vs 11.9%, p<0.05); however, no statistically significant improvements were seen in leg movement index, percentage of sleep time with leg movements, or any objective sleep architecture measures. The authors concluded that pergolide provided some symptomatic benefit but did not objectively improve sleep continuity or architecture in this small uremic cohort.

summary: This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter crossover trial tested bedtime levodopa/benserazide (100/25 mg or 200/50 mg) versus matched placebo across two 4-week periods in 32 patients with RLS who had both sleep disturbances and polysomnographically confirmed PLMs. Levodopa/benserazide significantly reduced PLMs per hour (26.2 vs 53.0, p<0.0001), increased the proportion of time in bed without limb movements (96.2% vs 92.6%, p<0.0001), and improved subjective sleep quality (p=0.0004), with full efficacy evident from the first dose and symptoms returning immediately upon discontinuation. All three primary outcomes and multiple secondary outcomes (sleep latency, duration, RLS severity, quality of life) showed statistically significant benefit for levodopa/benserazide, while daytime RLS severity was slightly higher on active treatment, suggesting an early augmentation signal.

summary: This 12-week single-arm open-label dose-finding pilot study evaluated cabergoline (a long-acting D1/D2 dopamine agonist, 1–4 mg/day; mean 2.1 mg) in 9 patients with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS who had previously responded insufficiently to levodopa and/or developed augmentation. All patients achieved cabergoline monotherapy by study end, with statistically significant reductions in total PLM count (195.8 to 26.4; p=0.002) and improvements in total sleep time (302.7 to 379.4 min; p=0.018), sleep efficiency (63.1% to 79.1%; p=0.017), and subjective RLS symptom ratings across all time periods. No serious adverse events occurred and no patient withdrew, though the uncontrolled open-label design precludes causal conclusions.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) This is a single-arm pre-post open-label study, NOT an RCT; 'between_group_effects' fields represent within-subject pre-post comparisons (paired t-tests) rather than true between-group comparisons. 2) Table 2 in the original has OCR artifacts in some cells (e.g. 'PLMS arousal' row shows '96449' and '1042.0' which appear to be garbled versions of '9.6±4.9' and '1.0±2.0' based on the text reporting '10.4±7.8 vs 1.0±1.7' for arousal index and '9.6±4.9 vs 1.0±2.0' for awakenings — values extracted from text-reported means and best interpretation of table). 3) The 'PLMS awakening' table row shows baseline mean 9.6 (SD 4.9) and week 12 mean 1.0 (SD 2.0) based on OCR interpretation; the abstract reports '10.4±7.8 vs 1.0±1.7 (p=0.001)' which corresponds to the PLMS arousal index, not awakenings — there is some ambiguity. 4) Quality of life data (Hamburger Visual Analogue Scale) is reported only in figures with no numeric table values — not extractable. 5) Patient Global Impression severity and improvement scores are reported categorically (counts per category) rather than as means/SDs. 6) The paper_id provided does not correspond to the DOI of this article; the article appears to be from Sleep Medicine journal circa 2000. 7) RLS duration in years: mean 23.1±13.7, range 5–47 years. 8) PLMS index baseline SD in table reads '£10.8' (=±10.8); week 12 reads '1542.3' likely garbled '1.5±2.3'. 9) PLMW index week 12 reads '6949.8' likely garbled '6.9±9.8'. 10) Some restlessness/sleep diary values at baseline appear duplicated between outcome_id 13 and 16 (both 4.9±4.3 / 0.4±0.7, p=0.02) — this is consistent with the paper reporting the same metric in two sections (subjective ratings and sleep diary).

summary: This single-blind, open-label, single-arm pre-post study evaluated cabergoline (0.5–2 mg/day, mean 1.1 mg) in 12 patients with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS naive to dopaminergic therapy, with a 1-week placebo run-in followed by 2 months of active treatment. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post study, not a true RCT; the 'placebo arm' is a 1-week run-in period, not a concurrent control group. Arm_id=2 represents the placebo run-in phase (T0) which is the same patients before active treatment. The baseline IRLSSG score is reported as both 23.4±4.4 (for all 12 patients, results section) and 24.3±4.4 (for 10 completers at T0 re-labeled as 'B' in the abstract/figure); both values extracted where applicable. CGI data are reported only descriptively (shift from 'no change/minimally improved' to 'much improved/very much improved') with no numeric values. Actigraphic data appear in Figure 2 but numeric values are also stated in the text, so result_source is 'verbatim'. No PSG data were collected post-treatment. summary: This open-label single-arm multicenter study enrolled 302 idiopathic RLS patients from 37 German centers to assess the 26-week safety and efficacy of cabergoline (median dose 1.5 mg/day once daily). Cabergoline produced significant improvements in all RLS symptom domains: the IRLS total score decreased from 26.8 to 9.7 (mean change -17.2 ± 10.2, p<0.0001), and 68.1% of patients achieved ≥50% symptom reduction, with 23.3% becoming symptom-free. Drug-related adverse events occurred in 48% of patients (most commonly nausea 16.6%), were predominantly mild and transient, emerged mainly in the first 4 weeks, and led to premature dropout in 39 patients (12.9%); augmentation criteria were noted in only 3% of patients, suggesting a low risk with long-term cabergoline therapy.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm open-label study with no control/placebo arm; therefore no between-group effects can be extracted. All p-values represent within-arm pre-post comparisons using paired t-tests with LOCF. The 'n_any_ae' of 238 for any AE was calculated from the text statement that 78.8% of 302 patients experienced at least 1 AE (0.788 × 302 ≈ 238). The distinction between 'patients with AE' (302 safety population) and 'patients with drug-related AE' (146, 48.3%) is maintained. The paper states IRLS baseline was 26.8 ± 5.9 in both Table 1 (safety population, n=302) and Table 6 (efficacy population, n=301); Table 6 values used for outcome extraction. Intermediate timepoints (weeks 4, 8, 12, 16, 20) were assessed per protocol but only graphically displayed (Figure not reproduced in text); numeric data for intermediate timepoints not available in text/tables. RLS-6 scale direction: severity items 0–10 (higher=worse); quality of sleep 1–7 (higher=better). The paper notes effect sizes > 1.0 for severity ratings but does not provide Cohen's d values explicitly.

summary: This 12-week double-blind, placebo-controlled parallel-group RCT (RESET PLM) evaluated ropinirole (0.25–4.0 mg/day, mean 1.8 mg/day) versus placebo in 65 adults with RLS and PSG-confirmed PLMS at 15 US centers. Ropinirole significantly reduced the primary endpoint of PLMS per hour (48.5 to 11.8 vs. 35.7 to 34.2 with placebo; adjusted treatment difference −27.2, 95% CI −39.1 to −15.4, p<0.0001) and key secondary endpoints including PLMA/hour, PLMW/hour, sleep latency, and Stage 2 sleep. Subjective sleep adequacy on the MOS Sleep Scale was also significantly improved with ropinirole (adjusted difference 12.1, 95% CI 1.1–23.1, p=0.032), though IRLS total score and most other MOS domains did not reach statistical significance, likely reflecting insufficient power for subjective endpoints.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. summary: This was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled 2-period crossover trial (n=38 mITT=34) evaluating XP13512 (gabapentin enacarbil) 1800 mg/day for 14 days in treatment-naive adults with moderate-to-severe primary RLS. XP13512 significantly reduced IRLS total score at Day 14 compared with placebo (mean change -12.1 vs -1.9, p<0.0001) and also significantly improved PSG-measured sleep architecture including reduced stage 1 sleep and increased slow-wave sleep. The drug was generally well tolerated, with somnolence (30.6%) and dizziness (27.8%) as the most common adverse events, and no serious adverse events were reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) This is an RLS trial, not a Long COVID trial — all Long COVID-specific fields (long_covid_definition, min/max_time_since_infection, percent_previously_hospitalized, percent_vaccinated, comorbidities, required_symptoms for COVID) are null/not applicable. 2) Crossover design: arm assignments refer to treatment sequence groups at baseline (Sequence 1: XP13512 first n=21; Sequence 2: Placebo first n=17), but all efficacy analyses are pooled across periods; per-arm results therefore represent pooled treatment-period data for n=34 analyzable subjects per treatment. 3) Several PSG outcomes (latency to sleep stages, latency to persistent sleep) had no significant treatment differences (all adjusted p=1 after Holm-Bonferroni); their baseline and change values are in Table 3 and extracted in this JSON. 4) Sleep architecture (stage 1, stage 3/4) change-from-baseline SDs are extracted from the abstract (text only) as these were the only verbatim values available; full table data were not provided for sleep architecture. 5) PLM figures (Figure 4) appear to contain individual subject data; mean/SD for PLMI, PLMSI, PLMSAI, PLMWI are from Table 3. 6) Post-sleep questionnaire outcomes (Table 2) are categorical/ordinal — no continuous means available; these were not included as separate outcome objects but could be derived from Table 2 categorical distributions. 7) The between_group_effects effect_value for the primary outcome (outcome_id=1) is calculated as XP13512 change minus placebo change (-12.1 - (-1.9) = -10.2); the paper reports ANOVA-based LS mean differences which may differ slightly. 8) Total follow-up of 5 weeks calculated as: 14-day baseline/washout + 14-day period 1 + 7-day washout + 14-day period 2 = ~7 weeks total from study start; however treatment duration per arm is 14 days. Follow-up set to 5 weeks (35 days = approx 2 treatment periods + washout). 9) The number of subjects n=36 in the adverse events table (safety population) vs n=34 in efficacy (mITT) reflects the 4 withdrawals. AE table uses n=36 per arm (crossover: each subject received both treatments). 10) Omitted from outcomes array due to output size: latency to stage 1 sleep (p=0.9687), latency to stage 2 sleep (p=0.3982), REM latency (p=0.2152), latency to persistent sleep (p=0.6273), total time in bed change (p=0.5926) — all non-significant and complete data in Table 3.

summary: This single-blind, placebo-controlled RCT examined the acute effects of a single oral dose of pramipexole 0.25 mg versus placebo on sleep architecture and NREM sleep microstructure (cyclic alternating pattern, CAP) in 34 treatment-naive RLS patients (19 pramipexole, 15 placebo). Pramipexole significantly reduced the PLMS index (from 40.2 to 7.9/h; p=0.00013) and improved sleep efficiency (72.1% to 79.4%; p=0.022) and stage 2 sleep percentage (40.3% to 51.2%; p=0.0017), and reduced WASO (p=0.036), while placebo showed no significant changes in any sleep parameter. Despite these benefits on sleep architecture and PLMS, no significant effects of pramipexole were observed on any CAP parameter, indicating that the heightened NREM sleep instability characterizing RLS persists after acute dopaminergic treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an RLS trial, not a Long COVID trial — all Long COVID-specific fields (long_covid_definition, min/max_time_since_infection, percent_previously_hospitalized, percent_vaccinated, comorbidities) are not applicable and set to null. The study also includes a healthy control group (n=13) that did not receive any intervention; baseline comparisons between controls and RLS patients (Tables 1 and 3) are reported in the paper but not extracted as arm-level results since controls were not randomized to treatment. Within-arm p-values (Wilcoxon, paired) for pramipexole vs. placebo within each group are reported in Tables 2 and 4; between-group treatment effects (pramipexole vs placebo arm at treatment night) were not explicitly reported and have been calculated as mean differences from Table 2/4 values. CAP rate during stage 1 sleep in the pramipexole group at baseline shows an unusual SD of 157.99 (verbatim from Table 4), which is likely a data anomaly or typo in the original paper. Additional outcomes from Table 2 not included as separate outcome objects: percentage stage 1 sleep, percentage SWS sleep, percentage REM sleep, TIB, SPT — all were non-significant; their per-arm data are available in Table 2. Additional CAP subtype mean duration outcomes from Table 4 (A1, A2, A3 mean duration in seconds) also not extracted separately but all were non-significant.

summary: This randomized crossover trial compared clonazepam (1 mg h.s.) and temazepam (30 mg h.s.) versus baseline in 10 patients with insomnia associated with nocturnal myoclonus (periodic leg movements during sleep). Both benzodiazepines significantly improved objective sleep parameters including sleep duration, sleep efficiency, and wake time during the night, as well as reducing leg jerks with EEG arousals and awakenings, though neither reduced the total number of leg jerks. No statistically significant differences were detected between clonazepam and temazepam on any outcome, suggesting temazepam is a suitable alternative to clonazepam for this condition.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a 3-condition crossover study (baseline, clonazepam, temazepam) rather than a traditional 2-arm RCT. Arm 3 (baseline/drug-free) is the reference condition; the p-values reported are from one-tailed paired t-tests comparing each drug to baseline (not between-drug comparisons). No direct clonazepam vs. temazepam p-values are reported (only described as non-significant in text). The paper does not report a clearly designated primary outcome; all 13 PSG parameters were co-equal. Outcomes 10, 12, and 13 (arousal-related jerk parameters) were only available for 8 of 10 subjects (those studied at Scripps; the 2 Stony Brook subjects lacked these data). Total study protocol was 30 nights but the follow-up duration in the conventional sense (post-treatment) was not reported as outcome data was collected only during treatment weeks. summary: This single-arm prospective study enrolled 31 patients with moderate-to-severe RLS who received a single IV infusion of 1000 mg ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) and underwent quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) brain MRI at baseline, 6 weeks, and 24 weeks post-treatment. FCM treatment significantly improved RLS symptom severity (IRLS score decreased from 29.7 to 19.5 at 6 weeks, p<0.001), sleep quality (PSQI, ISI), and serum iron parameters. QSM values in the caudate nucleus, putamen, and pulvinar thalamus changed significantly over the three timepoints (p=0.035, 0.048, and 0.032, respectively); caudate nucleus QSM increase at 6 weeks was inversely correlated with IRLS improvement (r=-0.466, p=0.011), and pulvinar thalamus QSM change was positively correlated with IRLS change (r=0.361, p=0.050), providing neuroimaging evidence linking IV iron treatment to brain region-specific iron changes associated with clinical improvement in RLS.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is not an RCT — it is a single-arm prospective cohort study with a healthy control group that only underwent baseline assessment (no treatment). The paper_id in the request does not match this paper's actual DOI (the paper appears to be published in Sleep Medicine, not Sleep). The 'between_group_effects' entries for most outcomes represent within-subject pre-post comparisons (t1 vs t0, t2 vs t0, t2 vs t1), not between-group comparisons in the standard RCT sense. summary: This open-label extension study evaluated 24 weeks of tonic motor activation (TOMAC) — a wearable peroneal nerve stimulation device — in 44 adults with medication-refractory moderate-to-severe primary RLS, compared to 59 controls receiving standard of care. summary: The RESTFUL study was a multicenter, double-blind, sham-controlled RCT of the TOMAC device (bilateral transcutaneous peroneal nerve stimulation) in 133 adults with medication-refractory moderate-to-severe RLS over 4 weeks (stage 1) followed by 4 weeks of open-label treatment (stage 2). The device was well-tolerated with predominantly mild, transient adverse events, and improvements continued to grow during open-label stage 2, supporting TOMAC as a safe and efficacious option for this refractory population.

summary: This preclinical animal study used iron-deficient (ID) rats as an animal model of restless legs syndrome (RLS) to investigate the role of histamine H3 receptors (H3R) in RLS pathophysiology and test the H3R antagonist thioperamide as a potential treatment. Thioperamide dose-dependently decreased periodic leg movements in sleep (PLMS) in both control and ID rats without altering sleep architecture (wake, SWS, or REM time), while the H3R agonist alpha-methylhistamine increased PLMS in control rats but had no effect in ID rats. Striatal H3R protein levels were highest in ID rats and positively correlated with PLMS index (R2=0.6, p<0.01, n=24), and declined with iron replacement, suggesting striatal H3R overexpression contributes to RLS-like motor hyperactivity and that H3R antagonists may be a candidate treatment for RLS.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a preclinical animal study (rat model of RLS), NOT a human clinical trial. The paper does not contain a human participant population, Long COVID definition, or standard RCT elements (randomization, allocation concealment, blinding). Most quantitative outcome data (means, SDs) are presented only in figures (Figures 1-5) and not extracted in the text or tables, so per-arm means/SDs cannot be extracted and are set to null throughout with result_source='not_reported'. Statistical results for between-group effects are reported as significance thresholds (p<0.001, p<0.05) from one-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc rather than exact p-values or effect sizes with CIs. The study uses a within-animal crossover design for drug injections (doses 2 days apart, drug types 1 week apart) in n=7 per group (control vs ID). A separate group of n=4 per iron-replacement week subgroup (IR1-IR4) was used for western blot and hematocrit measurements. The Pearson correlation coefficients (R2=0.6 for H3R vs PLMS; R2=-0.65 for H3R vs hematocrit) are explicitly stated in text. Arms as modeled here reflect distinct experimental groups/conditions rather than parallel treatment arms in the clinical trial sense. RoB2 assessment is not formally applicable to animal studies but is completed conceptually given study limitations. All quantitative outcome values are in figures only.

summary: This single-center RCT in China compared a novel acupuncture protocol (HTDRAS Acupuncture targeting Du and Ren meridians) versus conventional acupuncture in 66 adults with RLS and comorbid anxiety, treated daily for 4 weeks. The HTDRAS group showed significantly greater reductions in IRLS scores (7.09 vs 9.79, p=0.004) and HAMA anxiety scores (7.21 vs 10.33, p=0.006), as well as greater increases in serum 5-HT levels (374.76 vs 360.73 ng/mL, p=0.036) compared to conventional acupuncture. Overall clinical efficacy (total effective rate) was also significantly higher in the HTDRAS group (93.94% vs 81.82%, p=0.024), though both interventions produced meaningful symptom improvement.

summary: This uncontrolled prospective pilot study tested evening use of pneumatic sequential compression devices (SCDs) worn for ~1 hour daily in 10 adults with confirmed RLS at a military sleep clinic. Of the 9 patients who tolerated therapy, all showed improvements in RLS severity (mean score 24 to 8, p=0.001), daytime sleepiness (ESS 12 to 8, p=0.05), and all four RLS-QLI quality-of-life domains (p=0.003 to 0.05), with complete symptom resolution in 3 of 9 (33%). summary: This 12-week multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial tested twice-daily ropinirole (0.5–6.0 mg/d) versus placebo in 359 adults with primary RLS and late-afternoon/early-evening symptom onset (IRLS >= 20). summary: This phase 2b, 14-day, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 95 treatment-naive adults with moderate-to-severe primary RLS to evaluate gabapentin enacarbil (GEn) at 1200 mg or 600 mg once daily versus placebo. summary: This open-label, single-arm pre-post study examined 10 patients with severe RLS who received cabergoline (titrated to 2 mg/day) for 90 days, with TMS measurements of cortical silent period (cSP) and IRLSSGRS clinical ratings at baseline, 14 days, and 90 days, compared to 7 healthy controls. Cabergoline produced significant clinical improvement in IRLSSGRS scores at both 14 days (p=0.0002) and 90 days (p=0.0001), and normalized the initially shortened cSP at 14 days (p=0.007), though cSP tended to shorten again by day 90 (p=0.06) while clinical symptoms continued to improve. There was no significant correlation between cSP duration and clinical severity, suggesting cSP normalization is not the primary mechanism of symptom relief.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is NOT an RCT — it is a non-randomized, open-label, single-arm pre-post study with a separate healthy control comparison group that received no treatment. IRLSSGRS figure (Figure 2) shows data for n=7 evening measurements only; exact means and SDs for IRLSSGRS at days 14 and 90 are only in figures and not tabulated in text, so numeric endpoint values for those timepoints are not_reported. The RMT morning data in Table 1 uses the same values for morning and evening at each timepoint (both labeled 62/63/63% and 63/64% respectively) — extracted as given. summary: This open-label, 2-period crossover RCT (n=40 hemodialysis patients with RLS, Iran, 2022) compared valerian 530 mg vs gabapentin 100 mg, each given nightly for 1 month with a 1-month washout. Both treatments significantly reduced RLS severity and improved sleep quality within groups; gabapentin produced a significantly greater reduction in RLS score than valerian in Period 1 (mean difference in change ~3.94 points, p=0.027) and this difference was confirmed by the generalized linear mixed model treatment effect (p=0.01), while no significant between-group difference was found for sleep quality (p=0.31), suggesting valerian is comparable to gabapentin for improving sleep but inferior for RLS symptom reduction.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a crossover trial. arm_id=1 represents the 'valerian' treatment condition and arm_id=2 represents the 'gabapentin' treatment condition across both sequences. The paper states Kolmogorov-Smirnov test confirmed normality (noted as p<0.05 which may be a typo — normal data typically shows p>0.05 on K-S; this may mean the distribution was NOT rejected as non-normal). summary: This secondary analysis of a double-blind RCT compared carbamazepine (n=84) versus placebo (n=90) in 174 patients with restless legs syndrome over 5 weeks, focusing on discriminating responders from non-responders within the carbamazepine arm.
