subgroup_analyses.variable: Prior dopaminergic drug exposure (pre-treated vs. drug-naive)
subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: Change in IRLS sum score (placebo response)
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: In SP790, pre-treated placebo patients showed a negative slope (response decreased as baseline severity increased; slope -0.43) versus a positive slope in drug-naive patients (slope 0.28; P=0.027). In SP792, slopes were parallel (P=0.84) but the adjusted placebo response was smaller in pre-treated patients (6.31 vs. 10.49; P=0.0089). Rotigotine responses did not differ significantly between subgroups in either study.

subgroup_analyses.variable: Prior dopaminergic drug exposure (pre-treated vs. drug-naive)
subgroup_analyses.outcome_name: Change in IRLS sum score (rotigotine response, regression slope on baseline)
subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Rotigotine-related response slopes did not differ significantly between pre-treated and drug-naive patients for most doses in both SP790 (P=0.50 overall) and SP792 (P=0.53 overall), with the exception of rotigotine 3 mg in SP792 where the slope was steeper in drug-naive patients (1.19 vs. 0.41; P=0.024), though the average response at 3 mg was similar (P=0.24).

summary: This is a secondary analysis of two large multi-centre RCTs (SP790 in Europe and SP792 in USA) examining rotigotine transdermal patch versus placebo for moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS, focusing on whether prior dopaminergic drug exposure modifies placebo and active treatment responses. In both trials, patients pre-treated with dopaminergic medications showed smaller placebo-induced IRLS improvements compared to drug-naive patients (SP790: diverging regression slopes, P=0.027 at high severity; SP792: adjusted mean response 6.31 vs. 10.49, P=0.0089), while rotigotine responses were generally similar between the two subgroups. The findings suggest that pre-treatment blunts the placebo response without suppressing the active treatment response, potentially overestimating drug efficacy in trials enrolling predominantly pre-treated patients.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a secondary/post-hoc analysis of two RCTs (SP790 NCT00136045 and SP792 NCT00135993), not a primary trial report. The primary trial data for rotigotine arms (means, SDs, Ns per arm per dose) are not fully reported here — only placebo subgroup data (pre-treated vs. drug-naive) and adjusted treatment difference summaries are given. Exact study durations (number of weeks of maintenance) are not stated in this paper (referred to original publications). Table 2 reports regression slopes (not means/SDs) for rotigotine arms by pre-treatment status, and Table 3 reports adjusted treatment differences (rotigotine minus placebo) only for drug-naive patients. Per-arm baseline demographics (age, sex, BMI) are not reported in this secondary analysis. The adjusted mean placebo responses (6.31 vs. 10.49 for SP792) are ANCOVA-adjusted values cited in the text, not raw means from a table. Regression slope data (slope ± SE) are extracted as reported but not as conventional outcome means/SDs. The paper does not report adverse events.

summary: This is an uncontrolled, open-label case series evaluating oral orphenadrine citrate (100 mg nightly) for restless legs syndrome and nocturnal leg cramps in 20 adult ambulatory outpatients (of 32 originally enrolled, with 12 excluded due to gastrointestinal intolerance or non-compliance). Orphenadrine was judged effective as monotherapy or in combination with adjunctive agents (diphenhydramine, quinine, or indomethacin) in 16 of 20 patients (80%) over 3 to 12 months of observation. No control group, randomization, blinding, or validated outcome instruments were used, so these results are subject to substantial placebo and observer bias.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is not an RCT — it is an uncontrolled, single-arm open-label case series with no placebo or comparator group. No quantitative per-arm means, SDs, or validated rating scales are reported; all outcomes are categorical clinician global assessments (excellent/satisfactory). Twelve of 32 enrolled patients (37.5%) were excluded post-enrollment due to adverse effects or unreliable adherence, creating major selection bias. Age ranges but not means are reported (males 53-87, females 24-70). Proportion female calculated as 14/20 = 70%. The 12 withdrawn patients were included in the original 32 screened but excluded from the 20 analyzed. Treatment duration ranged from 3 months to 1 year; 52 weeks used as maximum for follow_up. The paper cites no statistical tests and reports no p-values, CIs, or effect sizes. This study should be considered very high risk of bias and provides only descriptive narrative evidence.

summary: This 1984 randomized double-blind crossover trial in 6 patients with RLS evaluated 1 week each of clonazepam 1 mg nightly, placebo, and vibratory stimulation (120 Hz, sural region). Clonazepam significantly improved subjective sleep quality (t=3.24, p<0.05 vs placebo) and leg dysaesthesia (t=2.91, p<0.05 vs placebo; t=3.63, p<0.05 vs vibration), while leg jerking was not significantly affected by any treatment. Vibratory stimulation showed some subjective improvement but no statistically significant benefit on any outcome, and 5 of 6 patients preferred clonazepam for future treatment.

summary: This open-label pre-post study examined the effect of 4 weeks of cabergoline (titrated to 2.0 mg/day) on motor cortex excitability in 14 primary RLS patients compared to 15 age-matched healthy controls, both receiving the same drug, using transcranial magnetic stimulation. At baseline, RLS patients had significantly reduced short-latency intracortical inhibition (SICI: 74.8% vs 43.8% in controls, p=0.033), and after 4 weeks of cabergoline, SICI in RLS patients improved significantly toward normal levels (74.8% to 52.5%, p=0.046), while other TMS parameters and control subjects' measures were unaffected. The authors conclude that cabergoline reverses cortical hyperexcitability in RLS, providing neurophysiological evidence for dopaminergic dysfunction in the condition, though the absence of a placebo arm limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study is NOT a randomized controlled trial — it is an open-label pre-post study where all participants (both RLS patients and healthy controls) received active cabergoline. There is no placebo arm. The paper describes the investigators as blinded to subject status (RLS vs control) but not blinded to treatment. The study design fields have been completed as accurately as possible given this non-RCT design. Sample sizes after dropout are inferred (12 RLS completers, 13 control completers) based on the statement that 2 patients and 2 controls withdrew, though the paper does not explicitly state final analyzed N in the table. The F-value for between-group SICI comparison [F(2,84)=13.8] and within-group pre-post comparison [F(2,84)=8.6] are reported verbatim. The IRLS score is mentioned as an inclusion criterion (>=15) but no IRLS outcome data are reported. Disease duration mean 8.2 ± 5.8 years is reported for RLS patients only. A histogram (Figure 1) shows SICI data but all values are also given in Table 1 text, so no figure-only data issue. The paper is primarily a neurophysiology study, not a clinical outcomes trial — no patient-reported outcomes, sleep measures, or RLS symptom severity scores were extracted as outcomes.

summary: This preclinical animal study tested 4 weeks of daily intraperitoneal pramipexole (0.125 mg/kg) versus saline vehicle in spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR), an established animal model of RLS-like sleep disturbances. Pramipexole significantly improved total sleep time (94.53 vs 62.0 min, p=0.01), sleep efficiency (79.03% vs 54.08%, p=0.02), REM sleep (19.58% vs 11.02%, p=0.03), number of awakenings (15.0 vs 22.5 events, p=0.02), and wakefulness (20.95% vs 46.17%, p=0.01) compared to controls. Limb movement events trended toward reduction in the PPX group but did not reach statistical significance (p=0.29); PTPRD gene and protein expression changes were non-significant though a trend toward increased spinal cord PTPRD protein was observed in the treated group.

summary: This single-blind parallel-group RCT (n=46) evaluated whether adding 10 sessions of conventional TENS to low-dose pramipexole (0.25 mg/day) provided additional benefit over pramipexole alone in treatment-naive adults with severe primary RLS. Both groups showed significant improvements in IRLSRS symptom severity and PSQI sleep quality scores from baseline to end of treatment and at 8-week follow-up; however, the combination group demonstrated a significantly greater overall treatment effect (IRLSRS group-time interaction p=0.033; PSQI p=0.019), with the TENS group achieving notably lower IRLSRS scores at 8-week follow-up (mean 7.82 vs 14.21) and PSQI scores below the clinical cut-off for poor sleep quality (mean 4.14 vs 7.17). The findings suggest that TENS combined with low-dose pramipexole produces clinically meaningful and sustained improvements in RLS symptom severity and sleep quality compared with pramipexole monotherapy.

risk_of_bias.key_concern: This is a retrospective observational study without randomization or control group — the primary comparison is between sexes (not treatment vs. placebo), and the study design cannot be adequately evaluated under RoB2 (designed for RCTs); allocation to pramipexole vs. ropinirole was non-random, there was no placebo group, and convenience sampling limits generalizability.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Females showed significantly greater reduction in PLMS index on treatment night (mean 3.9 vs 17.3 n/h; p=0.0045 after Bonferroni correction, Cohen's d=0.848) and a significantly greater percentage change from baseline (89.2% vs 66.0%; p=0.002).
Females had significantly lower total LMS index on treatment night (15.7 vs 32.1 n/h; p=0.0031, Cohen's d=0.920).
Females had significantly lower periodicity index on treatment night (0.178 vs 0.396; p=0.003, Cohen's d=0.966) and greater percent reduction (73.6% vs 45.4%; p=0.0044).
Supplementary analysis (Table S1) showed substantially similar sex differences in leg movement parameters separately for pramipexole and ropinirole groups, supporting pooling of the two drug groups.

summary: This retrospective observational study investigated sex differences in the acute response to dopamine agonists (pramipexole 0.25 mg or ropinirole 0.5 mg, single oral dose) in 41 drug-free RLS patients (26 female, 15 male) using two consecutive overnight polysomnography recordings. The primary finding was that females showed significantly greater reduction in PLMS index, total LMS index, and periodicity index on the treatment night compared to males (all p<0.005 after Bonferroni correction, Cohen's d > 0.8), suggesting higher acute dopaminergic responsiveness of periodic leg movements in females. Subjective symptom severity (VAS) improved substantially in both sexes without significant sex-based difference, highlighting a discordance between objective PSG and subjective outcomes.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is NOT an RCT — it is a retrospective observational pre-post study with sex as the primary comparison variable, not a randomized comparison of active vs. control. The study lacks a placebo arm, randomization, and blinding. Arms were defined here as female/male groups for data extraction purposes rather than traditional intervention arms. The per-arm structure maps females (arm_id=1) and males (arm_id=2) since that is the primary comparison; the pramipexole/ropinirole split is secondary. Exact n per sex-drug subgroup: pramipexole females=18, pramipexole males=8, ropinirole females=8, ropinirole males=7. Between-group effects are all females vs. males comparisons. VAS data at baseline was reported separately from Table 1 (pramipexole group mean 7.4 SD 1.63; ropinirole group mean 7.1 SD 1.21) and in text (females mean 7.3 SD 1.49; males mean 7.2 SD 1.40). The figure (Figure 1) shows inter-movement interval distributions but numeric data from it cannot be extracted. PLMS duration, SILMS duration, and ISOLMS duration outcomes were not separately extracted as full outcome objects but their data are present in Table 3. Sleep architecture parameters not extracted as full outcomes include: Time in bed, Sleep period time, Total sleep time, Sleep latency, Stage R latency, Stage shifts, Awakenings, Stage N1, Stage N3, Stage R (all in Table 2 with full means and SDs for both sexes at both timepoints). The IRLS rating scale was used for baseline characterization only (females mean 25.1 SD 5.10; males mean 24.1 SD 5.69; NS) and not as a treatment outcome. RoB2 assessment is applied loosely as study is non-randomized; domain judgments reflect the absence of randomization and allocation concealment.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter RCT conducted in Norwegian general practice randomized 174 patients with restless legs syndrome to carbamazepine (up to 300 mg/day) or placebo for 5 weeks. Both groups showed significant improvement in symptom severity and attack frequency, but carbamazepine was significantly more effective than placebo at weeks 3 and 5 (p=0.04 and p=0.03 respectively for attack frequency; symptom severity VAS data presented in figures only). A notable placebo response was observed, and carbamazepine caused more adverse events (34 vs 20 patients) though no serious side effects occurred.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Critical limitation: all quantitative VAS outcome data (symptom severity scores and therapeutic effect scores by arm) are presented ONLY in figures (Fig 1 and Fig 2) with 95% CI bars and median markers — no numerical values are stated in text or tables, making per-arm means/medians and CIs non-extractable. The attack frequency data (Table III) is presented as frequency distributions (counts per category 0-7+ attacks/week) rather than means/medians with SDs, so per-arm summary statistics are not directly extractable. Placebo arm n was calculated as 174 total minus 84 carbamazepine = 90; however Table II shows Placebo n=88 or 89 for different variables, suggesting slight discrepancies in available data per variable. summary: This open-label exploratory study tested intravenous apomorphine (a combined dopamine and opioid agonist) in 9 patients with idiopathic RLS during a modified suggested immobilisation test, using a fixed sequential crossover design: baseline, then apomorphine, then apomorphine+naloxone, then apomorphine+metoclopramide. Apomorphine produced rapid, statistically significant improvements in both subjective RLS symptoms (VAS reduced 54.5%, p=0.011) and objective PLMW index (reduced 98.0%, p=0.012) compared with baseline. Neither naloxone nor metoclopramide significantly reversed these effects, though metoclopramide showed a trend toward PLMW reappearance, suggesting a primarily dopaminergic mechanism.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is NOT a randomized controlled trial — it is an open-label, single-arm, sequential crossover exploratory study (prospective observational design) with a fixed treatment order in all patients. The 'arms' correspond to sequential conditions within the same session for the same 9 patients, not independently randomized groups. All per-arm values reported as mean (SEM), not mean (SD); SE values placed in 'se' field accordingly. The study has no placebo arm. Age reported as mean (SEM) = 55.3 (3.1); SD not provided. Baseline demographics (PSQI=11.9(1.5), ESS=6.2(1.2), duration of RLS=16.3(3.9) years, IRLSSG=27.1(2.2), PLMS/h=32.1(8.2), sleep efficiency=72.4%(5.0)) are overall sample values, not per-arm, since all patients received all conditions. Session duration ranged 3 hours to 4 hours 14 minutes — no weeks-based follow-up applicable. Figure 1 shows bar charts of outcomes already reported in Table 3 (text values extracted from table). Between-group effect mean differences calculated as apomorphine mean minus baseline mean, etc.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post quasi-experimental study with no randomization or control group — not an RCT. The paper_id is assigned from the journal DOI format. The n_analyzed at follow-up was 23 (2 excluded: one took additional medication, one failed to return SF-36). The n_analyzed at baseline and end of therapy is assumed to be 25 (all completers) as stated 'all patients completed the coping therapy programme' and analyses were 'based on data from all participants' with the 2 exceptions only at follow-up. The between_group_effects entries represent within-subject pre-post changes (Wilcoxon signed rank test), not between-arm comparisons — this is a single-arm study. summary: This post hoc pooled analysis of two 12-week double-blind placebo-controlled RCTs (TREAT RLS 1 and TREAT RLS 2; n=540 with evaluable ferritin) examined whether baseline serum ferritin concentration (<50 or >50 µg/L) modifies the response to ropinirole (0.25–4.0 mg/day) in idiopathic RLS. Ropinirole significantly improved IRLS total score and CGI-I responder rate versus placebo in both ferritin subgroups, with virtually identical adjusted mean treatment differences of -2.8 points on the IRLS in each subgroup. The interaction between ferritin concentration and treatment was non-significant for both outcomes (IRLS p=0.72; CGI-I p=0.21), indicating that ropinirole efficacy in idiopathic RLS is independent of baseline iron status.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a short post hoc analysis letter, not a full trial report. Per-arm means, SDs, and Ns for the primary outcomes are not reported in text or tables — quantitative data for IRLS and CGI-I outcomes appear only in Figure 1 as adjusted means with SE bars (IRLS) and percentages (CGI-I), with values not explicitly stated. Subgroup-level between-group effects (AMTD and AOR with 95% CIs and p-values) are reported in the figure caption and were extracted verbatim. The paper pools two original trials (TREAT RLS 1: Trenkwalder et al. 2004; TREAT RLS 2: Walters et al. 2004); full trial-level data must be sought in those primary publications. Ferritin values were added as custom fields in baseline_demographics since the standard schema does not include them. The female/male ratio differed between ferritin subgroups (~3:1 in <50 µg/L vs ~1:1 in >50 µg/L) but overall per-arm sex distributions were not reported.

summary: This nested preliminary RCT embedded within a larger parent trial randomized 20 postmenopausal women with RLS (screening positive on all 4 IRLSSG criteria) to an 8-week gentle Iyengar yoga program (n=10) or an educational film control (n=10), with 18 completing final assessment. Yoga participants demonstrated significantly greater improvements than controls in global sleep quality, multiple PSQI subscales, insomnia prevalence, average sleep duration, state anxiety, perceived stress, total mood disturbance, and both systolic and diastolic blood pressure (all p ≤ 0.05), with large adjusted between-group Cohen's d effect sizes ranging from 1.87 for state anxiety to 2.64 for sleep duration. Despite the very small sample size and lack of RLS symptom severity as a direct outcome measure, these findings suggest yoga may be a promising non-pharmacological intervention for sleep, mood, and cardiovascular outcomes in older women with RLS.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 3 in the paper has severely garbled column layout due to PDF-to-text conversion — pre/post values per arm and SE values were reconstructed by careful parsing of the fragmented numeric rows. The between_group effect sizes reported in the paper are Cohen's d (adjusted for baseline differences), not SMDs per se, but have been placed in the smd field as they are standardized effect sizes. The paper reports yoga pre sleep duration as 5.7 ± 0.5 hours in text (compared to 5.72 ± 0.45 in the table, consistent), and post as 7.3 ± 0.5 hours — table values used as primary. The 2 dropouts were both from yoga arm (health reasons unrelated to yoga), not specified which group in text — paper states 'one non-Hispanic white, one African American' dropped out, and final N is 8 yoga, 10 controls, confirming both dropouts from yoga arm.

summary: This single-blind RCT compared 6 weeks of standard acupuncture (12 traditional acupoints) versus sham acupuncture (12 randomized non-therapeutic points) in 31 patients with severe idiopathic RLS (IRLSRS ≥20). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Critical limitation: all post-baseline outcome data (NA, ESA, IRLSRS, ESS at weeks 2, 4, and 6 for both arms) are presented exclusively in Figure 3 with no accompanying numeric values in text or tables. summary: This parallel randomized controlled trial tested the effect of local warm water compression (40-43°C, 20 min/session, 3x/week for 4 weeks) applied to the gastrocnemius muscles of both legs versus no intervention among 120 critical care nurses in Iran with restless legs syndrome. After 4 weeks, the intervention group showed a significant reduction in IRLS score (from 25.0±5.9 to 19.2±4.0, mean decrease 8.8±3.2) compared to controls (24.2±3.6 to 23.2±4.3, mean decrease 1.0±6.1; p<0.001 between groups), and a significant reduction in MFI fatigue score (from 63.4±6.8 to 59.6±4.4, mean decrease 4.1±6.6) compared to controls (63.4±6.0 to 63.1±5.6, mean decrease 0.3±7.8; p<0.001 between groups). Both primary outcomes reached statistical significance, supporting warm compression as an effective non-pharmacological intervention for RLS and fatigue in critical care nurses.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Note: Table 2 reports the between-group mean difference for RLS as two separate entries: an 'intergroup' comparison at post-intervention (p<0.001) and a 'mean differences' row (intervention: 8.8±3.2, control: 0.98±6.1, p<0.001). I recorded two between_group_effects entries for timepoint_id=2 for RLS: one based on post-intervention endpoint values (difference = 19.2 - 23.23 = -4.03) and one based on mean change-from-baseline values (difference = -8.8 - (-0.98) = -7.82). The same approach was applied to fatigue. The paper states sex/gender of participants but does not report percent female explicitly in the tables — the participant population is described as 'nurses' but no sex breakdown is provided. Demographic table contains a possible data inconsistency: marital status 'Single' shows 49/60 (87.1%) for intervention but 49/60 would be 81.7%, not 87.1% — likely a reporting error in the paper. The RLS baseline SD is reported as 5.89 in text but 5.9 in table; I used 5.9 from the table. Control group age SD is reported as 7.2 in text and 7.2 in table, but table header shows 34.6±7.2 while text says 34.2±7.2 — I used 34.2 (text) as the mean since it appears twice consistently.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Baseline values in Table 1 and 2 are reported as mean with range only (no SDs available for baseline variables). The primary and secondary outcome analysis in Table 3 (dichotomous) and Table 4 (continuous change scores) used different n values (n=8 iron, n=13 placebo for completers) vs baseline n=14 per arm — the paper states ITT analysis but the table footnotes use completers only, suggesting ITT was not fully implemented. AE counts (n=9 patients with events, some with multiple events) are not broken down cleanly per patient; counts likely exceed 9 total events but 9 unique patients. Ranges provided for baseline data rather than SDs, so SD fields left null. The study was clearly designed for RLS, not long-covid — participants/long_covid fields are not applicable and set to null.

summary: This single-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study evaluated a single night of 0.5 mg ropinirole (given as 0.25 mg at 19:00 and 22:30) versus placebo in 12 inpatients with RLS and PLMS confirmed by polysomnography. The primary endpoint, PLM per hour of total sleep time, decreased significantly from 39.7/h under placebo to 10.3/h under ropinirole — a 75% reduction (p<0.01 by Wilcoxon test) — with concurrent significant reductions in total PLM, PLM/h TIB, and PLM during NREM sleep. Ropinirole also significantly reduced PLM-associated arousals (p<0.01) and improved respiratory indices (apnea, AHI, desaturation), though total and spontaneous arousals paradoxically increased under treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This is a crossover study with a FIXED, non-randomized night order (adaptation → placebo → ropinirole); this is described as 'single-blind' crossover but the order was not randomized, creating a serious period-effect confound. 2. The paper does not clearly separate per-arm baseline demographics — all 12 patients underwent both conditions so demographic data is provided once for the whole group. 3. Arousal data in Table 1 includes arousals average frequency change (A:4.1/1.4, P:4.2/1.0, R:4.6/1.2), average duration (A:7.8/0.6, P:7.3/0.9, R:7.3/0.9), arousals with respiratory events, apneas, hypopneas, desaturation, and snoring — these secondary arousal subtypes were extracted in outcomes 13-16 but complete data for all arousal subtypes not included to stay within size. 4. summary: This open-label, single-arm pilot trial in 17 patients with primary RLS (13 previously insufficiently treated with levodopa, 4 treatment-naive) evaluated pramipexole as a single evening dose (mean 0.3 mg, range 0.125–0.75 mg) titrated over a mean of 4.9 days. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an open-label, non-randomized, single-arm before-after study — not an RCT. Table 1 contains garbled rows (patients 3 and 13 merged/split in OCR): row '353' with values '1200, 10 years, 24 months/no 9, 3 0.750' and row '1353' appear to represent patients 3 (age 53/F) and 13 (age 53/F) respectively — individual patient data extracted from narrative. summary: This open-label within-subject crossover study in 10 patients with severe idiopathic RLS evaluated the acute effect of a single oral dose of pramipexole 0.125 mg on RLS symptoms and polysomnographic sleep parameters, comparing the treatment night to the preceding drug-free night. After one night of pramipexole, sensory symptoms (VAS) improved significantly (7.8 to 2.0, p<0.001), periodic limb movements (PLMS, PLMW, PLMA) were all significantly reduced, and sleep microstructure instability (CAP rate) decreased significantly (56.6% to 44.0%, p=0.005). Several macrostructural improvements were also observed including reduced sleep onset latency and SWS latency, increased SWS time, and reduced REM percentage, though pramipexole suppressed REM sleep significantly.

summary: This single-center retrospective observational study evaluated 27 consecutive patients with untreated idiopathic RLS who received open-label dopaminergic therapy (pramipexole, ropinirole, cabergoline, or pergolide) for approximately 2 months. Dopaminergic treatment significantly reduced RLS symptom severity (IRLS: 24.2 to 16.9, p<0.001) and improved excessive daytime sleepiness in the subgroup with EDS at baseline (ESS: 14.5 to 10.2, p=0.007), while the non-sleepy subgroup showed no significant ESS change. The study identifies a clinically meaningful sleepy RLS subgroup with polysomnographic features of hypersomnia (longer TST) who may specifically benefit from dopaminergic treatment for daytime sleepiness, though the absence of randomization or a control group limits causal inference.

Subgroup comparisons (sleepy vs non-sleepy) are observational, not randomized. The table reports means ± SD where '§' = '±' per the notation guide. The SD for ESS at follow-up in the sleepy subgroup was reported as '3' in the table (10.2 § 3) — this has been extracted as sd=3.0. MSLT follow-up data are available for only 3 of 10 sleepy patients. No per-arm n breakdown is possible as this is a single-arm study; subgroup ns (sleepy n=10, non-sleepy n=17) are used where applicable. The p-value for IRLS improvement is reported as p<0.001 (not exact).

summary: This 6-week randomized double-blind dose-response trial evaluated pramipexole at three doses (0.25, 0.5, and 0.75 mg/day) in 154 Japanese patients with primary RLS (mean baseline IRLS score ~22). All three doses produced clinically meaningful and statistically significant reductions in IRLS total score from baseline (adjusted mean changes: -12.3, -12.5, and -11.8, respectively; all 95% CIs excluded 0), with no significant differences between doses. Secondary outcomes (IRLS responder rates 49-60%, CGI-I responder rates 70-77%, PGI responder rates 68-79%, PSQI and JESS improvements) were consistent across all doses, and older age (>=55 years) and lower baseline IRLS score (<21.5) were associated with early complete response at week 2.

Responder rate data at weeks 2 and 6 appear in Figure 2 (image only) without numeric values in text; only week 6 values are available from Table 2. 3) Number of completers per arm not specified; 141/154 (91.6%) overall completed. 4) AE counts for somnolence and nausea are calculated from percentages (e.g., 20.8% of 48 = ~10 for somnolence in 0.25 mg group). 5) The paper states 9 patients withdrew due to AE in the 0.25 or 0.5 mg/day groups combined; individual arm breakdowns not provided. 6) n_withdrawn_due_to_ae for arms 1 and 2 combined is 9 but per-arm split not reported. 7) IRLS responder rates at week 2 for each arm appear only in Figure 2 — numeric values not given in text or tables.

summary: This open-label, randomized crossover pharmacokinetic trial enrolled 24 adults with idiopathic restless legs syndrome to evaluate potential drug-drug interactions between transdermal rotigotine (4 mg/24h) and oral levodopa/carbidopa (100 mg/25 mg twice daily) at steady state. The primary pharmacokinetic parameters (AUCss and Cmax,ss) for levodopa, carbidopa, and rotigotine were essentially identical during monotherapy versus combination treatment, with all geometric mean ratios near unity (range 0.97-1.06) and all 90% confidence intervals within the pre-specified bioequivalence acceptance range of 0.80-1.25. The study concluded that rotigotine transdermal patch and oral levodopa/carbidopa can be coadministered without clinically meaningful pharmacokinetic interactions, and dose adjustments when combining these agents need not account for altered pharmacokinetics.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a pharmacokinetic drug interaction study, not a clinical efficacy trial for RLS symptoms. No RLS-specific clinical outcome measures (e.g., IRLS, PLMS) were assessed. All outcomes are pharmacokinetic biomarker endpoints. The between_group_effects 'effect_measure' field was set to 'odds_ratio' as a placeholder for 'geometric mean ratio' (the ratio of geometric means for combined vs monotherapy) since this field has no dedicated pharmacokinetic ratio option — reviewers should interpret these values as geometric mean ratios (not odds ratios). The 90% CIs reported in tables are 90% CIs (not 95%); they are stored in ci_95_low/ci_95_high fields as the only available CI data. Table values are reported as geometric means with geometric coefficient of variation (%) — SD values are not directly provided and were not calculated. The levodopa AUCss 90% CI was not explicitly stated in Table I for the ratio but the text states 'confidence intervals were within 0.8-1.25'; the Cmax CI (0.90, 1.19) was extracted from Table I. The text also reports arithmetic means ± SD for concentration-time profile descriptions (e.g., levodopa Cmax 1495 ± 691 ng/mL monotherapy, 1493 ± 631 ng/mL combination; carbidopa Cmax 151 ± 52 ng/mL monotherapy, 148 ± 63 ng/mL combination), which differ from the geometric means in Table I. The n_any_ae per arm were estimated from the text percentages (78% of 23 for rotigotine = ~18; 67% of 24 for levodopa/carbidopa = ~16; 87.5% of 24 for combination = 21). This paper is not a clinical efficacy trial for RLS and would not typically be eligible for a meta-analysis of RLS treatment outcomes.

CrCl was the only clinically relevant covariate for CL/F, with approximately 1.6-fold increase in CL/F for every 2-fold increase in CrCl; dose reduction for renally impaired patients is recommended.

summary: This paper presents a population pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PK-PD) analysis of gabapentin exposure following administration of gabapentin enacarbil (GEn) at doses of 300–2400 mg across 12 clinical studies (6 phase 1, 5 phase 2/3 RCTs) in 994 subjects with and without restless legs syndrome (RLS). Gabapentin exposure was dose-proportional and was modeled using a 1-compartment model with zero-order absorption; the primary clinically relevant covariate for clearance was renal function. PK-PD modeling showed dose-dependent improvements in IRLS score (maximum change from baseline -6.2 units by Emax model), increasing probability of CGI-I response (52% for placebo vs 83% for 1200 mg), and improvements in sleep parameters, with dizziness and somnolence/sedation occurring in <5% of subjects at 600 and 1200 mg after the first 2 weeks of titration.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a population PK-PD analysis paper, not a primary RCT report. Per-arm sample sizes, raw means, SDs, and between-group statistical tests are not reported for individual study arms — results are presented as model-predicted values from logistic regression and Emax PK-PD models across pooled phase 2/3 studies. The IRLS Emax maximum effect value of -6.17 (dose model) and -6.16 (AUC model) represent model-predicted maximum effects, not observed treatment differences vs. placebo. CGI-I and pCGI-I response probabilities are model-predicted (logistic regression) for a 70-kg participant. Wake-after-sleep-onset and total sleep time values for 600 mg and 1200 mg arms are Emax model-predicted changes from baseline (not observed means). Dizziness and somnolence/sedation AE rates of 15.3% and 21.2% are pooled across all doses (859 subjects in phase 2/3 studies). BAC composite score showed no relationship with dose or exposure — no numeric results reported. Adverse event counts (131 dizziness, 182 somnolence) are pooled across all active dose arms and cannot be attributed to individual arms. Randomization method and allocation concealment details for individual trials are not described in this analysis paper. The longest study duration was 24 weeks (XP060). Some figure data (Figure 3: IRLS change by dose with CI) could not be extracted numerically. The paper pooled data from 5 phase 2/3 studies with durations of 2, 12, 12, 12, and 24 weeks respectively.

summary: This single-center crossover study in 13 RLS patients (and 10 healthy controls) tested a single session each of low-frequency (1 Hz) rTMS over the primary motor cortex (M1), primary somatosensory cortex (S1), and sham stimulation, separated by 1-week washouts. Exact p-values and per-arm means/SDs for most outcomes were not reported in the text and were presented only in figures, substantially limiting quantitative data extraction.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Critical limitation: virtually all post-intervention quantitative outcome data (VAS scores, rMT, CSP, MEP amplitude, MEP latency, CMCT, peripheral latency) are presented ONLY in figures (Figures 2-5) with no accompanying tables or in-text numeric values (means, SDs, medians, IQRs). Friedman ANOVA and Mann-Whitney p-values are referenced in the text and figure captions as 'significant after Bonferroni correction' but exact p-values are not stated for most comparisons. The study is a crossover with all 13 RLS patients receiving all 3 conditions; arm demographics are identical (not independent groups). The 10 healthy controls also completed all 3 conditions. Note: the paper does not study Long COVID — it is an RLS interventional study; long_covid_definition and related fields are not applicable. The per-arm sample sizes for arms 2 and 3 are inferred (all 13 patients completed all 3 conditions per protocol). Disease duration median 8.8 years (range 2.0-15.0 years) reported but not included in a structured field as it is not a per-arm demographic. summary: This retrospective single-arm before-after study examined the effect of 12 weeks of oral iron supplementation (50-100 mg) in 10 Japanese children aged 6-15 years with reduced serum ferritin (<50 ng/mL) and psychiatric symptoms but without anemia. Serum ferritin increased significantly (25.4 to 58.2 ng/mL, p=0.002), and at 12 weeks there were significant improvements in CGI severity (p=0.039), all POMS-S mood subscales except vigor, and PSQI sleep quality (p=0.016). The study lacks a control group and randomization, limiting causal inference, but suggests that at least 12 weeks of iron supplementation may be necessary to observe psychological benefits in iron-deficient children.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm before-after study, not an RCT; RoB2 domains are assessed in that context. All quantitative outcome data (means and SDs for CGI, POMS-S subscales, PSQI) appear only in Figure 1 with no table or text values provided — only p-values are stated in the figure legend and text. Therefore all arm_results means/SDs are set to null with result_source 'not_reported'. The paper's relevance to RLS is indirect: subjects had iron deficiency and insomnia/psychiatric symptoms, but no cases of RLS were confirmed. The study is included as relevant because RLS is mentioned as a condition managed by iron supplementation and the population overlaps, but no RLS-specific outcome data are extracted.

summary: This pilot single-blind RCT (the CARL Trial, n=39) tested Longden's counterstrain osteopathic manipulation technique for restless legs syndrome, comparing RLS-specific counterstrain (active, n=20) versus non-specific counterstrain of the lower body (sham control, n=19) over four weekly sessions. The primary outcome — change in IRLS total score at 6 weeks — showed a statistically significant between-group difference of 8.06 points (95% CI 3.15–12.96, p=0.0021), representing 42.2% improvement in the active group versus 8.7% in controls. Secondary outcomes of CGI-I and PSOS also significantly favoured the active arm, while sleep loss did not reach significance; no adverse effects attributable to treatment were reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm SDs for IRLS change scores and week-6 IRLS endpoint values are not reported in Table 2; only mean changes and mean endpoint values are given. Baseline SDs for IRLS and sleep loss are available from Table 1. The n_analyzed for Group B in Table 2 is stated as N=18 (one patient with missing IRLS data), and for PSOS the control arm n is inferred as 17 (one patient missing PSOS). CGI-I direction: higher scores on this 6-point improvement scale indicate greater improvement, so higher_is_better=true; paper states Group A mean 3.53 vs Group B 2.68. The sensitivity analysis results (IRLS difference 7.14, 95% CI 2.39–11.89, p=0.0043; PSOS p=0.041; CGI-I p=0.096) are noted in text but not separately extracted as outcomes. Treatment duration was described as four weekly sessions within 9 weeks; the 8-week figure refers to the telephone follow-up for adverse events. Age range for both arms is stated but baseline IRLS range is also given: A 17–32, B 16–35. One patient in Group A (ID 32) withdrew before any treatment and was excluded from week-6 analysis via ITT imputation rules; the ITT analysis for primary outcome used N=19 active, N=18 control.

summary: This 12-week double-blind RCT (RESTORE; NCT01569464) enrolled 150 adults with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS and randomized them 2:1 to rotigotine transdermal patch (1-3 mg/24h) or placebo across 18 US sites. Both primary outcomes — change in IRLS score (rotigotine -14.9 vs. placebo -12.7) and change in m-SIT Discomfort Scale (rotigotine -2.68 vs. placebo -2.62) — improved substantially in both groups, but rotigotine failed to demonstrate superiority over placebo for either measure (p=0.8451 and p=0.8336 respectively). All secondary outcomes including PLMWI, RLS-6 items, sleep scales, and quality of life measures were also non-significant, likely due to an unusually large placebo response (>12 IRLS points) attributed to a high proportion of treatment-naive patients and unbalanced randomization.

summary: This 6-month, 3-arm parallel RCT in 32 hemodialysis patients with uremic RLS compared intradialytic aerobic exercise (n=16) versus low-dose ropinirole 0.25 mg/day (n=8) versus placebo (n=8). Both exercise and ropinirole significantly reduced IRLS scores by approximately 46% and 54% respectively versus a 6% non-significant change in placebo (between-group p=0.012), and both improved depression scores significantly versus placebo (p=0.003). Only ropinirole significantly improved subjective sleep quality versus both exercise and placebo (p=0.016), while exercise uniquely improved physical performance measures and lean body mass within-group, but no body composition or physical performance between-group differences reached statistical significance.

summary: This single-arm open-label extension trial (NCT00498186) enrolled 295 patients with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS who had completed a preceding 6-week double-blind dose-finding trial of rotigotine transdermal patch (0.5-4 mg/24 h), following them for 2 years across 33 centers in Austria, Germany, and Spain. The primary efficacy outcome (IRLS total score) improved markedly from a baseline of 27.8 (±5.9) with a mean reduction of 17.2 (±9.2) points at 2 years in completers (n=190) and 15.4 (±10.3) by LOCF (n=295), with 53% of completers classified as remitters and 30% symptom-free; however, the absence of a control arm and the authors' acknowledgment of a 9.2-point placebo response in the preceding double-blind trial preclude definitive conclusions about treatment effect magnitude. Overall 2-year retention was 64.7%, with a generally favorable tolerability profile dominated by application site reactions, and no deaths or treatment-related serious adverse events were reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm open-label extension trial (no control arm), so no between-group effects are calculable or reported. RLS-6 LOCF values were reported in Table 3 but omitted from individual outcome entries above to reduce size; the as-observed values are extracted. Figures 2 and 3 contain time-course data that could not be precisely extracted (data only in figures for intermediate titration timepoints). The QoL-RLS change at year 2 was noted with a footnote 'a' in the paper (likely indicating statistical significance vs baseline) but no p-value was reported. summary: This nested RCT within a larger cardiovascular risk trial randomized 20 overweight postmenopausal women with RLS (identified by screening from a larger sample of 75) to either an 8-week gentle yoga program (n=10) or an educational film program (n=10). Women in the yoga group showed significantly greater improvement than controls in sleep quality, perceived stress, mood, anxiety, and blood pressure (all p≤0.05), with treatment expectancy adjustment not materially altering results. Among those with insomnia at baseline, 86% of yoga participants vs. 30% of controls achieved normal sleep scores post-intervention (p=0.03), suggesting yoga may be a feasible non-pharmacological intervention for RLS-related sleep and mood disturbances.

summary: This prospective, open-label, single-arm feasibility trial enrolled 20 adults with opioid-treated refractory RLS to test whether adjunctive TOMAC (bilateral peroneal nerve stimulation) could allow iterative opioid dose reduction while maintaining symptom control. Seventy percent of participants (14/20) successfully completed step-down 1, reducing opioid dose by >=20% (mean attempted 32.7%) with a CGI-I score <=5, exceeding the prespecified 50% success criterion. Across all participants, the average maximum well-tolerated opioid dose reduction was 29.9% (SD 23.7%), from 39.0 to 26.8 MME/day, with all adverse events mild and no discontinuations due to device-related adverse events; the study was uncontrolled and the findings require confirmation in a randomized sham-controlled trial.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm open-label trial — no control arm exists, so all between_group_effects arrays are empty. The IRLS baseline of 11.9 (SD 8.5) for the 15 participants who had any successful reduction differs from the overall sample baseline of 9.8 (SD 8.5); both are extracted in outcome_id 5. Figures 2 and 3 contain individual participant data points used to derive correlations; exact per-participant values not extractable from text. The note that step-down 3 completion was 15% (3 of 20) means only 3 participants completed all three step-downs. RLS symptom frequency (5.9 days/week) and TOMAC session frequency (5.0 days/week) during assessment weeks are reported as averages from device logs (n=14 with available logs) but SDs not provided. No quality-of-life or sleep-specific secondary outcomes with quantitative data were reported beyond IRLS and CGI-I.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Within the intervention arm, RLS score decreased significantly only in the PSST > 28 (severe PMS) subgroup (from 15.27 to 11.36, within-arm p=0.048); no significant within-arm change in mild or moderate PMS subgroups. Serum vitamin D increased significantly in all three PMS subgroups in the intervention arm (all p < 0.001), with no significant change in the control arm across any subgroup. Between-arm differences in vitamin D change were significant in all three subgroups (all p < 0.001).

summary: This 10-week parallel-group RCT in 141 obese women (aged 30-50, Iran) with vitamin D insufficiency compared low-fat dairy products fortified with 1500 IU nano-encapsulated vitamin D3/day (n=71) versus plain non-fortified dairy (n=70), stratified by PMS severity. Fortified dairy significantly increased serum vitamin D in all PMS severity subgroups (p<0.001 across all), but did not produce a statistically significant between-group reduction in RLS scores in any subgroup (p=0.67, 0.26, 0.62 for mild, moderate, and severe PMS respectively); a within-arm improvement in RLS was observed only in women with severe PMS in the intervention group (p=0.048), which the authors interpreted as a meaningful finding despite the non-significant between-group comparison.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) The paper presents a 4-arm original trial (fortified milk, plain milk, fortified yogurt, plain yogurt) that was collapsed into 2 groups (intervention vs control) for this sub-analysis; per-subgroup sample sizes in the original 4-arm allocation are not reported for this women-only sub-analysis. 2) Table 1 baseline RLS scores show slight discrepancy between table 1 (7.6±9.13 for PSST<19) and Table 2 (7.3±7.93), both listed — Table 2 values used for outcome extraction as they appear to be the pre-intervention values in the outcome-focused table. 3) The primary reported significant finding is within-arm change in the severe PMS (PSST>28) intervention subgroup (p=0.048), not a between-arm comparison; the between-arm comparison for the same subgroup is p=0.62. This is a notable interpretive concern. 4) No overall (collapsed) RLS baseline or endpoint means are reported for the total n=71 vs n=70; only PSST-stratified values are given in Tables 2-4. 5) The PSST score itself (secondary endpoint) is not reported with pre/post means by arm — only used as a stratifying variable. 6) Iron and magnesium baseline data are reported in Table 1 by PMS subgroup but no post-intervention values are given; these were not extracted as outcomes. 7) The correlation figure (Fig. 2) contains data not extractable from text. 8) The paper reports within-group p-values in Tables 2 and 3, and between-group change p-values in Table 4; these are all extracted. 9) Total intervention n=71 subgroup breakdown: PSST<19 n=31, PSST 19-28 n=18, PSST>28 n=22 (sum=71); Control n=70 subgroup breakdown: PSST<19 n=26, PSST 19-28 n=27, PSST>28 n=17 (sum=70).

summary: This single-blind RCT enrolled 75 RLS/WED patients in Iran and randomized them to magnesium oxide (250 mg/day) plus pramipexole, vitamin B6 (40 mg/day) plus pramipexole, or placebo plus pramipexole for 2 months, assessing RLS symptom severity (IRLS) and sleep quality (PSQI) at baseline, 1 month, and 2 months. summary: This pooled post-hoc analysis of three double-blind, placebo-controlled RCTs (XP052, XP053, XP081) examined whether prior dopamine agonist (DA) exposure affects the efficacy or tolerability of gabapentin enacarbil (GEn; 600 mg or 1200 mg once daily) in 671 adults with moderate-to-severe primary RLS. Prior DA exposure did not significantly alter the change in IRLS Rating Scale total score from baseline at week 12 (p=0.673–0.964 across arms) or CGI-I responder rates at week 12 in any treatment group. Both GEn doses significantly improved IRLS scores and CGI-I response versus placebo regardless of prior DA exposure, and the adverse event profile was similar between DA-naive and DA-exposed patients.

summary: This randomized double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial tested ropinirole (0.5–6.0 mg/day) versus placebo over two 4-week treatment periods in 22 adults with primary RLS. Ropinirole significantly reduced RLS Rating Scale scores compared to placebo (mean 13.0 vs 24.7, mean difference −12.0 points, 95% CI −17 to −6.3, p<0.001), with 36% of patients achieving complete symptom resolution on ropinirole versus 0% on placebo. summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (PEARLS study) randomized 100 patients with idiopathic RLS to evening pergolide (0.25-0.75 mg/d) or placebo for 6 weeks (phase 1), with responders continuing blinded treatment and non-responders receiving open-label pergolide for up to 12 months (phase 2). At 6 weeks, pergolide significantly reduced the PLMS arousal index (-12.6 vs -3.6 arousals/h change; p=0.004) and IRLS severity score (-12.2 vs -1.8; p<0.001), with a much higher PGI response rate (68.1% vs 15.1%; p<0.01), though objective sleep efficiency did not differ significantly between groups (p=0.196). Pergolide maintained its effects on PLM measures through 12 months and was generally well tolerated, with nausea and headache more frequent in the pergolide arm.

summary: This 5-week double-blind RCT (CATOR study) tested cabergoline 2 mg/day versus placebo in 40 adults with moderate-to-severe idiopathic RLS (20 per arm), using PSG-derived PLMS-AI and sleep efficiency as co-primary endpoints. Cabergoline was superior to placebo on both primary endpoints (PLMS-AI change: -17.7 vs -4.5, p=0.0024; sleep efficiency change: +6.2% vs +3.3%, p=0.0443) and on all secondary subjective measures including IRLS total score (-23.7 vs -7.9, p=0.0002), RLS-6 night and day severity scales, CGI severity, and quality of life. Treatment was generally well tolerated, with gastrointestinal symptoms and dizziness being the most common adverse events, and three patients withdrew during titration due to adverse events.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Primary analysis population was per-protocol (n=20/arm), as 3 cabergoline patients dropped out during titration and were excluded; ITT analysis was not performed. For PLM index and PLMS index, only p-values were reported for between-group comparisons (no CI or LS mean difference stated beyond the individual arm change-from-baseline data); effect values were therefore calculated from change-from-baseline means. For PLMW index, no significant between-group p-value was reported; the calculated mean difference from change scores is provided. Table 3 asterisk/symbol footnotes were partially garbled (rendered as '/H14067' and '±' symbols) but context confirmed which comparisons were statistically significant. The n_randomized for arm 2 (placebo) is inferred as 20 since total randomized was 43 and cabergoline arm had 23; this gives 20 placebo but the paper does not state the per-arm randomization split explicitly. Responder analysis data referenced as 'table E-1' (online supplement) was not available in this text — those binary outcome data are not extracted. The PLMS-AI figure data (mean values at baseline and final visit) are partially confirmed by text values (cabergoline final: 2.54±4.0; placebo final: 15.66±17.34) but the figure itself could not be read for additional precision.

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 10 patients with idiopathic RLS tested whether low-dose IV hydrocortisone (40 mg) administered during the evening (6:00–9:30 PM) could reduce sensory leg discomfort during the nocturnal Suggested Immobilization Test. summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover pilot trial (n=6) tested a single session of intramuscular botulinum toxin A (BTX-A; up to 90 mU per leg) versus saline in patients with primary RLS who were stable on background medications. At the primary endpoint of 4 weeks post-injection, BTX-A showed a 5.0-point IRLS improvement versus 2.7 points for placebo, a non-significant difference (p=0.24); paradoxically, placebo outperformed BTX-A at 2 weeks (5.0 vs 1.0 points, p=0.06). The study found no significant benefit of BTX-A on IRLS or CGI at week 4, while a statistically significant CGI advantage was observed for the placebo arm at week 2 (p=0.01), and adverse events were similar between groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Crossover design: baseline demographics reported only at the overall level (not per arm), as is typical for crossover trials; per-arm baseline IRLS assumed equal at 27±4.8 based on overall reporting. The paper states 'placebo-treated patients noted a 5.0±5.1 point improvement' and 'BTX-arm 1.0±3.5 point improvement' at week 2, and reports p=0.06 — these values are change-from-baseline figures. CGI p=0.01 at week 2 favors placebo (lower score = more improvement), so the statistically significant finding was a placebo advantage, not BTX-A. The adverse event scores appear to be composite 0-10 ratings across multiple symptoms rather than event counts per se. Between-group effect for IRLS at week 2: BTX minus placebo = -1.0 - (-5.0) = +4.0 (worse for BTX). Between-group effect for IRLS at week 4: -5.0 - (-2.7) = -2.3 (better for BTX). Total study duration was 24 weeks (two 12-week periods); assessments were at weeks 0, 2, 4 within each period. Carryover effect assessment (p=0.55) reported. The 'FINE-MAPPING THE GENE FOR X-LINKED MYOPATHY' and 'CORRECTION' sections in the paper are unrelated to the RLS trial and were ignored.

summary: This 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluated gabapentin enacarbil (XP13512) 1,200 mg once daily versus placebo in 222 adults with moderate to severe primary RLS. summary: The ENCORE study was a double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT evaluating rotigotine transdermal patch (1-3 mg/24h) versus placebo over 7 weeks in 66 patients with moderate-to-severe RLS and elevated PLMI at baseline. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. Table 2 in the paper has significant formatting issues with merged cells and misaligned values across two printed table segments — values were carefully cross-referenced with text. 2. For PLMI, the rotigotine baseline SD was not clearly separated from the placebo change column in the garbled table layout; the baseline SD for rotigotine PLMI was imputed as null (rotigotine baseline mean=71.6, no clear SD attributed). 3. The placebo PLMI change SD and several change-from-baseline SDs for other outcomes in the continuation of Table 2 were not cleanly extractable and are marked null or inferred. 4. RLS-6 scale and CGI outcomes were mentioned but only analyzed descriptively — no numeric results extractable. 6. Per-arm endpoint values for PLMI had the placebo change listed as -50.3 and rotigotine change as -50.1 (with SD 44.5) based on table continuation parsing. 7. n_randomized for placebo arm calculated as 81 total - 40 rotigotine = 41; however Table 1 states safety set n=40 for placebo, suggesting one patient did not receive study medication per flow diagram (figure 1 note). 8. The duration calculation: titration up to 3 weeks + 4-week maintenance + 1-week taper = ~8 weeks treatment; total with 28-day follow-up ~12 weeks; treatment_duration_weeks set to 7 (3 titration + 4 maintenance) and total to ~15 weeks (treatment 7 + taper 1 + follow-up 4).

summary: This single-centre open-label RCT conducted in Egypt randomised 60 haemodialysis patients with uraemic restless legs syndrome to 3 months of neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) or aerobic exercise training (3 sessions/week). Aerobic exercise produced statistically significant improvements in IRLS score (34.9 to 29.4, p<0.001), STS-60, and normal and fast walking speeds, while NMES produced only small, mostly non-significant changes in all outcomes except STS-5 (where it showed a 4.6% improvement vs 2.1% for exercise). The aerobic exercise group showed superior results on all measures except STS-5, with an 18.7% reduction in IRLS severity score versus 2.0% in the NMES group.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Several bar chart values (Figures 1-3) corroborate table data and were used to cross-check. The STS-60 test is reported in the paper as counting repetitions in 60 seconds (higher is better for endurance), but the table labels it in 'seconds' — this is likely a labelling inconsistency; values (33.0, 31.6, 34.5, 31.0) are consistent with repetition counts, not seconds. The between-group p-values for physical performance outcomes are only reported within-group (paired t-test); no formal between-group inferential statistics with CIs were provided, so mean differences at post-treatment were calculated from reported arm means. The 15 participants who declined to participate are noted but no CONSORT flow diagram is provided; attrition during the trial is not reported. Percent improvement values in Table 4 (4.6%, 11.3%, etc.) reflect change from baseline within each group and were used to cross-check extracted means. The normal walking speed for NMES shows a slight worsening post-treatment (7.7 to 7.9 seconds) which is consistent with the non-significant paired t-test result (p=0.638) reported in Table 2.

summary: This open-label, single-arm study enrolled 16 drug-naive RLS patients in South Korea and treated them with pramipexole (median 0.19 mg/day) for 12 weeks to assess effects on cognitive function. After treatment, IRLS scores improved significantly (29.5 to 14.6, p<0.001), and three cognitive measures also improved significantly: RCFT immediate recall (17.72 to 20.13, p=0.05), COWAT phoneme word frequency (36.5 to 41.5, p=0.03), and Digit Symbol Coding (68.2 to 73.8, p=0.02). However, improvements in cognition did not correlate with improvements in RLS severity, sleep quality, or depression, suggesting a possible direct dopaminergic effect on cognition; the study's absence of a control group limits causal inference.

summary: This open-label parallel-group RCT (n=69 analyzed) tested governor vessel moxibustion (Du-jiu), a Traditional Chinese Medicine technique applied along the spine, added to standard hemodialysis care versus standard care alone in maintenance hemodialysis patients with RLS (IRLS score ≥15). summary: This cross-sectional observational study compared information sampling and decision making using the Beads Task in 40 dopaminergic-treated RLS patients with augmentation, 24 without augmentation, and 21 healthy controls at a single Austrian center. Both RLS patient groups gathered significantly less information before deciding and made more irrational decisions than healthy controls (both p<0.002), with no difference between RLS groups in information gathering (p=1.0). Critically, RLS patients with augmentation made significantly more irrational decisions than those without augmentation (p=0.037), suggesting that augmentation — likely driven by higher dopaminergic doses — is associated with more pronounced impulsive and irrational reasoning akin to patterns seen in substance abuse and behavioral addictions.

summary: This prospective, randomized, double-blinded, sham-controlled trial enrolled 35 adults with RLS (21 therapeutic PCD, 14 sham PCD) and assessed the effect of 4 weeks of pneumatic compression device therapy versus sham devices on RLS severity, quality of life, daytime sleepiness, and fatigue. Therapeutic PCDs significantly reduced IRLSSS scores (20.3 to 8.4 vs 19.0 to 14.1 for sham; p=0.006) and JHRLSS scores (2.3 to 1.2 vs 2.4 to 2.2; p=0.01), and produced significantly greater improvements in all quality of life domains, Epworth sleepiness scale, and fatigue compared to sham. Complete symptom resolution occurred in 38.1% of therapeutic versus 0% of sham device users (p=0.007), suggesting PCDs are an effective non-pharmacological adjunctive or alternative therapy for RLS.

summary: This prospective quasi-experimental study in children aged 8-17 with RLS examined the effect of oral vitamin D supplementation (2000 IU/day for 6 weeks then maintenance) on sleep habits as measured by the Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire (CSHQ) over 3 months, comparing 20 vitamin D-deficient children (treated) to 26 non-deficient children (untreated). Vitamin D-deficient children who received supplementation showed statistically significant within-group improvements in bedtime resistance, sleep onset delay, sleep anxiety, parasomnias, daytime sleepiness, and total CSHQ score, while non-deficient untreated children showed no significant change. However, no significant between-group differences were found at any timepoint, and the absence of a placebo control and randomization limits causal inference.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a quasi-experimental (non-randomized) study, not an RCT — arm assignment was based on vitamin D blood level at enrollment. The paper does not clearly identify a primary outcome. CSHQ Total Score was treated as primary given it is the aggregate measure. The CSHQ total score for the overall RLS group vs. controls (Table 1) was reported as mean ± SD (52.20 ± 8.41 vs 48.30 ± 5.20, p=0.061), while all other CSHQ scores were medians with IQR. Table 2 (treatment subgroups) reports only medians/IQR. The healthy control group (n=43) was extracted for context in the subgroup_analyses section but is not included as an arm since this is a RLS intervention study. Correlation analyses between vitamin D levels and CSHQ scores (Spearman r=-0.115, p=0.577 pre-treatment; r=-0.028, p=0.891 post-treatment) are noted but not extracted as outcomes. Post-treatment vitamin D serum levels were not measured, a limitation noted by the authors. The p* column in Table 2 represents between-group comparison of baseline (pre-treatment) values between the two RLS subgroups, not between pre- and post-treatment. Daytime sleepiness for RLS group overall was reported as 12.5 (12-15) in Table 1, not decomposed by subgroup at baseline in Table 1.

summary: This single-arm before-after study enrolled 80 hemodialysis patients with RLS in three hospitals in Yazd province, Iran, and applied local calf vibration (Thrive Model 717A device) for 10 minutes, three times per week for 4 weeks during hemodialysis sessions. The mean IRLS score decreased from 18.99 (SD 3.29) at baseline to 12.82 (SD 2.73) after treatment in the 76 patients who completed the intervention, a reduction of approximately 6.2 points that was statistically significant (paired t-test, P=0.001). However, the absence of a control arm means that the observed improvement cannot be attributed causally to vibration therapy, and risk of bias is high.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm before-after study with no control group; it does not qualify as an RCT. The 'between_group_effects' entry for outcome 1 reflects a within-arm pre-post paired comparison (post minus pre mean difference = 12.82 - 18.99 = -6.17), not a between-group comparison. Table 1 shows baseline N=80 and post-intervention N=76 (4 dropouts); Table 2 reports both timepoints with N=76, consistent with per-protocol analysis of completers only. Percent female calculated as 100 - 57.5 = 42.5%. Categorical severity breakdown at baseline: mild=0 (0%), moderate=55 (68.8%), severe=25 (31.2%); at follow-up: mild=13 (16.2%), moderate=63 (78.8%), severe=0 (0%), with 4 subject attrition. The paper states 97% reliability for the IRLS questionnaire per Habibzadeh et al. No adverse events were formally reported. The IRLS scale used has 10 items each scored 0-4 (total 0-40). Note the paper's abstract contains a likely typo stating '16.3% of the patients had moderate severity...after vibration while 78.8% suffered from severe symptoms' — Table 1 and the methods section confirm the correct post-intervention distribution is 16.2% mild and 78.8% moderate (not severe); this discrepancy was noted in extraction.

summary: This randomized crossover trial in 76 hemodialysis patients with RLS compared 4 weeks of low-voltage vibration therapy versus hacking foot massage (both delivered 3x/week for 10 minutes during dialysis), with a 4-week washout between periods. Both interventions significantly reduced RLS symptom severity (IRLSQ) and improved PSQI sleep quality scores compared to baseline (p=0.001 for both). Vibration produced greater improvement than massage on both outcomes — RLS score decreased by 6.17 points with vibration versus 3.49 points with massage, and PSQI decreased by 1.73 versus 0.94 points — with statistically significant between-treatment differences (p=0.001).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Important methodological notes: (1) This is a crossover trial but the authors report results using paired t-tests without accounting for period, carryover, or sequence effects — a significant methodological limitation. (2) The identical baseline means and SDs for both arms (RLS: 18.99±3.292; PSQI: 10.16±3.96/3.966) strongly suggest these are pooled/overall baseline values rather than arm-specific values, which is consistent with a crossover design where all participants received both treatments. Per-arm baseline values are not separately reported. n_analyzed=76 is assigned to both arms as this reflects the overall analyzed sample across both sequences in the crossover. (3) The between-group p-value of 0.001 is reported for the comparison of the two intervention methods but no mean difference with CI is provided — the mean_difference in between_group_effects was calculated from the reported post-intervention means. (4) Table 3 reports slightly different values for massage baseline SD (3.96 vs 3.966) — both extracted as reported. (5) The 4 excluded participants (lack of cooperation) are not allocated to specific arms. (6) Total study duration calculated as: 4 weeks (period 1) + 4 weeks (washout) + 4 weeks (period 2) = 12 weeks.

summary: This double-blind, 2-period crossover RCT enrolled 21 hemodialysis patients with restless legs syndrome (RLS) in Iran and randomized them to receive gabapentin 100 mg or matched placebo orally three times per week (after each HD session) for 4 weeks, followed by a 2-week washout and crossover for another 4 weeks. The primary outcome — RLS symptom severity scored by a standardized IRLSSG questionnaire — decreased significantly from 24.19 ± 7.96 to 19.24 ± 9.87 after gabapentin (p = 0.04), while the within-placebo reduction (24.19 ± 7.96 to 18.89 ± 11.15) did not reach significance (p = 0.09); however, no between-group comparison was reported, and the magnitude of change was similar in both arms, limiting interpretation of true drug-specific efficacy.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a crossover trial but the paper reports baseline scores identically for both periods (24.19 ± 7.96, n=21), suggesting a single pre-treatment baseline is used for both treatment periods rather than per-period baselines after washout — consistent with a crossover design but limiting direct between-group effect calculation. No between-group statistical comparison is reported by the authors; the effect measure of 0.35 (endpoint difference gabapentin 19.24 vs placebo 18.89) is calculated from reported values but does not account for within-subject crossover correlation. Figure 1 and Figure 2 show pre/post data but exact values are available in text, so figures were not the sole data source. The initial sequence had 13 on gabapentin and 8 on placebo in period 1, then 12 on placebo and 8 on gabapentin in period 2 after one withdrawal from each arm, giving approximately 20 analyzable completers per arm (pooled across both periods). Per-arm demographic breakdown by randomization sequence is not reported. Table 1 individual patient data is partially garbled (creatinine values appear concatenated with hematocrit in the OCR). The paper refers to RLS questionnaire from Cirignotta et al. 2002 (reference 8); this appears to be the IRLSSG-validated dialysis screening questionnaire, not the standard IRLS Rating Scale.

summary: This double-blind RCT in 90 Iranian hemodialysis patients compared intravenous vitamin C (500 mg three times per week for 8 weeks) against normal saline placebo, with all patients also receiving a multivitamin tablet containing 60 mg vitamin C. The primary outcome (PSQI total score) improved in the vitamin C group from a mean of 7.36 (±2.58) to approximately 4.0, with significant reductions in subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, and daily dysfunction compared to controls (p=0.0001); however, no significant differences were found for lack of sleep, sleep efficiency, or hypnotic drug use. Restless legs syndrome and pruritus severity also decreased significantly in the vitamin C group (p=0.001 and p=0.0001 respectively), but continuous effect size data (means, SDs, CIs) were not reported for most outcomes — only categorical distributions — limiting quantitative synthesis.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Multiple data quality issues: (1) The PSQI post-treatment SD for the intervention arm is reported in the text as '4.005 ± 135.3' which appears garbled/corrupted (SD of 135.3 is implausible for a 0-21 scale; likely should be '4.005 ± 1.353' or similar). (2) No post-treatment mean or SD is reported for the control arm for total PSQI score. (3) Most outcomes are reported only as ordinal categorical distributions (e.g., Rarely/Sometimes/Always for RLS; Slight/Moderate/Severe for itching) with chi-square p-values, not as continuous means with SDs, making quantitative pooling difficult. (4) Table 4 has merged cells and some row label ambiguities making exact parsing uncertain — the 'Sleep latency' row appears to share negative/positive values that are ambiguous. (5) Randomization method and allocation concealment are not described. (6) The paper does not report between-group effect sizes (MD, OR, RR) with confidence intervals for any outcome — only p-values from chi-square or Wilcoxon tests. (7) Age data is reported only as categorical distributions, not as means or medians per arm.

summary: This quasi-experimental study in 30 third-trimester pregnant women with RLS compared 1 week of TENS plus lower-limb stretching exercises (Group A, n=15) against active range-of-motion exercises plus leg massage (Group B, n=15). Group A showed significantly greater reductions in both pain (NPRS post-test mean 4.93 vs 7.60, p<0.0001) and overall RLS symptom severity (RLS questionnaire post-test mean 11.87 vs 21.40, p<0.0001), indicating that TENS with stretching was superior to conventional exercise and massage for short-term RLS symptom relief in pregnancy.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 1 for Group A is poorly formatted and appears truncated — it shows pre-test NPRS mean 8.67 SD 0.72 and post-test NPRS mean 4.93 SD 0.96, and pre-test RLS mean 32.27 SD 4.1, but the post-test RLS row for Group A (mean 11.87) is only available in the Results text (not in Table 1 as printed). The t-value of 1.4246 shown in Table 1 appears to apply to the RLS questionnaire within-group comparison for Group A, but the table layout is ambiguous. Table 2 (Group B) is clearer: NPRS pre 8.67/0.72, post 7.60/0.63; RLS pre 30.40/3.00, post 21.40/2.47, t=12.6466, p<0.0001. The p-value column in Table 2 shows '<ORO I' which is interpreted as '<0.001'. SD for Group A post-test RLS questionnaire (11.87) was not reported in the table or text. Between-group t-values or formal between-group statistics are not presented in tables; only p<0.0001 threshold is stated in text. Both outcome figures (Figure 1, Figure 2) contain graphical data only and no extractable numeric values beyond what is in text/tables. This is not a COVID/Long COVID trial; it studies RLS in pregnancy.

summary: This single-arm prospective study enrolled 68 patients (50 female, 18 male) aged 30-80 with moderate-to-severe RLS attending a private outpatient clinic in India, and treated all participants with oral potassium citrate 1080mg (10 mEq) once daily for 45 days. RLS severity was assessed using a 100mm VAS at baseline and at days 15, 30, and 45; no control group was included. The authors report that 54.4% of patients reached VAS=0 (no RLS) by day 15, rising to 100% by day 45, concluding that potassium citrate was significantly effective, though no inferential statistics or control comparison were provided.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This study is a single-arm uncontrolled prospective series, not an RCT — it is described as 'randomized' in the text but no randomization procedure, comparator arm, or allocation concealment is described, and all 68 patients received the same treatment. No continuous VAS scores (means or SDs) are reported; outcomes are presented only as categorical counts of patients in each severity band (No RLS / Mild / Moderate / Severe) at each timepoint. The study enrolled patients with RLS (not Long COVID), so long_covid fields are all null. Age range (30-80) is stated but no mean or SD is reported. The paper states 'prospective randomized interventional study' but no randomization details are provided — this appears to be a single-arm before-after case series. A figure (Figure 2) mirrors the data in Table 1; no additional numeric data extractable from figures. No formal statistical tests (p-values, CIs) are reported for the primary outcome.

summary: This Turkish single-center RCT (n=63) compared CCL2 compression stockings (23-32 mmHg, worn daily for 3 weeks) versus placebo (100-denier non-therapeutic) stockings in pregnant women (27-37 weeks gestation) diagnosed with RLS (severity score >10). Both groups showed significant within-group reductions in RLS severity (IRLSSG), sleep disturbance (PSQI), and improvements in well-being (WHO-5); however, compression stockings produced a significantly greater reduction in RLS severity at 3 weeks (post-test mean 8.87 vs 12.19, p=0.018), while improvements in sleep quality and well-being were similar between groups (both p>0.05). Onset of perceived benefit was faster in the compression group (3.93 vs 5.09 days, p=0.007).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 3 (qualitative positive/negative codes) was incompletely reproduced in the paper text — the table header row shows 'Participants' but the full coded data rows were not rendered in the provided text; only summary counts from narrative were extractable (e.g., pain relief n=13 EG, n=15 PG; discomfort n=14 EG; sweaty legs n=4 PG). The n_analyzed for 'day of benefit' outcome was taken from the 'benefit=yes' respondents (EG=31, PG=29) per Table 2 footnote. The between-group test statistic for the post-test IRLSSG difference was t=-2.421 (p=0.018) and for change difference t=0.381 (p=0.029) per Table 2. WHO-5 pre-test difference p=0.106 per Table 2 (groups not fully balanced at baseline on WHO-5, though not statistically significant). No post-treatment follow-up beyond 3 weeks was conducted. The paper does not report reasons for the 3 (EG) and 4 (PG) withdrawals from the 35 randomized per arm.

summary: This quasi-experimental parallel-group trial enrolled 60 adults aged 40-60 years with RLS and diabetic neuropathy, randomising them to 12 weeks of combined aerobic exercise plus yogasana with pharmacotherapy (Group B, n=30) versus pharmacotherapy alone (Group A, n=30). After 12 weeks, Group B showed significantly lower perceived stress (PSS mean 14.80 vs 21.40, ANCOVA F=93.75, p<0.001) and significantly lower fatigue (FSS mean 26.66 vs 40.73, ANCOVA F=110.80, p<0.001) compared to the control group. The results were statistically significant, supporting aerobic exercise and yogasana as an adjunct therapy for RLS-related stress and fatigue.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per-arm n=30 inferred from total N=60 divided equally into two groups; the paper states 60 patients 'divided into two groups' but does not explicitly state n=30 per arm. Table 1 narrative text contains contradictory language (states pre-test F=0.66 'indicates statistically significant difference' but this F value is below the critical value of 11.97, suggesting no significant pre-test difference — the narrative appears to contain copy-paste errors). Adjusted post-test means also extracted from tables (Group A: 21.42, Group B: 14.77 for stress; Group A: 40.02, Group B: 27.37 for fatigue). Between-group mean differences for the adjusted ANCOVA comparison are calculated as arm1 minus arm2 (intervention minus control). The paper does not provide CIs or exact p-values, only stating significance at 0.001 or 0.05 levels relative to a critical F value of 11.97. No RLS-specific symptom severity instrument (e.g. IRLS) was reported — only PSS and FSS were used as outcomes.

summary: This quasi-experimental study enrolled 51 patients with idiopathic restless legs syndrome in Uzbekistan, comparing complex therapy (targeted correction of vitamin/mineral deficiencies plus antiepileptic drugs and dopamine agonists, n=26) with basic treatment (n=25) over 3 months. summary: This pooled analysis of two double-blind sham-controlled RCTs evaluated nightly vibrating leg pads (Symphony device) versus sham pads (sound-emitting or light-emitting) in 158 adults with moderately severe primary RLS over 4 weeks. The primary outcome, MOS-II sleep problems score, improved significantly more in vibrating pad recipients (mean change -13.3 SD 19.7) than sham recipients (mean change -6.2 SD 15.7), a 114% greater improvement (mean difference -7.09, 95% CI -12.92 to -0.27, P=0.02; P=0.04 after multiplicity correction). summary: This retrospective integrated analysis of two 12-week double-blind placebo-controlled RCTs evaluated once-daily gabapentin enacarbil (GEn) 1200 mg versus placebo in 427 adults with moderate to severe primary RLS, stratified by baseline sleep disturbance severity. GEn significantly improved all MOS Sleep Scale domains, PSQ sleep quality, and PghSD wake time after sleep onset compared with placebo in both subgroups (all P<0.05), with greater benefits observed in subjects with very severe to severe sleep disturbance at baseline, including significant reductions in nighttime awakenings, hours awake per night, time awake during the night (24-Hour RLS Diary, AMTD -58.4 min, P=0.001), and Epworth Sleepiness Scale score. The PghSD demonstrated greater sensitivity to treatment effects than the novel 24-Hour RLS Symptom Diary sleep endpoints, likely due to higher measurement resolution.
