summary: This pilot study pooled IRLS subscale data from two single-blind RCTs (N=58: 41 NIR treatment, 17 sham) to examine whether the IRLS symptom severity (SS1) and symptom impact (SS2) subscales responded differently to 4 weeks of near-infrared light therapy versus sham treatment in RLS patients. Both subscales improved significantly within the NIR group (P<0.005), but only SS1 showed a significantly greater improvement versus the sham control (P=0.0004); SS2 did not differ between groups (P=0.178). Within the sham group, SS1 changed significantly (P=0.002, placebo effect), but SS2 did not (P=0.196), suggesting the placebo effect in RLS is primarily attributable to perceived symptom severity rather than symptom impact on daily functioning.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a post-hoc pooled subscale analysis of two prior trials (Mitchell et al. 2011a and 2011b), not an independently powered RCT. The SS1 and SS2 change-from-baseline values in Table 3 represent absolute mean change in average item score (0-4 scale), not change in summed subscale score. The SD for within-sham SS2 change is not separately provided in Table 4 (only p-value given as 0.196). The paired t-test p-value for SS1 in NIR group is reported as P<0.005 (not exact). The between-group SS1 p-value 0.0004 is verbatim from Table 3. Individual question-level means are reported in Tables 2 and 4 without SDs. The symptom duration data (NIR: 15.9±16.0 years; sham: 12.7±13.3 years) is in Table 1. Percent female computed: 24/41=58.5% NIR, 8/17=47.1% sham. The NIR arm (n=41) pools subjects from two different treatment arms (n=13 variant 1, n=11 variant 2 from study 2, plus n=17 from study 1), which were shown to be non-significantly different (P=0.88); the sham group (n=17) comes only from study 1. The change_from_baseline mean for SS1 in Table 3 (1.31 for NIR, 0.62 for sham) represents the reduction in average item score, not summed subscale score.

summary: This single-center quasi-experimental study from China assessed dynamic cerebral autoregulation (dCA), measured as phase difference via transfer function analysis, in 120 RLS patients classified by IRLS severity (mild, moderate, severe, very severe, n=30 each) and 30 matched healthy controls. Phase difference was significantly lower (compromised dCA) in moderate, severe, and very severe RLS groups (approximately 37-39°) compared to controls and mild RLS patients (approximately 50-52°, p<0.001), and correlated negatively with IRLS score, arousal index, and PLMI. In a non-randomized open-label substudy of 35 patients with moderate-to-very severe RLS treated with pramipexole 0.125 mg/day plus gabapentin 300 mg/day for one month, phase difference improved significantly from a pre-treatment median of 36.41° to 48.56° post-treatment (p<0.001), suggesting pharmacological therapy may restore cerebrovascular autoregulation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is an observational study with a nested pre-post treatment substudy, NOT an RCT. The study design fields have been completed to reflect this: design_type set to quasi-experimental. The arm structure is complex: arms 1-4 represent the 4 RLS severity groups and arm 5 is the healthy control group; only moderate-to-very severe patients received pharmacological treatment. Age data are reported only in categorical bins (not as continuous means/SDs), so age_mean is null for all arms. The pre-post treatment substudy enrolled 35 patients (12 moderate, 11 severe, 12 very severe) and the pre-treatment IRLS was reported as 24.91 ± 8.27, post-treatment as 20.26 ± 8.89. Stage N2 results were not statistically significant (p=0.743) and are omitted from outcomes but values were: Controls 50.47±6.97, Mild 51.29±10.06, Moderate 50.82±7.22, Severe 51.93±10.53, Very Severe 48.63±12.70. AHI was also not significant (p=0.781): Controls 2.12±1.61, Mild 2.31±0.99, Moderate 2.56±1.37, Severe 2.30±1.39, Very Severe 2.22±1.23. Transfer function figure data (Figure 1B, Figure 3B) are only in graphical format with no extractable numeric values. The between-group p-values for phase difference comparisons are stated as P<0.001 in text; exact post-hoc p-values for individual pairwise comparisons are not numerically reported. The F-statistic for phase difference overall ANOVA was 18.353. Spearman correlations reported: PD vs IRLS r=-0.343 p=0.0001; PD vs arousal index r=-0.213 p=0.0193; PD vs PLMI r=-0.230 p=0.0113. Univariate regression betas also extracted in Table 4. Treatment substudy pre-treatment PD reported as median with IQR [33.05-40.45] and post-treatment as [39.99-54.35]; the pre-treatment substudy n=35 does not equal any single arm because it pools moderate+severe+very severe patients.

summary: This paper reports a retrospective pooled analysis of three 12-week double-blind, placebo-controlled RCTs (XP052, XP053, XP081) evaluating gabapentin enacarbil (GEn) at doses of 600 mg, 1200 mg, 1800 mg, and 2400 mg in 752 adults with moderate-to-severe primary RLS. GEn 600 mg significantly reduced IRLS total score versus placebo at week 12 LOCF (adjusted mean change: -13.6 vs -9.3; adjusted mean treatment difference: -4.3; 95% CI -6.01, -2.52; p<0.0001), with 70.2% vs 42.2% responders on the CGI-I scale (AOR 3.1; p<0.0001). All four doses demonstrated significant efficacy versus placebo, with a dose-dependent increase in somnolence and dizziness but no unexpected safety signals.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a pooled retrospective analysis, not a single trial; individual study-level data (XP052, XP053, XP081) are not reported separately. IRLS change-from-baseline values at intermediate timepoints (weeks 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10) are stated to exist in Figure 1 but numeric values are only provided in text for weeks 2 and 12; all other intermediate timepoints are data-only-in-figures. CGI-I responder rates at timepoints other than week 2 and week 12 (i.e., weeks 1, 4, 8) are mentioned as assessed but not reported numerically in text; data only in Figure 2. The mITT n for the 1200 mg arm baseline characteristics footnote states n=265 (footnote b), suggesting a minor discrepancy vs n=266 in the mITT table row; this appears to reflect the footnoted exclusion for duration of disease. The n_any_ae for the placebo arm (182/245 = 74%) and all GEn arms combined (434/515 = 84%) are verbatim; individual arm completion rates are not reported per arm (only overall 82-83%). Randomization method and allocation concealment details are not described for the pooled analysis.

summary: This small RCT (n=15 HIV-positive males) tested 16 weeks of EEG neurofeedback versus placebo in patients with sleep disorders at a Tehran hospital. Neurofeedback produced significant improvement in stress levels (p<0.05) and reportedly improved quality of life indicators, with approximately 60% of anxiety and 40% of depression cases reaching normal range in the treatment group. Polysomnographic changes (Leg Movement Index, EMG, respiratory hypopneas, snoring index) were not statistically significant between groups, and no baseline pre-intervention measurements were reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. Major methodological and reporting limitations: (1) No baseline (pre-intervention) measurements are reported for any outcome — all data appear to be post-treatment only, making it impossible to assess within-group change; the paper states it is a pre-test/post-test design but only post-test data appear in tables. (2) PSQI and DASS tables appear to pool both arms together (n=15 total) rather than separate per arm, making arm-level extraction ambiguous — the 'treatment' and 'placebo' labels in Table 3 may be post-intervention categories, not group assignments. (3) PSG Table 5 values are reported as mean±SD (e.g., 0.980±0.2) but are ambiguously formatted — extracted as mean/SD accordingly. (4) The paper states 30 were randomized but only 15 were analyzed (9 treatment, 6 placebo); the discrepancy is unexplained beyond notation in CONSORT diagram about 'special conditions of patients.' (5) Age is reported confusingly as 'mean and standard deviation of age were 25±1 and 45±1' — this likely refers to two different individuals or the range, not a valid mean/SD for the sample; not extracted. (6) The RLS-specific outcome (Leg Movement Index) is included as a PSG metric but the study is primarily about HIV/sleep disorders, not RLS specifically. (7) No p-values are reported for PSG outcomes beyond 'not significant'; stress improvement p<0.05 is stated verbally. (8) The WHOQOL-BREF data are reported only as frequency distributions (satisfied/dissatisfied categories) with no summary scores.

summary: This parallel-group RCT (n=40 hemodialysis patients with RLS) compared 6 weeks of cold dialysate (35.5°C) versus isotonic stretching exercises on IRLS severity scores, assessed weekly. Both interventions significantly reduced RLS severity over time (Friedman test p=0.001 in each arm), with mean IRLS scores declining from 27.0 to 16.7 in the cold dialysis group and from 23.4 to 14.1 in the stretching exercise group. No statistically significant difference was found between the two active interventions (group effect p=0.09; interaction p=0.25), suggesting comparable efficacy for both non-pharmacological approaches.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is an active-comparator RCT with no placebo or usual-care control arm, which limits the interpretability of between-group effects for meta-analysis purposes. Per-arm means and SDs were fully reported at all 7 timepoints (baseline + 6 weekly assessments). The between-group p-value (p=0.09) is from repeated measures ANOVA group effect; no confidence intervals for between-group differences were reported. The mean difference at end of treatment (week 6) of 2.6 points (cold dialysis minus stretching) was calculated from reported means. The paper does not report whether analysis was ITT or per-protocol; given 4 dropouts excluded from final n=40, this appears to be per-protocol. The study is framed as hemodialysis-related RLS, not idiopathic RLS — relevance to general RLS meta-analysis should be assessed by the reviewer.

Between-group comparisons after treatment showed the massage group had significantly lower TOC and OSI and significantly higher PON1 than controls (all p<0.05), suggesting a favorable oxidative stress profile with massage, though numeric IRLS scale scores were not tabulated.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Several issues: (1) The paper states in the methods section that 'Blood samples were taken before and after treatment from 42 female patients over the age of 40 who were diagnosed with knee OA' — this appears to be a copy-paste error from a different study; the actual study population is hemodialysis patients with RLS. summary: This quasi-experimental study tested 8 weeks of intradialytic strength training (twice weekly, upper and lower extremity exercises with 0.5 kg weights) versus usual care in 32 Indonesian hemodialysis patients with RLS (15 intervention, 17 control) across two hospital sites. The intervention group showed a mean IRLS score decrease of 1.0 points post-treatment while the control group worsened by 1.29 points; the between-group difference was statistically significant (p=0.035). The authors concluded strength training has a beneficial effect on RLS severity in hemodialysis patients, though study limitations include non-individual randomization, small sample size, and a significant baseline TIBC imbalance between groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This is a quasi-experimental study with cluster randomization by hospital site (two sites only), not true individual RCT — RoB2 applied with appropriate downgrading. 2. The paper reports 'unpaired t-test' for between-group analysis; p=0.035 is stated as the between-group comparison at post-intervention. However, the paper also states pre-intervention p=0.035 in the same table cell which appears to be the between-group comparison at post-test (Δmean row), not pre-test — the pre-intervention comparison is implied to be non-significant per text. 3. The between-group mean difference at endpoint was calculated as 20.13 - 23.29 = -3.16 (intervention minus control). 4. Within-group p-values are reported: intervention p=0.271 (non-significant), control p=0.028 (significant worsening). 5. summary: This Indonesian quasi-experimental study tested the effect of intradialytic stretching exercise (20 minutes, twice weekly for 4 weeks, 8 total sessions) versus no exercise on RLS severity in 20 chronic kidney disease patients on routine hemodialysis, using the IRLS ordinal scale. Within-group analysis (Friedman test) showed a statistically significant improvement in RLS scale scores in the intervention group (p<0.001) but not the control group (p=0.282); however, no formal between-group statistical comparison was reported, and the final mean scores at session 8 were 5.20 (SD 1.135) for the intervention arm versus 4.90 (SD 0.994) for the control arm, limiting the interpretability of the between-group effect. The study has a high risk of bias due to its non-randomized quasi-experimental design with purposive sampling.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. The paper is written primarily in Indonesian (Bahasa Indonesia); all numeric data extracted verbatim from Table 3 and results text. 2. The p-value reported (p<0.001) is for the within-group Friedman test on the intervention arm only, NOT a between-group test; the control arm p=0.282 is its own within-group test. No formal between-group statistical test result with p-value is reported. The calculated between-group mean difference at session 8 is 5.20-4.90=0.30 in favor of the intervention arm, but the pattern across sessions is non-monotonic and the control arm also shows substantial score reductions at some sessions. 3. The RLS scale used appears to be an ordinal condensed version of IRLS (range 0-8) rather than the standard 0-40 IRLS total score; the paper refers to it as 'skala ordinal' with categories: very severe (7-8), severe (5-6), moderate (3-4), slightly severe (1-2). 4. Figure 1 and Figure 2 contain graphical data that may supplement Table 3; the per-session means in Table 3 are extracted verbatim. 5. Hemodialysis duration (years): intervention group mean 2.50±0.70 years, control group mean 2.00±0.81 years — not mapped to any JSON field as this is not RLS duration. 6. The paper describes a non-equivalent control group design (purposive sampling, not true randomization), which is classified here as quasi-experimental. 7. The oscillating pattern in Table 3 (scores rising and falling alternately across sessions) suggests the measurements may alternate between pre-session and post-session assessments within sessions, though this is not explicitly clarified in the text.

summary: This quasi-experimental parallel-group controlled trial (n=30 male hemodialysis patients aged 55-75 years) evaluated 6 weeks of selected core stability exercises (3 sessions/week, 45 min/session using a Swiss ball) versus usual care on restless legs syndrome (RLS) severity and health-related quality of life (KDQOL-SF). The exercise group showed a statistically significant reduction in RLS severity score (from 28.0 to 20.3, approximately 20% improvement) and significant improvements across most KDQOL-SF subscales (overall health score increased from 29.9 to 53.5, approximately 24% improvement), while the control group showed no meaningful change; all between-group differences were statistically significant (p<0.001 for most outcomes). No blinding was employed and the randomization method was not adequately described, limiting confidence in the findings.

The 'overall health score' (نمره کلی سلامت) row in Table 4 shows baseline values of 29.9±17.5 (experimental) and 25.4±12.4 (control) and post values of 53.5±12.6 and 25.5±8.5 — these appear to duplicate values from the energy/fatigue subscale row in the table as rendered; this may be a table rendering artifact in the OCR/extraction, but values were taken as printed. summary: This open-label RCT enrolled 43 patients with RLS comorbid with diabetic polyneuropathy who had failed gabapentin, randomizing them to 30 days of pramipexole monotherapy (n=21) or pramipexole plus zopiclone 7.5 mg (n=22). The authors conclude that zopiclone add-on to pramipexole provides clinically meaningful additional benefit for sleep quality and daytime functioning beyond motor symptom control.

summary: This pooled analysis of three 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials evaluated gabapentin enacarbil (GEn) 600 mg and 1200 mg versus placebo in 671 adults with moderate-to-severe primary RLS, stratified by baseline sleep disturbance severity. Both doses of GEn significantly reduced IRLS total scores and increased CGI-I responder rates vs placebo in both no-to-moderate and severe-to-very severe sleep disturbance subgroups (all P<0.01), with LS mean IRLS reductions of -12.3 and -11.3 (vs -7.7 for placebo) in the no-to-moderate subgroup and -16.6 and -17.0 (vs -12.7 for placebo) in the severe-to-very severe subgroup. GEn also significantly improved pain scores, mood subscales (POMS), and individual IRLS items (sleep disturbance, daily affairs, mood disturbance) compared with placebo, with somnolence and dizziness as the most frequent treatment-emergent adverse events.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a pooled analysis (not an individual RCT) of three parent trials (XP052, XP053, XP081). All primary efficacy results are reported stratified by sleep disturbance subgroup rather than for the total pooled population. Age and sex demographics at the arm level were calculated as weighted averages across the two sleep subgroups. Quantitative LS mean changes from baseline for IRLS items 4, 9, and 10 at week 12 and for the RLS pain score at week 12 are only available in figures (not in tables or text), so per-arm change-from-baseline values for these secondary outcomes at week 12 could not be extracted numerically — only baseline values and between-group significance levels (from the text) are reported. POMS subscale outcomes for anger-hostility, confusion-bewilderment, tension-anxiety, depression-dejection (severe subgroup), and fatigue-inertia (severe subgroup) are reported in Table III but were not extracted as separate outcome objects to manage output size; all values are available in Table III. The adverse event table splits counts by sleep disturbance subgroup with differing denominators (no-to-moderate: placebo n=135, GEn 600 mg n=89, GEn 1200 mg n=151; severe-to-very severe: placebo n=110, GEn 600 mg n=74, GEn 1200 mg n=118), these are safety population denominators. Total n_any_ae for each arm was calculated by summing both subgroups. Spearman correlation coefficients between POMS subscores and IRLS items 4, 9, and 10 were reported in text (range 0.20-0.49) but not extracted as formal outcomes.

summary: This parallel-group RCT compared two near-infrared (NIR) light devices — Anodynes (890nm, 292Hz) and HealthLight (880nm + 650nm red, 4698Hz) — in 25 adults with moderate-to-severe RLS who received 12 treatments over 4 weeks. At 3 weeks, bupropion produced a significantly greater reduction in IRLSSG scores (mean change -10.8 vs -6.0 points; p=0.016), but this difference was not statistically significant at 6 weeks (-10.4 vs -7.6 points; p=0.108) due to continued placebo group improvement. The study concluded that bupropion does not exacerbate RLS symptoms and may be a reasonable antidepressant choice for patients with RLS, though the trial was underpowered to definitively establish efficacy as a primary RLS treatment.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Two between_group_effects entries are provided for each of the 3-week and 6-week IRLSSG timepoints: one for the endpoint score comparison (t-test on absolute scores, p=0.032 at week 3 and p=0.152 at week 6 per Table 4) and one for the change-from-baseline comparison (p=0.016 at week 3 and p=0.108 at week 6, as stated in Table 4 and the abstract). The t-statistics reported in the table (-1.90 for endpoint at week 3, 2.20 for change at week 3) correspond to these two distinct comparisons. The paper does not report 95% CIs for any between-group effects. The miscarriage withdrawal in the bupropion arm was listed under reasons for withdrawal but was not characterized as a drug-related AE by the authors. Overall n_completed per arm estimated as: 60 total - 14 total lost to follow-up at week 6 = 46 completers; distribution by arm not explicitly stated, estimated as approximately 23 per arm based on 48% active drug among completers (Table 2). The BDI p-values are reported as one-tailed t-test results per the table (p=.383 at week 3, p=.129 at week 6); these are presented as between-group comparisons. No data appeared only in figures.

summary: This 6-week parallel-group RCT (n=18) compared once-weekly tension and trauma release exercises (TRE) — a program of progressive lower-limb muscle fatigue exercises designed to invoke therapeutic tremors — against a matched discussion group control in adults with idiopathic RLS. No significant between-group differences were found at week 6 on any outcome (IRLS, global RLS VAS, PIRS-20, MDI, or stress VAS), and there were no significant group-by-time interaction effects. Both groups showed clinically meaningful within-group reductions in RLS severity and depression over time, with the authors concluding the improvements were likely attributable to non-specific factors (regression to the mean, repeated assessment, or group social effects) rather than to TRE specifically.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The control group baseline n is reported as 7 in Tables 3 and 4 (not 9), suggesting 2 participants withdrew before week 1 and only IRLS data (not secondary outcomes) were imputed for them via last observation carried forward. The paper notes 'only IRLS scores could be analyzed using imputation of missing data for the 2 participants who withdrew before week 1.' Week-by-week intermediate scores (weeks 1-5) appear only in Figure 2 with no accompanying tables or text values — these are marked not_reported. The between-group mean difference CIs at baseline for PIRS-20 appear sign-reversed in Table 3 (printed as '−18.3 to 9.6' rather than '−9.6 to 18.3'); extracted as stated in paper. Change scores for the intervention group are stated as mean 6.9, SD 5.7 and control as mean 5.0, SD 4.6 (text says '5 [4.6]'); these are entered as negative values (improvement) in arm_results. The paper does not report weekly intermediate numeric data in tabular form.

summary: This quasi-experimental study tested the effect of daily hot water bag application (40-43°C, 20 minutes/day for 4 weeks) versus routine care on RLS severity and sleep quality in 80 elderly Iranians (aged ≥65 years) recruited from community health centers. RLS severity (IRLS) decreased significantly in the intervention group (from 16.7±0.46 to 10.68±1.52) compared to the control group (from 16.50±1.17 to 15.55±1.79), with a statistically significant between-group difference at post-test (p=0.0001). Sleep quality (PSQI) also improved significantly in the intervention group (from 10.4±1.93 to 8.3±1.5) versus control (10.53±1.95 to 10.42±1.89), with a significant post-intervention difference (p=0.0001), though sleep quality remained in the 'poor' range for both groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The paper is quasi-experimental, not a true RCT, despite using computer-generated randomization for group assignment. The abstract reports sleep quality post-test values with groups appearing reversed (control=8.3±1.5, experimental=10.42±1.89) but Table 3 and the results section text clarify experimental=8.3±1.5 and control=10.42±1.89, confirming that the abstract had the labels transposed. The total analyzed sample is stated as 80 (4 withdrawn from each group), but the exact per-arm n at analysis is inferred as 40 each. No CIs or exact mean differences were reported; between-group mean differences were calculated from reported arm means. Adverse events were mentioned only as an exclusion criterion (skin reactions) but not systematically reported as outcomes. The paper lacks polysomnography data and iron status assessment, noted as limitations by authors. No subgroup analyses were conducted.

summary: This open-label pilot study assessed the efficacy of ropinirole 0.25 mg in 5 patients with chronic insomnia secondary to restless legs syndrome, using polysomnography on four nights (night 1 baseline, night 2 with ropinirole, night 30 after 30-day treatment washout, night 31 with ropinirole). Ropinirole produced statistically significant improvements in sleep efficiency (62.6% vs 82.8% on night 1/2, p=0.010; 64.9% vs 88.8% on night 30/31, p=0.014), total sleep time (295 vs 398 min, p=0.006; 295 vs 391 min, p=0.025), and number of periodic limb movements (91 vs 31, p=0.011; 190 vs 36, p=0.013). Subjective sleep quality by Spiegel questionnaire also improved significantly (p=0.0005), and no adverse events were reported at this low dose.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a within-subject crossover design (not a parallel-arm RCT): each of 5 patients underwent 4 polysomnographic nights. Arm 1 (ropinirole) and Arm 2 (no treatment) represent conditions within the same patients, not separate randomized groups. Statistical analysis was paired t-test. The between_group_effects p-values are from within-subject paired comparisons. The no-treatment mean for PLM at night 30 (189.8) is much higher than night 1 (91.0) — authors note a rebound increase in PLM after 30-day treatment withdrawal. The Spiegel questionnaire results are reported only as significant (p=0.0005) with no per-patient numeric scores provided. Individual patient data for all three polysomnographic outcomes are fully extractable from tables and were verified against reported means and SDs. The text states 'primera noche de polisomnografía sin tratamiento y la segunda noche con 0,25 mg de ropinirol' confirming the acute dose design. One patient later required dose increase to 0.75 mg after 6 months but this was outside the study period.

summary: This 8-week pilot RCT tested intradialytic resistance exercise (elastic bands, 3x/week during HD) versus standard care in 42 Indonesian hemodialysis patients with moderate-to-severe RLS (IRLS >= 11). The IRE group showed significantly greater reductions in IRLS scores at week 4 (mean difference -5.6, 95% CI -8.5 to -2.7, p=0.001, Cohen's d=0.83) and week 8 (mean difference -8.4, 95% CI -11.7 to -5.0, p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.11) compared to controls, representing a large and clinically meaningful effect. Adherence was high (median 93% of sessions) and no serious adverse events occurred.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: PSQI was collected at baseline and described as an outcome instrument but no post-intervention PSQI data (week 4 or week 8) are reported in tables or text — only baseline PSQI values are extractable. The paper reports means ± SE (not SD) in Table 2 for weeks 4 and 8; SD values are only available at baseline (from Table 1 and narrative). The between-group p-value for week 8 is reported as '<0.001' (threshold, not exact). Cohen's d values are reported in Table 2: baseline 0.07, week 4 0.83, week 8 1.11. The MMRM group×time interaction F-statistic is F=9.34, p<0.001. Withdrawal reasons are described as 'relocation or hospitalization' combined for both arms (2 per group = 4 total); individual reasons per person not specified. The paper does not report a CONSORT flow diagram with screening/eligibility counts. Table 2 reports 'Between-group Δ' — these are labeled as MMRM-adjusted estimates for weeks 4 and 8 but the baseline comparison (Δ=-0.6) appears unadjusted; adjusted status set to false for baseline and true for weeks 4 and 8 accordingly.

summary: This prospective, open-label, single-arm study evaluated pregabalin (75–300 mg/day, mostly 75 mg) as add-on therapy to dopamine agonists in 32 RLS patients in South Korea who had persistent symptoms, intolerable side effects, or comorbid insomnia despite stable DA use. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm before-after study, NOT an RCT; RoB2 is not strictly applicable as there is no comparator arm — the 'between_group_effects' fields represent within-arm pre-post comparisons, not between-group contrasts, and effect_source is set to 'calculated' (post minus pre). summary: This single-center RCT (n=30 idiopathic RLS patients; n=20 healthy controls) compared 14 days of daily active transcutaneous spinal cord direct-current stimulation (tsDCS; 2 mA, 20 min) versus sham stimulation on RLS symptom severity (IRLS-RS) and sleep quality (PSQI), alongside resting-state fMRI neuroimaging measures. Active tsDCS produced statistically significant within-arm reductions in both IRLS-RS (27.2 to 15.0; p=5.09×10⁻⁶) and PSQI (14.9 to 10.3; p=1.09×10⁻⁵), whereas the sham group showed no significant change; however, between-arm comparisons on clinical outcomes were not formally reported. Neuroimaging analyses revealed tsDCS normalized fALFF in the right anterior insula/temporal pole, ReHo in the supplementary motor area, and weighted degree centrality in visual cortex and posterior cerebellum, providing neurophysiological evidence for tsDCS efficacy in RLS.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) Per-arm means and SDs for fMRI measures (fALFF, ReHo, weighted DC) are not reported numerically — only t-statistics for paired comparisons and figure bar graphs are provided (data only in figures for regional mean values). 2) The paper presents within-group pre-post comparisons as the primary clinical analysis; formal between-arm (tsDCS vs sham) statistical comparisons for IRLS-RS and PSQI are not reported in the text or tables — only within-arm paired t-test p-values are given. Between-group mean differences at endpoint were calculated from reported arm means. 3) The p-values reported as scientific notation (5.09×10⁻⁶, 1.09×10⁻⁵) were inferred from the table notation '5.09 10^-6' and '1.09 10^-5'. 4) Healthy control fMRI data were also collected (n=20, scanned once) and compared to RLS patients but controls are not a randomized arm — they are an observational comparator group. 5) The paper does not report blinding of outcome assessors or details of allocation concealment. 6) Correlation analyses: weighted DC in left V1 after tsDCS correlated with PSQI (r=0.58, p=0.025); fALFF in right anterior INS/TP before tsDCS marginally correlated with IRLS-RS (r=0.49, p=0.064). These were not extracted as separate outcome objects but are noted here.

The paper reports mixed-model fixed-effects SE and t-values rather than CIs; no CIs are available for between-group comparisons. summary: This pre-planned secondary analysis of the IronWoMan RCT randomized 176 iron-deficient blood donors to intravenous ferric carboxymaltose (1 g, single dose) or oral ferrous fumarate (10 g over 8-12 weeks) and evaluated self-reported RLS symptoms, fatigue, sleep quality, and other iron-deficiency-related symptoms before and after treatment. Across all five fatigue subscales, all four sleep quality items, and RLS symptom severity, statistically significant improvements were observed after iron supplementation (p<0.001 for most outcomes), as were significant reductions in headache, dyspnea, and dizziness prevalence. No significant differences were found between IV and oral iron for any clinical endpoint, though this trial lacked a placebo control arm, limiting causal interpretation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This paper is a secondary analysis of the IronWoMan RCT (primary endpoint: transferrin saturation); it has no placebo/control arm — all between_group_effects represent within-person pre-post comparisons (V0 vs V1), NOT between-arm comparisons. The RCT compared IV vs oral iron; arm-level data are NOT reported separately in the symptom tables — all medians/IQRs in Table 2 represent the entire study population combined. 2. The RLS severity analysis (outcome_id 2) was performed only in participants with RLS at baseline (n=31 for V0; n presented in 31 participants who had RLS at V0), not the full population. 3. RLS diagnosis prevalence denominators differ between Table 2 (N=134) and body text (156 at V0, 152 at V1); the text values are used as more precise. 4. Table 2 is garbled due to PDF conversion with interleaved row labels; values were reconstructed from text descriptions and table data. 5. The overall RLS symptom score change is also described in text as p=0.001 (exact) in the RLS section but p<0.001 in the abstract; both are noted. 6. Arm_id 1 is used to hold combined study population data since no per-arm symptom data are available. 7. Fatigue n=169 and sleep n=160 and different symptoms n=161-165 represent combined populations. 8. Quality of life: no statistically significant change reported; p-value not given. 9. The IQR values in Table 2 for the RLS overall severity row (0 to -10 to 13 / -7 to -14 to 3) appear to be the change score distribution (median change -7, IQR -14 to 3), not endpoint values; these are noted in the RLS severity outcome but median endpoint values from the body text (V0 median 4, V1 median 2) are used instead. 10. The percent female per arm is calculated: arm 1 (IV): 69/86=80.2%; arm 2 (oral): 69/90=76.7%. 11. Adverse events reported as 38% in both groups with no specific numbers disclosed.

summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial (n=24 enrolled, 21 completers) tested a single bilateral intramuscular injection of incobotulinumtoxinA (200 units total) versus normal saline into tibialis anterior, gastrocnemius, and biceps femoris in patients with refractory moderate-to-severe RLS. IncoA produced a statistically significant improvement in IRLS categorical severity (severe to mild/moderate) at 4 weeks (p=0.0036) and 6 weeks (p=0.0325), significant improvement in pain (VAS) at 4 weeks (p=0.01), quality of life (Johns Hopkins QoL) at 6 weeks (p=0.04), and patient global impression of change at 4 weeks (p=0.012; 7/21 vs. 1/21 with definite or marked improvement), with no adverse effects observed.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 appears to have garbled columns: the values listed under 'Standard Deviation' for the Botulinum Toxin arm (0.06, 0.04, 0.08, 0.01, 0.09, 0.09, 0.73, 0.46, 0.22) are clearly p-values (confirmed by text), while the values listed under 'p Value' (9.52, 9.55, 9.88, 2.74, 2.82, 2.73, 6.36, 6.29, 6.48) are clearly standard deviations. Extraction reflects the corrected interpretation: SD column values used as p-values, p Value column values used as SDs for the IncoA arm. Baseline n per sequence group (placebo-first n=10, IncoA-first n=14) differ from the analysis n=24 per arm due to crossover design — all 24 completed at least one period. MOS sleep scale data were reported at baseline only (Table 1); no post-treatment MOS values were extractable from tables or text. The IRLS primary outcome was analyzed as a binary proportion (severe vs. mild/moderate, Fisher's exact test) — no continuous IRLS means or SDs at post-treatment timepoints were reported in Table 2 or text. The abstract states VAS p=0.04 at 6 weeks and QoL p=0.01 at 6 weeks; the Results section states VAS p=0.01 at 4 weeks and QoL p=0.04 at 6 weeks — the Results section values were used as they are more specific. Note: 'higher_is_better' for QoL questionnaire set to false as higher score likely indicates worse quality of life (consistent with direction of results showing IncoA group has higher scores post-injection), though this is not explicitly confirmed in the paper.

summary: This open-label RCT compared pramipexole 0.18 mg/day versus gabapentin 100 mg/day over 4 weeks in 60 hemodialysis patients with moderate-to-severe RLS (30 per arm). Both treatments significantly reduced IRLSSG severity scores from baseline (pramipexole: 24.2±6.6 to 7.4±5.4; gabapentin: 20.3±7.9 to 7.3±7.3, both p<0.001), but the mean improvement was significantly greater with pramipexole (16.8±6.5 vs 13.0±7.3 points; p=0.036), suggesting pramipexole may be superior to gabapentin for RLS in dialysis patients.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a study of RLS in hemodialysis/CKD patients, not Long COVID; long-COVID-specific fields (infection timing, vaccination status, hospitalization) are all not applicable. The between-group comparison at endpoint (outcome_id 1, timepoint 2) shows virtually identical post-treatment means (7.4 vs 7.3), so the primary between-group difference is best represented by the change-from-baseline comparison (outcome_id 2), which is the comparison the authors report with p=0.036. Note that baseline IRLSSG scores differed significantly between arms (pramipexole 24.2 vs gabapentin 20.3), raising concerns about adequate randomization or chance imbalance. Table 3 (categorical severity distribution) contains counts and percentages per category per arm at baseline and follow-up but these are ordinal categorical data without summary statistics suitable for a continuous arm_results entry; the data are: Pramipexole baseline — mild 0%, moderate 33%, severe 54%, very severe 13%; Pramipexole follow-up — mild 77%, moderate 17%, severe 6%, very severe 0%; Gabapentin baseline — mild 0%, moderate 80%, severe 10%, very severe 10%; Gabapentin follow-up — mild 74%, moderate 23%, severe 0%, very severe 3%. No adverse event data were systematically reported. Attrition not explicitly described but implied to be zero. Randomization method beyond 'random allocation' not described.

summary: This quasi-experimental study tested 8 weeks of intradialytic stretching exercise (20 minutes per dialysis session, 3x/week) versus usual care in 40 hemodialysis patients with RLS (n=20 per arm) in Indonesia. The intervention group showed a mean reduction of 8.3 points on the IRLSSG scale (from 24.5 to 16.2), compared to 1.2 points in the control group (from 23.7 to 22.5), yielding a calculated between-group difference of 6.3 points. No formal between-group statistical test or p-value was reported, and the study had high risk of bias due to unclear randomization, no allocation concealment, and no blinding.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) No formal between-group statistical test (t-test or ANOVA comparing groups) was reported; only within-group paired t-tests are mentioned analytically, and no p-value or CI for the between-group comparison was provided. The between-group mean difference of -6.3 at endpoint was calculated from reported arm means. 2) The paper mentions 'paired t-test' as the analytic method but reports no actual test statistics or p-values in the results section. 3) The text below Table 2 contains a copy-paste error referencing 'bekam' (cupping therapy) and pain scores — this appears to be erroneous boilerplate from a different paper and was ignored. 4) Age distributions are reported in categorical bands (50-59, 60-69, ≥70 years) only; no mean or SD for age is provided per arm. 5) Change-from-baseline SD is not reported for either arm, only the mean change. 6) The paper is in Indonesian with an English abstract; the primary results table (Table 2) is in Indonesian but values are clear.

summary: This quasi-experimental study tested progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) therapy performed twice weekly for 4 weeks versus health education (control) in 24 hemodialysis patients with restless legs syndrome (RLS) in Indonesia. Mean IRLSSG scores decreased significantly in the PMR group (22.92 to 17.42, p=0.001) and showed minimal change in the control group (24.33 to 23.50, p=0.001 within-group), with a calculated between-group difference of approximately 6.1 points favoring PMR at end of treatment. However, no between-group inferential test result was explicitly reported, and the lack of randomization and blinding limits the strength of these conclusions.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) The study is quasi-experimental with convenience sampling, not a true RCT — allocation method not described. 2) Table 5 reports within-group paired t-test p-values (both p=0.001) but does NOT report a between-group independent t-test statistic or p-value despite the Methods section stating one was planned; the between-group mean difference at post-treatment (-6.08) was therefore calculated. 3) The abstract states p<0.005 for PMR efficacy which may be a typographical error for p<0.05 or p=0.001. 4) The paper title mentions 'RPM' (Spanish acronym) while English text uses 'PMR'; these refer to the same intervention. 5) Minimum and maximum RLS scores per arm at each timepoint are reported in text (baseline PMR: min=21, max=27; post PMR: min=13, max=22; baseline control: min=22, max=28; post control: min=22, max=27) but not extracted as separate fields since the schema does not include min/max fields. 6) No adverse events were reported anywhere in the paper.

summary: This 3-arm parallel-group RCT compared foot reflexology massage, Swedish foot massage, and sham touch (control) in 90 hemodialysis patients with RLS in Iran, delivered 3x/week for 4 weeks. Immediately post-intervention, reflexology produced the greatest reduction in RLS severity (mean 6.80 vs. 14.60 vs. 19.46) and PSQI score (mean 9.97 vs. 12.57 vs. 14.57), with all pairwise comparisons statistically significant (all p<0.003). However, at the 1-month follow-up these benefits had fully regressed to near-baseline in all three groups, with no significant between-group differences remaining.

Mann-Whitney test statistics (U values) are reported in Table 4 and Table 6; p-values extracted as stated. 4. The sham group PSQI SD at immediately-post-intervention is listed as 1.14 in Table 5 (same as baseline), which appears to reflect no change — extracted verbatim. 5. The Friedman test statistic for the sham PSQI row appears incomplete in the original table (shows '44' without a full value); extracted what was available. 6. The p_value for arm1_vs_arm3 RLS immediately-post (p<0.001 stated as Mann-Whitney statistic=0.001 in Table 4) is recorded as p<0.001 (p_value_exact: false). 7. No adverse events were reported. 8. summary: This quasi-experimental pre-post study in 34 insomniac adults (aged 21–45) in India compared three nutritional interventions — intramuscular vitamin B12 (n=12), beetroot powder drink (n=12), and poppy seed powder drink (n=10) — over 15 days, with arm assignment based on individual biomarker deficiencies rather than randomization. All three interventions yielded improvements in insomnia (B12: 33.4%, beetroot: 54.6%, poppy seeds: 63.6%) and restless leg syndrome (B12: 66.8%, beetroot/poppy seeds: 50%), with B12 producing a statistically significant increase in serum B12 (p<0.01) and cortisol reduction (p<0.01). Quality of life (SF-36) improved across all groups, though the lack of randomization, no control arm, small sample sizes, and non-blinded design preclude causal conclusions.

summary: This open-label RCT (n=42) compared 8 weeks of acupoint catgut embedding targeting heel vessel acupoints (Shenmai, Zhaohai, and adjunct points) versus oral Madopar 125 mg nightly in Chinese outpatients with primary RLS. Both treatments significantly reduced IRLS, PSQI, and SAS scores from baseline; the catgut embedding group showed statistically significantly greater reductions in all three scores compared to Madopar (p<0.05), and a higher overall response rate (95.2% vs 90.5%, p<0.05). However, the absolute between-group differences were small, the design was open-label with subjective outcomes, and randomization details were not reported, raising substantial risk of bias concerns.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. Age was reported only as ranges (observation: 45-72 years; control: 43-74 years), not as means/SDs — age_mean fields left null. 2. Disease duration was reported only as ranges, not means/SDs. 3. Between-group p-values are reported only as thresholds (p<0.05), not exact values. 4. No CIs were reported for any between-group comparisons. 5. The between-group mean differences for IRLS, PSQI, and SAS were calculated from the post-treatment endpoint means (arm1 minus arm2): IRLS = 24.67 - 25.00 = -0.33; PSQI = 11.48 - 12.05 = -0.57; SAS = 58.67 - 59.25 = -0.58. Note: the paper claims observation group had greater decreases than control (p<0.05), but the endpoint means are nearly identical — this likely reflects differences in baseline-adjusted change scores or within-group analyses rather than a large absolute post-treatment difference. 6. No adverse events were reported. 7. No flow diagram or CONSORT reporting; dropout/completion data not reported. 8. Randomization method and allocation concealment not described. 9. This is an RLS trial, not a Long COVID trial — all Long COVID-specific fields (long_covid_definition, time_since_infection, percent_vaccinated, percent_previously_hospitalized) are not applicable and set to null.

summary: This quasi-experimental pre-post study examined 12 drug-naive RLS patients (IRLS >19) before and after 12 weeks of open-label pramipexole treatment, compared to 16 age-matched healthy controls using overnight polysomnography with 19-channel EEG. At baseline, RLS patients showed significantly elevated delta-band EEG power (44.28 vs 41.36 dB, p=0.017) and disrupted small-world network properties during N3 sleep compared to controls, and the delta power correlated with IRLS severity (r=0.606, p=0.037). Pramipexole treatment significantly reduced IRLS scores (29.92 to 13.50, p=0.028), PLMS index (23.80 to 5.29, p=0.006), improved sleep efficiency (77.78% to 87.76%, p=0.019), and normalized EEG spectral power across all frequency bands and small-world network characteristics, with post-treatment values no longer differing from healthy controls.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is NOT an RCT — it is an open-label, uncontrolled, single-arm pre-post study with a separate matched healthy control group. There was no randomization and no placebo arm, making this quasi-experimental. The 'RLS follow-up' arm in the design is the same patients post-treatment, not a separate arm. For between_group_effects, comparisons labeled 'arm1_baseline_vs_arm2_control' compare RLS patients at baseline to healthy controls; 'arm1_baseline_vs_arm1_followup' are within-patient pre-post comparisons (Wilcoxon signed-rank); 'arm1_followup_vs_arm2_control' compare post-treatment RLS to controls. Table 1 shows follow-up SD values missing for several outcomes (IRLS, BDI-II, ISI, PSQI) — only means reported for post-treatment column. Table 4 graph-theory data includes SWI and Cnorm values across all sleep stages (Awake, N1, N2, N3, REM) for all three groups — only the N3 values are extracted here as primary comparisons; full stage-by-stage data also available in Table 4. PLMS arousal index (control 1.77±2.37, RLS baseline 6.53±9.24, RLS follow-up 2.34±2.50, p=0.133/0.169/0.478), sleep latency, WASO, stage percentages (N1, N2, N3, REM), apnea-hypopnea index, and arousal index all reported in Table 2 but omitted from outcomes for brevity as all p-values non-significant. SWI during stages Awake, N1, N2, REM also available in Table 4 but omitted. Epworth Sleepiness Scale data collected but values not reported in tables. Dosage SD for pramipexole is unusually large (0.28±0.32 mg/day) suggesting wide dose variation.

summary: This 12-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 78 Korean adults with moderate-to-severe RLS (IRLS ≥15) to evaluate flexible-dose pregabalin (75-300 mg/day; mean final dose 107.8 mg) versus placebo across four tertiary centers. The primary outcome — baseline-adjusted change in IRLS score at week 12 — was -6.8 in the pregabalin group and -5.4 in the placebo group, a between-group difference of 1.5 points that was not statistically significant (p=0.420); no secondary outcomes differed significantly between groups. The study was negative, with the authors attributing this to a low achieved pregabalin dose, modest sample size, and a substantial placebo response (mean IRLS reduction of 8.0 points in the placebo arm).

summary: This Japanese open-label, non-randomized study investigated Holter ECG recording of periodic limb movements (PLM) during hemodialysis sessions for diagnosing RLS and evaluating the efficacy of pergolide mesylate (50–100 µg/day for 2 weeks) in 19 hemodialysis patients with neurologist-confirmed RLS. Among the 12 patients who completed treatment, subjective RLS symptoms improved by approximately 70% on VAS across all four symptom domains, and mean PLM frequency significantly decreased from 31.0±23.8 to 5.6±9.4 per 30 minutes (p<0.05), with a significant positive correlation between PLM reduction and symptom improvement (r=0.67, p<0.05). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This is NOT a randomized controlled trial; groups were formed by patient preference and adverse event occurrence, so the study_design quasi-experimental classification is most accurate and all RoB2 domains are high/some_concerns. 2. The VAS improvement rates for individual symptom domains (~70% for all four) are presented in Figure 10 (bar graph) without precise per-domain mean±SD values in text; the ~70% approximation is the only quantitative value given in the text. 3. The abstract reports 'mean PLM frequency significantly decreased from 31.0±7.5 to 5.6±3.0/30min' — but these appear to be SE values (not SD), while the main text and summary report SD values of 31.0±23.8 and 5.6±9.4 for n=10. Both sets of values are extracted; the abstract values may represent SE. 4. The abstract also notes 'n_any_ae nausea and gastric discomfort in 10 of 19 patients and somnolence in 1 of 19', which differs slightly from the main text; the abstract values are used for the overall AE count (11/19 with AEs per main text). 5. Multiple outcome data points (PLM counts by group) are presented only in Figure 7 (bar graph) without full SD values in text for arm 4 (excluded) and arm 5 (control) — mean of 0 for both confirmed verbatim in text. 6. The paper is in Japanese with an English abstract; some nuance may be lost in translation. The SD values in the summary section (25.8±24.7, 2.4±3.7, 3.0±3.5) differ from those in the results section (31.0±23.8 for n=10 PLM-positive continuers); both sets are extracted as they refer to different subgroups (n=12 all continuers vs n=10 PLM-positive continuers). 7. Correlation coefficient (r=0.67) between PLM reduction and symptom improvement is reported across all 4 VAS symptom domains but no domain-level r-values provided.

summary: This 12-week multicenter US RCT (n=380 ITT) compared flexible-dose ropinirole (0.25-4.0 mg/day) to placebo in patients with moderate-to-severe primary RLS. Ropinirole produced a significantly greater reduction in IRLS total score at week 12 (adjusted mean difference -3.7 points, 95% CI -5.4 to -2.0, P<0.001) with improvements detectable as early as day 3. Ropinirole also significantly improved CGI-I responder rates, PLM index, sleep disturbance, sleep adequacy, sleep quantity, quality of life, and anxiety scores compared with placebo, and was generally well tolerated with nausea (42.8% vs 7.8%) as the most common adverse event.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: The adjusted mean (2 SE) values in the paper refer to ±2 SE (half-width = 1 SE), so per-arm SE values were computed as half the reported 2SE value. The IRLS change at day 3 and POMS analyses were post hoc (explicitly stated in paper). The HADS analysis used restricted subpopulations (anxiety n=68/68, depression n=24/27) rather than the full ITT population. Baseline and endpoint data for Johns Hopkins RLS QoL questionnaire were not reported in tables (only change-from-baseline values). POMS subscale data for Confusion-bewilderment, Fatigue-inertia, Anger-hostility, Depression-dejection, and Tension-anxiety were captured in Table 3 but only Total mood disturbance and Vigor-activity reached statistical significance; remaining POMS subscales omitted from outcome objects to manage length but fully reported in Table 3 of paper with non-significant p-values (0.05-0.25). Median time-to-response values are in days (7 days and 21 days). Death for ropinirole arm occurred during follow-up phase (ill-defined disorder), not treatment phase; death in placebo arm occurred in follow-up phase (traffic crash). Neither was considered related to study medication.

summary: This randomized triple-blind controlled trial tested cool dialysate (35.5°C) versus standard dialysate (37°C) during hemodialysis in 63 patients with restless legs syndrome (RLS) over one month. The primary outcome was RLS severity measured by the IRLS questionnaire (0–40). After one month, the cool dialysate group showed a significant reduction in RLS severity from 31.51 to 11.66, while the control group remained stable (28.45 to 28.77); the between-group difference was highly significant (t=14.03, p=0.001), demonstrating that cool dialysate is an effective non-pharmacological approach for reducing RLS severity in hemodialysis patients.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Table 2 reports the baseline mean for the control group as both 28.48 (in the text) and 28.45 (in Table 2); the Table 2 value (28.45) was used as it is the primary data source. The between-group mean difference at baseline was calculated as 31.51 - 28.45 = 3.06 (intervention minus control); the text reports t=-2.11 and p>0.05 (not significant), consistent with this direction. The between-group mean difference at post-treatment was calculated as 11.66 - 28.77 = -17.11 (intervention minus control). The paper states the triple-blind design included blinding of patients, research assistant, and statistician; however, the specific allocation concealment mechanism (beyond permuted block randomization) is not described. No formal adverse event table is provided; the paper only states cool dialysate was 'well tolerated.' Attrition per arm is not explicitly reported in a CONSORT flow table. Duration of hemodialysis treatment means were 36.72 months (intervention) and 35.10 months (control).

summary: This open-label RCT conducted at a single tertiary care hospital in India compared clonazepam 0.5 mg/night versus nortriptyline 25 mg/night over 8 weeks in 120 women aged 40-65 years with RLS. Both drugs produced statistically significant within-group reductions in IRLSS total score from baseline at 4 and 8 weeks (p<0.001), but intergroup differences in IRLSS score were not statistically significant at any timepoint. summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT tested 10,000 µg/day oral biotin supplementation for 8 weeks versus placebo in 37 ESRD dialysis patients with restless legs syndrome (Study 2), preceded by an observational cross-sectional study (Study 1) showing that RLS patients had higher biotin deficiency markers than non-RLS patients (AC of PCC 1.17 vs 0.87, p=0.007). In Study 2, IRLS scores decreased significantly in both the biotin group (p=0.001, n=16) and the placebo group (p=0.01, n=15), but the between-group difference was not statistically significant, indicating a prominent placebo effect. Biotin supplementation did significantly improve the biotin status biomarker (AC of PCC decreased, p=0.01, n=8) versus no change in the placebo group, suggesting biological activity, but clinical benefit for RLS could not be established.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: CRITICAL DATA LIMITATION: All quantitative outcome data for Study 2 (IRLS scores at baseline and follow-up per arm, AC of PCC values at baseline and follow-up per arm) are reported ONLY in box-whisker plots (Figure 2A and 2B) with no numerical means, SDs, or medians provided in the text or tables. Only within-arm p-values and sample sizes are stated in text (biotin IRLS: p=0.001, n=16; placebo IRLS: p=0.01, n=15; biotin AC of PCC: p=0.01, n=8; placebo AC of PCC: n=7, not significant). No between-group effect size or p-value for IRLS is reported. The paper describes the arms as having 16 (biotin) and 15 (placebo) completing IRLS assessment, but the initial randomization numbers are not directly stated — only that 21 total were enrolled in biotin arm (Table 2 shows 2/21 died in biotin group) and 16 in placebo (1/16 died). One participant was excluded for noncompliance. Study 1 cross-sectional data (AC of PCC: RLS 1.17±0.65, n=30; No RLS 0.87±0.39, n=19, p=0.007) is verbatim and complete. The paper conflates Study 1 (observational) and Study 2 (RCT) — this extraction focuses on Study 2 for the RCT schema but notes Study 1 cross-sectional findings in outcome_id referenced biomarker results for context.

summary: This double-blind, double-dummy crossover RCT (n=39 per-protocol) conducted in six Swiss sleep centres compared pramipexole (0.25–0.75 mg/day) versus dual-release levodopa/benserazide (125–375 mg/day) over 4 weeks each in de novo RLS patients. Both treatments significantly reduced the primary endpoint (PLM index: mean reduction -11.5 for PPX vs -7.7 for L/B), with PPX meeting non-inferiority (p=0.00015). On the secondary IRLS score, PPX showed a numerically greater reduction (-7.2 vs -4.0) that trended toward significance (p=0.054), and in the subgroup with severe-to-very-severe baseline IRLS (>20), PPX was statistically superior (p=0.047); the overall conclusion was comparable efficacy for short-term treatment of mild-to-moderate RLS.

HADS scores appear unusually high (anxiety ~8, depression ~11) suggesting possible scoring variant. Between-group effect for PLMI is noted as non-inferiority test with p=0.00015 (ANCOVA/Wilcoxon), direction favours PPX; the calculated mean difference (-3.8) is derived from change-from-baseline means. The per-arm n_randomized breakdown is not stated — only total ITT (67) and total per-protocol (39) are given; these 39 per-protocol patients contributed data to both arms in the crossover. summary: This single-blind parallel-group RCT (n=30 completers) compared 6 weeks of aerobic training versus resistance training (3 sessions/week) in adults aged 40-60 with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and comorbid RLS. Both interventions produced statistically significant within-group improvements in IRLS total score, PSQI global score, and ESS total score (all p<0.001), but no statistically significant between-group differences were found on any primary outcome. The paper is an active-comparator trial (aerobic vs resistance training) with no passive control/placebo arm; arm_id=1 assigned to aerobic (primary intervention) and arm_id=2 to resistance training per convention. 2. PSQI subscale table (Table 5) has unclear row labels due to repeated 'Sleep' headers — rows matched to subscales by order and context (sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, habitual sleep efficiency, sleep disturbance, sleep medication, daytime dysfunction). The IQR values in Table 4 and 5 are reported as single numbers (e.g., '2(2)') likely representing median(IQR) but exact IQR bounds not provided. 3. Dropout allocation per arm (6 each) is inferred from total dropout of 12 and equal group sizes at completion (15 each); the text does not specify exact arm-level dropout counts. 6. IRLS subscale 'Need' refers to 'Need to move legs'; 'RLS' row appears duplicated with identical pre-values to 'RLS severity as a whole' — likely a data table parsing artifact. 7. Habitual sleep efficiency row in Table 5 has apparent transposition of U-value and p-value fields. 8. The between-group mean differences in Table 2 represent arm1 minus arm2 (aerobic minus resistance) based on the group ordering and reported values.

summary: This 3-arm open-label RCT (n=36) evaluated 6 weeks of physiotherapy (Relax Revive Technique) with self-affirmation (Group A), yoga (Utkatasana) with self-affirmation (Group B), or their combination on alternate days (Group C) in adults aged 20-45 with mild-to-moderate idiopathic RLS. summary: This quasi-experimental parallel-group study (n=60 pregnant women with moderate-to-severe RLS in the third trimester) compared daily leg stretching exercises (30 min/day for 7 days) versus nightly warm water leg immersion (43-47°C, 20 min/night for 7 days). Both interventions significantly reduced RLS symptom severity and pain and improved sleep quality, but stretching exercise was superior: 93.3% of the stretching group achieved mild RLS symptoms at one week vs. 63.3% in the thermotherapy group (p=0.020), and 93.3% vs. 73.3% had good sleep quality (p=0.038). The mean IRLS score fell from 24.13 to 6.80 with stretching exercise versus 23.27 to 10.43 with thermotherapy, with all between-group differences at one week reaching statistical significance.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. RLS mean scores with SDs are reported only in figure captions in the text (Figure 2 for RLS, Figure 3 for pain) — not in formal tables — but values are stated explicitly in the text narrative accompanying those figures and are therefore treated as verbatim. The sleep quality outcome does not report continuous mean scores, only categorical distributions. The pain level categorical data in Table 3 contains a likely transcription error: baseline moderate pain for stretching group is listed as '12 (20.0)' but should be '12 (40.0)' given n=30 (60% severe + 40% moderate = 100%); extracted as stated. The study self-identifies as quasi-experimental but is registered as an RCT (NCT05261035); allocation is by alternating assignment using a random number generator, not true random allocation concealment. No continuous sleep quality scores (GSQS totals as means/SDs) are reported. The paper notes 'good' sleep as 0-4 in Table 4 but the Methods describe 'normal refreshing sleep' as score 0-2 and 'slightly disturbed' as 3-9 — these categories differ between Methods and Table 4; Table 4 values extracted as reported. No adverse events section present.

summary: This single-arm pre-post study evaluated a 4-week home-based lower-limb self-stretching program in 200 adults aged 40-59 with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus at two Pakistani hospitals. The RLS-DI Sum Score decreased significantly from 7.39 to -0.79 (mean difference 8.17, 95% CI 7.06-9.28, p<0.001) and the Grand Total Score fell from 3.31 to -2.27 (mean difference 5.57, 95% CI 4.38-6.76, p<0.001). Item-level chi-square analyses showed significant reductions in urge to move, unpleasant sensations, worsening at rest, and sleep disturbance, though the study lacks a control group and cannot establish causation.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm pre-post study, not an RCT; there is no control/comparator arm and no randomization. The 'between_group_effects' arrays for continuous outcomes are empty because all analyses are within-subject (paired t-tests), not between-group comparisons. For categorical item-level outcomes, chi-square statistics (χ²) are reported as the test statistic for pre-vs-post distribution shifts; these are not true between-group effects but within-subject distributional comparisons coded as such for consistency. The RLS-DI sum score and grand total score had negative post-intervention means (-0.79 and -2.27 respectively), suggesting the scoring instrument allows negative values. The t-test statistics reported are t=14.556 for Sum Score and t=9.201 for Grand Total. The 95% CI values reported in the abstract/results for mean paired differences are extracted as change_from_baseline CI (negated to reflect decrease: -9.28 to -7.06 for Sum Score, -6.76 to -4.38 for Grand Total). Table 3 reports post-RLS n as '1 (1.5%)' for Grand Total which appears to be a typo (should be 3/200=1.5%); extracted as n=3 per the text description. No adherence monitoring data, no adverse events reported, no long-term follow-up.

summary: This non-randomized controlled study examined the effect of wet cupping therapy (hijama) at acupuncture points BL-40, BL-57, and GB-30 in 16 patients with RLS in Turkey; one arm (n=8) received pramipexole 0.5 mg/day plus two sessions of wet cupping, and the other arm (n=8) received wet cupping alone. Within-arm analyses showed significant improvements in IRLS total score in both groups (arm 1: z=-2.10, p=0.025; arm 2 showed improvement in 6 IRLS subscales), and the cupping-only arm additionally showed significant improvements in PSQI sleep latency, daytime dysfunction, and total PSQI score. Between-group comparisons showed no statistically significant differences in IRLS, PSQI, or NRS pain scores after treatment, though the cupping-only arm tended to show numerically greater improvements.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Paper is written in Turkish; values extracted from tables and results text. Table 1 reports arm 1 pre/post IRLS, PSQI, and NRS with means, SDs, medians, and within-arm Wilcoxon z and p values. Table 2 reports the between-group comparison of score reductions (change scores) for both arms with Mann-Whitney U p values. Per-arm baseline and endpoint values for arm 2 (cupping only) are NOT provided in tables — only change scores for arm 2 appear in Table 2. Individual PSQI subscale scores are not tabulated numerically; only within-arm Wilcoxon z and p statistics are reported in text. IRLS subscale item-level statistics are reported only as z and p in text (no means/SDs per item). Outcome 4 (PSQI change score) mean for arm 1 = 14.88 appears unusually large relative to arm 1 baseline PSQI of 11.50; this likely represents cumulative/different scoring — reported verbatim from Table 2 as stated. Note: the study is non-randomized (quasi-experimental); RoB2 applied but this design inherently has high risk. Figures 2 and 3 contain bar graphs of pre/post scores but no additional numeric data beyond what appears in the tables.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Participants with MT < 15 mA had greater IRLS improvement (mean difference -7.7, n=6) than those with MT 15–20 mA (-4.2, n=6) or MT > 20 mA (-2.4, n=8); lower MT predicted greater efficacy.

subgroup_analyses.results_summary: Responders had lower mean MT (15.8 mA vs 20.7 mA, P=0.042) and lower MT:TIL ratio (0.61 vs 0.77, P=0.058) compared with nonresponders; TIL, age, calf circumference, and BMI did not differ significantly between groups.
Participants with 100% tonic score had mean IRLS difference of -7.2 vs -0.3 for those with tonic score <100% (P=0.021).
Participants with 100% sustained score had mean IRLS difference of -6.6 vs -1.3 for those with sustained score <100% (P=0.085, not statistically significant).
No correlation between baseline IRLS and IRLS difference (r=0.02, P=0.910) in the full mITT population (n=37), indicating efficacy was independent of baseline RLS severity.

summary: This randomized, sham-controlled, participant-blinded crossover trial (n=20 from a 43-participant parent study) tested 14 days of bilateral high-frequency noninvasive peroneal nerve stimulation (NPNS) at bedtime versus sham control in adults with moderate-to-severe RLS, with a focus on characterizing the mechanism of action via surface EMG. NPNS produced a mean IRLS improvement of -4.8 (SE 1.1) compared with -0.3 (SE 0.7) for sham (difference approximately -4.5 points), and 75% of participants were PGI-I responders with active NPNS versus 0% with sham. NPNS evoked tonic and sustained tibialis anterior muscle activation at therapeutic intensity levels in 19 of 20 participants, lower motor thresholds predicted greater efficacy (r=0.45, P=0.046), and NPNS significantly improved self-reported sleep onset (52% vs 15% of nights, P=0.002) without interfering with sleep onset (16% vs 11%, P=0.629), supporting an afferent Hoffman-reflex mechanism of action.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1) This paper is a mechanistic sub-study of a parent RCT (NCT04700683, Buchfuhrer et al. 2021, n=43); all efficacy data here are for the 20-participant EMG sub-study subset only. 2) IRLS change-from-baseline SDs are not reported per arm — only SE values are given (-4.8 ± 1.1 for NPNS; -0.3 ± 0.7 for sham); SE placed in 'se' field. 3) Means for sleep onset outcomes (nights helped, interfered, RLS symptoms, usage) are reported without SDs. 4) The PGI-I data were only available for 16 of 20 participants per the text but responder rates are given as percentages of n=20 participants — this inconsistency is noted. 5) Adverse events are not reported in this paper; they reference the parent publication. 6) The 75% PGI-I responder rate for NPNS and 0% for sham is stated in the results but exact n values derived as 15/20 and 0/20 respectively. 7) Baseline IRLS (mean 24.6, SD 3.9) and demographics are for all 20 participants combined, not per treatment arm (crossover design). 8) Subgroup analyses (MT groups, tonic/sustained scores, baseline severity) are exploratory and not pre-specified. 9) The between-group IRLS difference for the full mITT (n=37) efficacy data is in the parent publication; this paper only reports the 20-participant subset values.

summary: This open-label single-arm pilot study tested 200 mg daily magnesium citrate supplementation for 8 weeks in 12 treatment-naive adults with primary RLS. IRLS scores improved significantly (mean difference 6.67 points, 95% CI 2.33-11.00, p=0.006), Kohnen QOL scores improved (mean difference 8.50 points, p=0.014), and objective PLMW indices on the multiple suggested immobilization test showed significant reduction (median 30.40 to 8.63 events/hour, p=0.043). Without a control arm, placebo effects on self-reported measures cannot be excluded, but the authors note that the improvement in objectively measured PLMW is less susceptible to placebo effects.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-arm open-label study with no comparator arm; all 'between_group_effects' entries reflect within-arm pre-post comparisons (not between randomized groups). The study is not an RCT; design_type is quasi-experimental. RoB2 applied with recognition that domain 1 (randomization) is not applicable in the strict sense. Table 4 correlation coefficients use '2' as a minus sign (artifact of PDF encoding); values extracted as negative correlations per NOTE in prompt. The CI lower bound for Mg level and PLMW trial 2 is listed as '0' in the paper (correlation coefficient -0.613, 95% CI -0.891 to 0). One participant withdrew before any active treatment (time constraints); 3 additional participants did not complete the m-SIT follow-up due to time constraints (1) or RLS discomfort during the initial immobilization test (3), leaving n=8 for all m-SIT outcomes.

summary: This within-patient crossover study (n=15 RLS patients, n=14 healthy controls) conducted 96-hour continuous skin temperature monitoring during 4 suggested immobilization tests to investigate whether peripheral hypoxia in RLS results from impaired blood flow. RLS patients off pramipexole showed no difference in foot skin temperature or distal-to-proximal gradient compared to healthy controls (31.1°C vs. 31.1°C, p=0.991), but pramipexole significantly increased foot skin temperature during immobilization (31.1°C vs. 32.9°C off vs. on pramipexole, p<0.05) and substantially reduced subjective discomfort (4.2 vs. 1.6, p<0.001). The authors conclude that pramipexole—not RLS itself—drives the peripheral thermoregulatory changes previously attributed to the disease.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: 1. This study is not a true RCT: treatment order was fixed (off-pramipexole days 1-2, on-pramipexole days 3-4) with no randomization of sequence; it is best classified as a non-randomized within-patient before-after design with a parallel healthy control group. 2. No SDs or CIs are reported for any outcome — only means and p-values are given in Table 1 and text. 3. Exact n analyzed after exclusions is 12 RLS patients (3 excluded for IRLSSG <15 post-discontinuation), inferred from text; this is not stated explicitly. 4. Daytime skin temperature data are presented only in Figure 1 with no numeric values in text or tables; result_source set to 'not_reported' for those arms. 5. The Spearman correlations reported (foot temperature ρ=-0.110; DPG ρ=-0.221) appear to use all 15 enrolled RLS patients. 6. The 4-day study duration equates to approximately 0.57 weeks; follow-up fields set to null as the study does not have a post-treatment follow-up phase. 7. summary: This randomized crossover trial enrolled 13 adults with RLS/WED to receive 2 weeks of whole-body vibration (WBV; 26 Hz, 2 mm, 10×30-second bouts, 3×/week) and 2 weeks of sham in randomized order. WBV significantly reduced IRLS scores by ~5.2 points vs. baseline (p=0.013, 95% CI −9.1 to −1.3) compared to minimal change with sham (−0.6 points, p=0.6), a clinically meaningful improvement exceeding the 3-point MCID. WBV acutely increased skin blood flow per session but did not significantly raise resting blood flow over 2 weeks, so the symptom benefit could not be attributed to sustained improvement in peripheral perfusion.

The 'control group' (n=11 healthy age/sex-matched subjects) is not a randomized arm but a separate matched cohort for skin blood flow comparison only — modeled as arm_id=2 only in outcome_id 3 (baseline SBF comparison). No formal RLS-6 between-group statistical test was performed or reported. Correlation between IRLS change and flux change: r=−0.2, p=0.56 (reported in discussion, not extracted as separate outcome).

summary: This exploratory parallel-group RCT randomized 41 adults with moderate-to-severe RLS to a 12-week gentle Iyengar yoga program (n=19) or an educational film control (n=22). Both groups improved in RLS symptoms (IRLS total), perceived stress, mood, and QOL-mental health, but yoga participants showed significantly greater reductions in IRLS total score (change -9.35 vs -4.11, p=0.015), RLS severity subscale (p=0.01), RLS ordinal severity scale (p=0.003), perceived stress (p=0.0009), and mood (p=0.04), with large within-group effect sizes (Cohen d 1.8-2.3 for primary RLS outcomes). By 12 weeks, 77% of yoga completers scored in the minimal/mild RLS range versus 23% in the educational film group.

summary: This randomized, participant-blinded, 2-period crossover trial (n=37 mITT) tested 14 nights of nightly noninvasive peripheral nerve stimulation (NPNS) of the common peroneal nerve versus sham in adults with moderate-to-severe RLS. summary: This single-blind placebo-controlled RCT enrolled 43 treatment-naive RLS patients who received a single oral dose of pramipexole 0.25 mg (n=25) or placebo (n=18) before a second polysomnographic night. Pramipexole significantly reduced PLMS index (from 61.9 to 11.1 vs 40.1 to 47.9 for placebo, p<0.01) and periodicity index, while improving sleep efficiency and Stage 2 sleep; crucially, isolated (non-periodic) leg movements were unaffected by treatment. The study further characterized that the pramipexole response was restricted to LM with duration 2–4 s and inter-movement intervals 6–46 s, suggesting a pharmacologically distinct subtype within the broader PLMS scoring criteria.

summary: This was a randomized, double-blinded, 3-way crossover trial in 85 adults with moderate to severe idiopathic RLS and associated sleep disturbance, comparing pregabalin 300 mg/day, pramipexole 0.5 mg/day, and placebo over three 4-week periods. Pregabalin significantly reduced WASO by 27.1 minutes versus placebo (p<0.0001) and by 26.9 minutes versus pramipexole, and increased slow wave sleep by 32.1 minutes versus pramipexole (p<0.0001), while also improving subjective TST and RLS-NDI versus placebo (both p<0.0001 and p=0.04 respectively). The effect of pregabalin on PLM arousal index was comparable to pramipexole (-3.7 PLMA/h vs placebo, p<0.0001), but pregabalin reduced total PLMS less than pramipexole, suggesting pregabalin's sleep benefits are partly independent of PLM suppression.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a crossover trial; per-arm LS means and SEMs are provided (not per-arm means and SDs in traditional sense). Baseline demographics are reported by treatment sequence (6 sequences), not by treatment arm, so per-arm baseline demographics are not extractable. The n_analyzed values for SSQ and MOS-SS outcomes are not explicitly stated per arm; 75/76/73 are used for PSG outcomes but exact n per arm for questionnaire outcomes is not reported. CGI-I responder percentages are reported without denominator counts. IRLS and RLS-QoL per-arm LS means not reported, only between-group differences. Total study duration calculated as: 14-day run-in + 3 x (29-day treatment + 13-day taper/washout) = 14 + 126 = 140 days ≈ 20 weeks total; treatment per period is 4 weeks. MOS-SS subscales for sleep disturbance, snoring, awakening short of breath/headache, sleep adequacy, somnolence, sleep quantity, and optimal sleep are all reported in Table 4 and fully extracted in outcomes 21-22; remaining MOS-SS subscales omitted from individual outcome objects but available in Table 4: sleep disturbance (PGB 34.1/PPX 40.2/PBO 48.7, diff vs PBO -14.6 [-20.9,-8.2], diff vs PPX -6.1 [-12.4,0.2]); snoring (PGB 15.3/PPX 16.0/PBO 18.0); awakening short of breath (PGB 11.6/PPX 13.1/PBO 10.9); sleep adequacy (PGB 55.0/PPX 43.9/PBO 40.8, diff vs PBO 14.2 [6.3,22.1], diff vs PPX 11.1 [3.2,18.9]); somnolence (PGB 21.3/PPX 21.3/PBO 23.7); sleep quantity (PGB 6.4/PPX 6.5/PBO 6.0); optimal sleep (PGB 0.4/PPX 0.4/PBO 0.3). summary: This is a single-center observational case series of 151 Japanese patients presenting with RLS symptoms to a neurology clinic; 113 were diagnosed with idiopathic RLS using IRLSSG criteria. The study was not an RCT — there was no randomization or control arm — but documented clinical features and uncontrolled treatment outcomes: 73% of idiopathic RLS patients improved with dopaminergic agents and 33% achieved complete remission. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a randomized controlled trial. It is a descriptive observational case series / clinical audit with no control arm, no randomization, and no blinding. It should not be included in a meta-analysis of RLS clinical trials as an RCT. The paper_id in the prompt was assigned externally and not verified. No per-arm quantitative outcome data with means/SDs exists because there is only one uncontrolled treatment group. All percentage figures were extracted from the abstract as the full text body was not fully provided. The n_randomized fields are null as there was no randomization. Event counts for binary outcomes were calculated from percentages × N=113 and rounded to nearest integer (e.g., 73% of 113 = ~82, 33% of 113 = ~37, 43% of 113 = ~49, 81% of 113 = ~91, 49% of 113 = ~55, 71% of 113 = ~80).
